16.1

INTRODUCTION

This is the most important section in a benami proceeding. The provisions of this section triggers the process of provisional attachment leading to confiscation of the benami property. This section deals with provisional attachment of benami property by the Initiating Officer. The attachment process commences with issue of notice under section 24(1) of the PBPT Act,1988. It is the first step in action to initiate a proceeding for 'Attachment, Adjudication and Confiscation'. Hence, the foundation for initiation of proceeding under section 24(1) should be in conformity with legal parameters as stipulated in this section. If the initiation of proceeding under section 24(1) is bad in law from the beginning and lacks jurisdictional foundation, all other consequential actions which follow the same, would also be bad in law. In this regard, reference may be made to the decisions in the case of CIT v. Kelvinator of India Ltd. [2002] 123 Taxman 433 (Delhi) affirmed by Supreme Court in [2010] 87 Taxman 312. The decisions in cases of Rawatmal Harakchand v. CIT [1981] 129 ITR 346 (Cal) and P.V. Doshi v. CIT [1976] 113 ITR 22 (Guj.). Hence, the need for proper initiation of proceedings by application of mind.

Steps to secure recovery of demand in high demand cases - It has been the experience in the past that on several occasions, the Assessing Officers create huge demands against assessees without obtaining the details of any known assets of the asses¬see. With the passage of time and in the absence of such details, no concrete action gets taken to recover this demand. As a re¬sult, Department is burdened with the responsibility to recover the huge arrears existing in its records, with little possibility of actual recovery in many cases. As on 1-4-2004, the arrears increased by 20% to Rs. 87,885 crore while the objective was to reduce arrears by 20% as compared to the preceding year.

2. The Board has, therefore, decided that in cases where demand of Rs. 5 lakh and above in big cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Kolka¬ta, Chennai, Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Pune and Bangalore and Rs. 1 lakh and above elsewhere, is likely to be created and it appears that the recovery, in full or in part, could become difficult, it shall be the responsibility of the Assessing Officer, during the assessment proceedings itself, to enquire into all assets of the assessee and place under provisional attachment, in terms of provisions of section 281B, before the assessment is completed, the assets sufficient to cover the demand in question (or to the maximum extent, as the case may be). After completion of the assessment, if the provisional attachment cannot be continued till recovery, the same assets can be considered for attachment, etc., under section 222/226. In each of these cases, the Assessing Officer shall mention in an Office Note to the Assessment Order in question, the efforts made to locate the assets of the assessee, the details of assets located, the details of assets placed under provisional attachment, etc.

3. In search and seizure cases, huge demands are raised under block assessment and the recovery of the same is tedious and time-consuming. In this regard, it is extremely important for Assessing Officers in Central Charges to explore the possibility of invoking the provisions of section 281B. At the time of prepa¬ration of Appraisal Report, the DDIT(Inv.)/ADIT(Inv.) should take particular care in identifying the properties of the assessees which could be attached under this section and make a specific mention of the same in the Appraisal Report itself.

4. It shall be the responsibility of all Assessing Officers to follow the above procedure. If any demand becomes irrecoverable due to the failure of the Assessing Officer to follow these guidelines, he shall be held accountable for the loss caused to the Government, regardless of his subsequent posting.

5. While making a review of scrutiny assessments, the Commission¬ers of Income-tax and Chief Commissioners of Income-tax concerned shall specifically comment on this aspect.—Instruction No. 8/2004, dated 2-9-2004.

The Counsel of the Respondents relied on the decision of Madras High Court in the case of Dinesh Chand Surana v. Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax reported in [MANU/TN/3340/2018] and Tulsiram v. Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax (Benami Prohibition) reported in [MANU/CG/0099/2020]

The Court after hearing, observed as under:—

"12. Let us examine the nature of the impugned proceedings passed with reference to the provisions of the Act. As discussed above, section 1 sub-section (3) clarifies that the provisions of sections 3, 5 and 8 shall came into force at once, and the remaining provisions of the amendment Act shall be deemed to have came into force on 19 th day of May, 1988. Section 3 contemplates "Prohibition of benami transactions". Though the petitioner has relied on sub-section (3) to section 3, stating that whoever enters into any benami transaction on and after the date of commencement of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016, shall, notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (2), be punishable in accordance with the provisions contained in Chapter VII, section 1 sub-section (3) clarifies that the other remaining provisions of the Act shall be deemed to have come into force on the 19th day of May, 1988. Thus, in respect of the transactions prior to the amendment i.e. on 1-11-2016, the actions were taken under section 24 is valid and in accordance with law. In the present case, investigations and search were conducted prior to the amendment Act. The alleged benami transactions were also occurred prior to the amendment. But, the provisional attachment under Section 24 was made after the amendment, which is certainly permissible under section 1 sub-section (3) of the Act. Thus, the reference made by the learned counsel for the petitioner regarding sub-section (3) to Section 3 cannot have any application in respect of the facts and circumstances of the case on hand."

About issue of provisional attachment notice under section 24(4)(a)(i), it was observed as

"Therefore, the scheme of the Act is unambiguous under section 24(4)(a)(i). A provisional attachment of property shall be made in order to prevent the persons from encumbering the property during the process of adjudication and after passing the provisional attachment, if the proceedings are to be continued, then, an adjudication under section 25 and thereafter Section 26(1), show cause notice is to be issued. In the present case, it is not in dispute that the impugned order dated 12-05-2017, is an order of provisional attachment passed under section 24(4)(a)(i) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016 and the second amendment order dated 26-05-2016 is the notice to show cause under section 26(1) of the Act. Thus, for all purposes, it is only the commencement of proceedings under the Act and the petitioner has to respond to the show cause notice by submitting their explanations/objections along with the documents and evidences and thereafter, the authorities are bound to adjudicate the matter in the manner provided and take appropriate decision. This being the scope of the Act, the petitioner has misconstrued the provisions based on certain incorrect interpretations, filed the present Writ Petition."

1.4-3 Provisional attachment of property involved in money-laundering.

Section 5(1) of PMLA deals with provisional attachment of proceeds of crime. Section 5(1), as amended by the Finance Act, 2015 provides that where the Director or any other officer not below the rank of Deputy Director authorised by the Director for the purposes of this section, has reason to believe (the reason for such belief to be recorded in writing), on the basis of material in his possession, that—

(a)

any person is in possession of any proceeds of crime; and

(b)

such proceeds of crime are likely to be concealed, transferred or dealt with in any manner which may result in frustrating any proceedings relating to confiscation of such proceeds of crime under this Chapter,

he may, by order in writing, provisionally attach such property for a period not exceeding one hundred and eighty days from the date of the order, in such manner as may be prescribed.

First proviso to section 5(1) provides that no such order of attachment shall be made unless, in relation to the scheduled offence, a report has been forwarded to a Magistrate under section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974), or a complaint has been filed by a person authorised to investigate the offence mentioned in that Schedule, before a Magistrate or court for taking cognizance of the scheduled offence, as the case may be, or a similar report or complaint has been made or filed under the corresponding law of any other country.

Second proviso to section 5(1) provides that that, notwithstanding anything contained in the first proviso, any property of any person may be attached under this section if the Director or any other officer not below the rank of Deputy Director authorised by him for the purposes of this section has reason to believe (the reasons for such belief to be recorded in writing), on the basis of material in his possession, that if such property involved in money-laundering is not attached immediately under this Chapter, the non-attachment of the property is likely to frustrate any proceeding under this Act.

1.4-4 Adjudication [Section 8 of PMLA]

Finance Act, 2015 has inserted new sub-section (8) in section 8 of PMLA which provides that where a property stands confiscated to the Central Government under sub-section (5) of section 8, the Special Court, in such manner as may be prescribed, may also direct the Central Government to restore such confiscated property or part thereof of a claimant with a legitimate interest in the property, who may have suffered a quantifiable loss as a result of the offence of money laundering. The Special Court shall not consider such claim unless it is satisfied that the claimant has acted in good faith and has suffered the loss despite having taken all reasonable precautions and is not involved in the offence of money laundering.

17.2

PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT - VARIOUS STAGES

Provisional attachment under section 24 of the PBPT Act, 1988 has various statutory stipulations governing the procedure to invoke the said provisions. There are various stages involved in the process of such attachment. These are:-

Initial stage: The IO in consequence of material in his possession and after recording his satisfaction can issue a notice to the benamidar asking him to show cause within such period as indicated in the notice as to why the property should not be treated as benami property under section 24(1). This is the starting point of initiation of proceeding under the PBPT Act, 1988. A copy of this notice need be sent to the beneficial owner, if his identity is known. No approval from Adjudicating Authority is required for issue of initial SCN. [24(1)]

Second stage: Where the IO is of the opinion that the person in possession of the property held benami, may alienate such property, during the period allowed to him in the show cause notice under section 24(1), he may attach the subject property provisionally in the prescribed manner as specified Rule 5 of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transaction Rules, 2016. The procedure of attachment should be in the same manner as provided in Second Schedule of the Income-tax Act, 1961. This attachment shall be for a period not exceeding any 90 days from the last day of the month in which show cause notice under section 24(1) is issued (with effect from 1-9-2019). This can be done with previous approval of the Approving Authority. This is provided in sub-section (3) of section 24 of the PBPT Act, 1988. This order should be in writing specifying the property and indicating his satisfaction in resorting to provisional attachment. [24(3)]

Third stage: Where provisional attachment has been made under sub-section (3) of section 24, IO may, after making such enquiries, calling for such details as he may require and collecting evidence and taking into account all relevant materials, may extend the initial period for attachment. The section requires that the initial period of attachment can be continued by the IO only after consideration of relevant material in his possession. This means that the extension is not the ipse dixit of the IO. This extension can be made after consideration of relevant materials within a period of 90 days from the last day of the month in which show cause notice under section 24(1) is issued with effect from 1-9-2019.[S. 24(4)]

Fourth stage: After consideration of all relevant materials and evidences collected on enquiry, the IO may,

Continue the provisional attachment of the property made under this section with previous approval of the Approving Authority till passing of the order by the Adjudicating Authority under sub-section (3) of section 26. [24(4)(a)(i)], or

Revoke the provisional attachment of the property wherever it is not necessary with the previous approval of the Approving Authority. [24(4)(a)(ii)]

Fifth stage : Where no provisional attachment has been made under sub-section (3), the IO may pass an order provisionally attaching the property with previous approval of the Approving Authority till passing of the order under section 26(3) by the Adjudicating Authority [24(4)(b)(i)]. He may also decide not to attach the property as indicated in the SCN with previous approval of the Adjudicating Authority. [S. 24(4)(b)(ii)]

Sixth stage: Where the IO passes an order continuing the provisional attachment of the property under sub-clause (i) of clause (a) of sub-section (4) or passes an order provisionally attaching the property under sub-clause (i) of clause (b) of that sub-section, he shall, within fifteen days from the date of the attachment, draw up a statement of the case and refer it to the Adjudicating Authority. [S.24(5)]

The provisional attachment at all stages as indicated above shall be made after making enquiry, considering evidence or reports and taking into all relevant materials in possession of IO and with previous approval of the Approving authority. Attachment is made provisionally so as to thwart any attempt by the benamidar who was put to notice under section 24(1) not to alienate the subject property. However, the benamidar can approach the Court challenging the notice of attachment or its continuance by way of a writ where there is fatal jurisdictional error committed by the IO which goes to the root of the matter.

Q.14 Whether the provisions of Benami Law violate Article 20(1) of the Constitution? Ans. The benami law does not violate fundamental rights as enshrined in the Constitution of India and more particularly the violation of Article 20(1) of Constitution of India. There is no violation of Article 20(1) of Constitution of India for the reason that the proceedings under benami law are not Criminal proceedings. They are adjudicatory proceedings which are of civil nature. [General]

Q.15 Whether the authorities acting under the PBPT Act, 1988 enjoy protection from criminal action?

Ans. Under section 64 no prosecution, suit or other proceeding shall lie against the Government or any officer of the Government or the Appellate Tribunal or the Adjudicating Authority established under this Act, for anything done or intended to be done in good faith under this Act. The General Clauses Act defines good faith as "A thing shall be deemed to be done in good faith where it is in fact done honestly whether it is done negligently or not." There should be an element of honesty in ones act while performing his duties. [General]

Q.16 What is the meaning of the expression "Benami"?

Ans. The term "Benami" has its origin from a Persian compound word. This comprises of 'Be' which means 'without' and 'Nami' which means 'name'. This literally means without name. In a benami transaction, the benamidar is the ostensible owner of the property and the beneficial owner is the real owner who pays consideration and enjoys the benefit from the property. [Ref. Chapter 2]

Q.17 What is the distinction between a benami transaction and sham transaction?

Ans. Benami transactions are entered into solely to create an advantage for the creator himself. It has a dubious purpose. In the eye of law, a sham transaction has no existence. It is good in appearance but false in facts. Prior to enactment of the PBPT Act, 1988, a sham transaction was not considered as a benami transaction. However, after enactment of PBPT Act, 1988, sham transactions have been brought into the scope of benami transaction by bringing these transactions within the ambit of clauses (B), (C) and (D) to section 2(9) and by widening the scope of benami transaction under section 2(9)(A), which is the basic definition. [Ref. Chapter 3]

Q.18 Whether re-transfer of a benami property by the benamidar to beneficial owner is permissible?

Ans. It is barred. [Ref. Chapters 4 &12]

Q.19 What is scope of definition of 'property' in the Principal Act, 1988 and in the PBPT Act, 1988 ?

Ans. In the definition in the Principal Act, property referred to property of any kind without making the definition explicit leaving some scope for interpretation. Definition of property in the PBPT Act, 1988 refers to asset of any kind whether movable or immovable, tangible or intangible, corporeal or incorporeal, any right or interest, a legal document or instrument evidencing title or interest in property. The new definition has provided clarity, thereby reducing any debate in the matter of interpretation of the expression. [Ref. Chapter 5]

Q.20 Whether Benami Act applies to a property situated outside India?

Ans. No. This has been clarified the Finance Minister in Rajya Sabha that the benami property located outside India is beyond the scope of Benami Act. Such acquisition will be dealt with under Black Money Act. [Ref. Chapter 6]

Q.21 What is the effect of non-identification of Benami property ?

Ans. The proceedings under section 24(1) will be null and void, for the reason that the proceeding under this section is initiated for provisional attachment in respect of such property. [Ref. Chapter 6]

Q.22 Whether benami property only refers to immovable property?

Ans. No. Section 2(26) of the PBPT Act, 1988 has widened the definition of property to include both immovable and movable property of various kinds and forms. [Ref. Chapter 6]

Q.23 Whether a part of the property can be regarded as benami property?

Ans. Yes. In a multi-storeyed building where a person acquires a property in benami name such portion can be covered under benami transaction. [Ref. Chapters 6 & 17]

Q.24 What will be the position when proceeds of benami property are deposited in bank?

Ans. Such bank deposits will take the character of benami property. If this deposit is converted into fixed deposit or in any other form, such property will also be considered as benami property. But the same should exist on the date of initiation of section 24(1) of PBPT Act. [Ref. Chapter 6]

TRANSACTION COVERED IN CLAUSE (b)

A Transaction or an arrangement in respect of a property carried out or made in a fictitious name :-

This clause is applicable to a benamidar who is not identifiable or is a fictitious person. As per Dictionary.com a fictitious person refers to a created, taken, or assumed for the sake of concealment, which is not genuine but false. A fictitious person cannot be equated with a legal person who is identifiable. However, this clause does not postulate the complete absence of such a person. It cannot be said that there is no person at all in such a transaction. A transaction or arrangement presupposes the existences of two parties as one cannot transact with himself. On a reading of this clause, it would appear that fictitious person is that person whose name appears in a document but with a false or forged signature so that he cannot be identified easily. To apply this clause and before alleging that the transaction is carried out in the name fictitious name, IO is required to conduct enquiry on the basis material available with him. This enquiry cannot be half-hearted and based on suspicion. The record should show that all attempts have been made to trace the person before reaching an inference that the person is fictitious. The same should find mention in the satisfaction note before issue of show-cause notice. A fictitious person may refer to a person who has signed a document other than the benamidar.

ILLUSTRATION:

During demonetization period, on the basis of forged and fabricated documents like PAN and Aadhaar card, some persons having unaccounted money opened accounts in banks and deposited their unaccounted money in old currency in the said accounts. Later they withdrew the same in new currency. In such cases, the account-holder (benamidar) can be categorized as one who is a fictitious person in terms of section 2(9)(b). The beneficial owner is the person who deposited cash in the account opened in fictitious name and converted his unaccounted money in old currency and enjoyed the benefit. The property is the cash either in the same form or in the converted form. In such a case, law does not require to identify the benamidar. Here there could be a case where the beneficial owner may not be traceable creating difficulty for initiation of proceeding under section 24(1) of the PBPT Act, 1988. It is only if the property documents are found in course of search or inspection in the possession of beneficial owner or in the possession of searched party, the work would be easier being supported by evidence to advance enquiry.

ILLUSTRATION:

Acquisition of land and building in benami names in the past was a device resorted to by the various persons when the records maintained in SRO's office were manual and there was no insistence for providing KYC Norms (PAN/Aadhaar cards etc.). There was no full-proof method to ensure correct identity of the transferee. This practice was rampant. People having unaccounted money, acquired immovable properties in fictitious names so that they would remain anonymous and enjoy benefit from such property by realizing higher price by sale in future, although not immediately after purchase. This type of cases now can be covered under benami transaction as section 2(9)(b). In such cases, the person in whose name the property was purchased is a benamidar whose identity may not be verifiable. If the property documents may be found in course of search or inspection in the possession of beneficial owner or any other searched party, the work would be easier to advance further enquiry. It is further stated that if beneficial owner is not traceable, there will be no difficulty in initiating proceeding under section 24(1) as the notice can be sent to benamidar.

FACT: The applicant was a proprietor of a proprietary concern engaged in the business of trading of ferrous and non-ferrous metal scrap. It held a valid registration certificate under the provisions of the CGST Act and the GGST Act respectively.

A spot visit was carried out by the flying squad of the revenue department at the premises of the applicant. The department was prima facie of the view that the purchases made by the applicant from the JSK and UM were not genuine. In the course of the search carried out by the department, the registers, documents and books of account for the period between 1-7-2017 and 11-8-2020 were collected and taken into possession.

The Additional Commissioner passed an order under section 83 of provisional attachment of cash credit/current bank account and one savings bank account held by the applicant with the HDFC Bank Ltd.

Being dissatisfied with the order of provisional attachment, the applicant filed the instant writ-application.

HELD: Under the scheme of Act, levy and collection of tax are provided for in Chapter III, assessment is under Chapter XII and inspection, search, seizure and arrest are dealt with under Chapter XIV. Chapter XV which deals with the demand and recovery. This chapter provides for the provisional attachment under section 83. [Para 28]

Therefore, during the pendency of any proceedings under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 and 74, the Commissioner can provisionally attach any property including the bank account belonging to the taxable person. For this purpose, the Commissioner has to form an opinion that it is necessary to do so for protecting the interest of the Government revenue. These steps have to be taken in such manner as prescribed. Rule 159(1) deals with the provisional attachment of the property. [Para 29]

Rule 159(1) states that when the Commissioner decides to attach any property including the bank account, he shall pass an order in Form GST DRC-22. Various forms have been appended to the GST Rules 2017. Form GST DRC-22 lays down the format in which the order has to be issued provisionally attaching the property and the communication thereof to the financial institution. [Para 30]

The form of the order shows that it is to be addressed to the taxable person. The sections under which the proceedings are launched against such a taxable person are to be referred and then a direction is to be issued for not allowing any debit. [Para 31]

FACT: The Competent Authority provisionally attached under section 83 bank account of the assessee on the ground that it had created bogus records and claimed input tax credit for discharging the GST dues of about Rs. 121 crores.

The assessee, on writ petition filed before the High Court, contended that in terms of section 67 there could not be any attachment of future receivables so as to strangulate its entire business module and the recovery proceedings initiated by the department was contrary to the provisions of the GST Act.

The writ Court held that a sum of Rs. 5.68 crores, which was lying in the bank account of the assessee, was appropriated by the department and the assessee had also agreed to pay another sum of Rs. 1 crore against the estimated tax due of about Rs. 21 crores. The payment of Rs. 5.68 crores would amount to discharge of 27.05 per cent of the estimated tax dues. Therefore, there was no meaning in attaching the bank account further. It directed the assessee to deposit a sum of Rs. 1 crore within one week and on such deposit the attachment order was to be vacated. It also directed the Competent Authority to complete the investigation and issue appropriate show-cause notice as expeditiously as possible.

On writ appeal:

HELD: The observation made in the order impugned is premature. Admittedly what was put to challenge was only the order of provisional attachment and the statutory machinery provides for a mechanism for filing objections against such provisional attachment. The assessee appears to have understood the factual and legal provisions in a proper manner and has given a representation/objection dated 18-3-2021 seeking to lift the order of attachment under section 83. This application is undoubtedly an application to be reckoned under rule 159(5). However, the fact remains that the department has not disposed of the said application by passing a reasoned order. [Para 5]

The question is whether an order is required to be passed if an objection is filed in terms of rule 159(5). This issue has been answered by the Supreme Court in the affirmative in the case of Radha Krishnan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh [2021] 127 taxmann.com 26/86 GST 665. [Para 6]

Admittedly such an order has not been passed in the case of the assessee pursuant to its representation dated 18-3-2021.

been appended to the GST Rules 2017. Form GST DRC-22 lays down the format in which the order has to be issued provisionally attaching the property and the communication thereof to the financial institution. [Para 30]

The form of the order shows that it is to be addressed to the taxable person. The sections under which the proceedings are launched against such a taxable person are to be referred and then a direction is to be issued for not allowing any debit. [Para 31] Section 83 refers to the pendency of proceeding under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 and 74 respectively. Section 63 deals with the assessment of unregistered persons. Section 64 is regarding a summary assessment in respect of certain special cases. Section 67 falls in Chapter XIV and refers to the power of inspection, search and seizure. Section 73 is in Chapter XV wherein it deals with the determination of tax not paid or short paid or erroneously refunded or wrongly availed, utilised for any reason other than fraud or any wilful mis-statement made on suppression of facts. Section 70 confers power on the proper officer to summon any person whose attendance he considers necessary to give evidence or to produce documents or any other thing in any inquiry. Such inquiry is deemed to be a judicial proceeding under the Indian Penal Code. [Para 32]

Thus, the sine qua non for exercise of powers under section 83 is that the proceedings should be pending under section 62 or section 63 or section 64 or section 67 or section 73 or section 74. Where no proceedings under section 67 were pending on the date of the passing of the order of provisional attachment, the same would render the order illegal and contrary to the provisions of the Act, more particularly, section 83.[Para 34]

The amount as on date in the two bank accounts aggregates to Rs. 22,065. What good purpose the department is going to achieve by provisionally attaching the two bank accounts with balance of a paltry amount of Rs. 22,065.[Para 42]

The avowed object of exercise of power under section 83 for the purpose of provisional attachment of any property is to protect the interest of the revenue. Say for instance, tomorrow an order of assessment is passed and liability of the assessee to pay a particular amount is fixed. It is at that stage that the department may consider recovering the amount determined towards the tax liability from the amount lying in the bank accounts. In the same manner, if any immovable property has been provisionally attached and final liability towards the payment of tax is fixed under the order of assessment, then such immovable property can be put to auction for the purpose of recovering the dues. In the case on hand, the investigation already undertaken by the department cannot be interfered with. Ultimately, if sufficient material surfaces indicating the involvement of the applicant in some bogus transaction, the next step in the process can always be a show-cause notice under section 73 or section 74, as the case may be. However, to provisionally attach all the bank accounts and that too those accounts in which there is hardly any balance would only cause undue hardship to the assessee. This is the grey area where the revenue or the authority concerned needs to apply its mind before the power is exercised. This is the reason why in Valerius Industries v. Union of India [2019] 109 taxmann.com 218 (Guj.), this Court observed that the considerations are altogether different for the purpose of exercising the power of provisional attachment under section 83. Just because some proceedings are initiated under section 67 by itself may not be sufficient to arrive at the subjective satisfaction that it is necessary to provisionally attach the property for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue. An order of provisional attachment cannot be as a matter of course. It is one of the drastic measures which the authority may be compelled to take if the situation demands for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue.[Para 43]

The expression 'is of the opinion' or 'has reason to believe' as noted above are of the same connotation and are indicative of the subjective satisfaction of the Commissioner, which depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is settled law that 'opinion' must have a rational connection with or relevant bearing on the formation of the opinion. The rational connection postulates that there must be a direct nexus or live link between the protection of interest and available property which might not be available at the time of recovery of taxes after the final adjudication of the dispute. The opinion must be formed in good faith and should not be a mere pretence. The courts are entitled to determine whether the formation of opinion is arbitrary, capricious or whimsical. The expression 'necessary' must also be taken care of. From the order and record, it must come out that actually it was necessary to take drastic action of provisional attachment.[Para 44]

The opinion must be formed in good faith and should not be a mere pretence. The courts are entitled to determine whether the formation of opinion is arbitrary, capricious or whimsical. The expression 'necessary' must also be taken care of. From the order and record, it must come out that actually it was necessary to take drastic action of provisional attachment.[Para 44] Section 83 is in pari materia with the provisions of section 281B of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Section 281B of the Act, 1961 also provides for a provisional attachment of the property of an assessee pending the adjudication an assessment/reassessment proceedings where the income tax department believes that such attachment is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue. The provisions of section 83 have been framed along identical lines as section 281B.[Para 47]

Although the provisions of section 281B is pari materia to section 83 of the State GST Act, yet one pertinent feature of section 281B of the Income Tax Act is that it gives guidelines for making the provisional attachment. Such guidelines are missing so far as section 83 of the State GST Act is concerned.[Para 49]

In the overall view of the matter, more particularly, having regard to the fact that there is hardly a balance of Rs. 22,065 in the two bank accounts, there is no good reason to continue the provisional attachment.[Para 50]

In the result, this writ-application succeeds and is hereby allowed. The impugned order of provisional attachment of the two bank accounts is quashed and set aside. The connected Civil Application would not survive and the same is disposed of accordingly.[Para 51]

It is clarified that this order shall have no bearing on the further proceedings that the authority may deem fit to initiate in accordance with law.[Para 52]

It has been noticed over a period of time that in each and every matter in which proceedings under section 67 are initiated, an order of provisional attachment of the bank accounts under section 83 would follow. This mechanical exercise of the power is not appreciated. The Legislature has thought fit to confer upon the authority the power to provisionally attach the property of the assessee in the hope that such power is not exercised casually but, only after due and proper application of mind. A mechanical or casual exercise of such power will dilute the very efficacy of the provisions of section 83. Every day there are not less than ten matters on the subject of section 83 in the cause-list. When there are plethora of judgments explaining section 83 in details, then why so much of litigation in the High Court. The only reason that can be attributed is the mechanical exercise of power under section 83. This should stop at the earliest. So much judicial time is wasted in all such matters wherein the law is so well settled.[Para 53]

The Union of India as well as the CBDT is directed to read this judgment thoroughly and consider issuing appropriate instructions or guidelines at the earliest with respect to the exercise of power under section 83.[Para 55]

HEADNOTE: Section 83, read with  section 74, of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and rule 159, of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Section 83, read with  section 74, of the Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and rule 159 of the Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Whether order of provisional attachment is required to be communicated to party affected and this requirement is necessary for a meaningful exercise of right conferred under rule 159(2) - Held, yes - Petitioner was a dealer engaged in B2B e-commerce trading in white goods including mobile handsets - Pursuant to investigation carried out by DGGI against few suppliers of petitioner for issuing fake invoices to pass fraudulent ITC, premises of petitioner were searched under section 67 and statements were recorded under section 70 - Thereafter, DGGI attached bank accounts of petitioner under section 83 by citing pendency of proceedings under section 74 and petitioner's failure to pay tax dues - Petitioner filed a representation before DGGI against attachment order but no hearing was granted by DGGI - Hence, petitioner filed instant writ petition to quash attachment order - Whether requirement of provisional attachment as contained under rule 159 would require passing of order to affected person to enable him in filing of objections, and passing an order after affording an opportunity of being heard - Held, yes - Whether since investigation against petitioner was an outcome of investigation against suppliers, no show cause notice under section 74 was issued to petitioner; FACT: The petitioner was engaged in the Business to Business ('B2B') e-commerce trading in 'white goods' including mobile handsets. The respondent No. 2 (Additional Director General of GST Intelligence) was conducting certain investigation in respect of Pal Overseas, a registered entity under the GST Act and also as regards other entities relating to the alleged issuance of bogus/fake invoices without supply of goods and were seeking to claim Input Tax Credit of Goods and Services Tax. It is stated that the petitioner was purchasing the mobile handsets from these suppliers and was selling to its customers. The respondent No. 2 conducted a search at the Head Office of the petitioner. During the search, the respondent No. 2 issued summons to the Associate Director of the petitioner Company and had recorded their statements.

The said representatives of petitioner Company responded to the notice, appeared before the Authorities and also made their statements, which had been duly recorded.

On 21-9-2020, the respondent No. 2 sought details of the bank accounts of the petitioner which were provided on the same day. It is stated that the respondent No. 2 attached the bank accounts of the petitioner purportedly in exercise of power under section 83.

The petitioner made representation in terms of rule 159(5) seeking release of attachment and defreezing of bank accounts, but such request was neither considered nor any order was passed as required under the applicable Rules.

On writ Petition:

HELD: At the very outset, it must be noted that the order of provisional attachment is required to be communicated to the party affected and this requirement is necessary for a meaningful exercise of the right conferred under rule 159(2) of CGST Rules.[Para 18]

It must be noted that while the petitioner has drawn attention to communication dated 21-9-2020, addressed to the Bank Manager, HDFC Bank, Bengaluru regarding the provisional attachment of bank account of the petitioner in exercise of power under section 83, it is pointed out that such communication does not have any copy addressed to the petitioner.[Para 19]

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with rule 159 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with rule 159 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority had provisionally attached bank accounts of petitioner under section 83 and copy of such order had not been served upon it - Whether notice required to be issued on Competent Authority - Held, yes [Para 3] [Matter pending]GST : Where Competent Authority had provisionally attached bank accounts of petitioner under section 83 of CGST Act and copy of such order had not been served upon it, notice was issued on Competent Authority

FACT: The Competent Authority of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Department had provisionally attached the bank accounts of the petitioner under section 83.

On writ:

HELD: No copy of any order under section 83 appears to have been served upon the petitioner. The order of provisional attachment of property under section 83 issued to the concerned bank is in Form DRC-22 which is referable to rule 159(1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017. Sub-rule (5) of rule 159 provides that any person whose property is attached may within seven days of attachment under sub-rule (1) file an objection as provided in the said rule. However, it appears that the general practice of the department is to issue provisional attachment order on the concerned banks without furnishing copy of any such order to the concerned supplier. It is difficult to comprehend as to how the supplier whose property is attached would be in a position to file objection under sub-rule (5) of rule 159 if a copy of such order is not furnished to such supplier. [Para 2]

In view of the aforesaid, notice required to be issued on the Competent Authority. [Para 3]

'. Evidently, except for the property exempted from attachment under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), other properties are liable to attachment. Section 60 CPC provides the property liable to attachment. Noticeably, section 60(1) CPC specifically states that money is an attachable property. Properties which are not liable to attachment have been specified in the proviso to the section. Therefore, money in bank account is property liable to attachment. [Para 10] ■

There could be instances where the assessee does not own immovable property sufficient enough to secure the likely demand, but there are sufficient funds in the bank account. The power for provisional attachment is provided to protect the interest of the revenue. There is no warrant to hold that money lying in a bank account is not liable to attachment. [Para 11]

■

The mere fact that bank account is not explicitly provided under section 281B, unlike the GST Act, 2017 which specifically mentions the same, cannot lead to the conclusion that bank account is not liable to be attached under section 281B. [Para 12]

■

On the above discussions it is held that money in bank accounts is a property liable for provisional attachment under section 281B. [Para 13]

■

Now it is to be considered whether the security furnished before the Judicial First Class Magistrate's Court could be considered as sufficient security for the purposes of the Act. Section 451 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 which corresponds to section 497 of the Bharathiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhitha, provides for interim release of property produced before any criminal Court. The interim order for custody in terms thereof is only regarding custody pending the conclusion of the criminal proceeding. The mere fact that the Judicial First Class Magistrate's Court released the money to the assessee on furnishing security cannot have any significance in relation to the proceeding of the Income Tax Department under section 281B. Furnishing security before the Magistrate's Court is to ensure compliance with production of the property on being ordered. The security so furnished before the Magistrate's Court in relation to the proceedings before the Court cannot be construed as enuring to secure a likely demand on assessment under section 147. Section 226(4) authorises the Department to apply to a Court in whose custody there is money belonging to the assessee, to meet the tax due from the assessee. However, at the stage when the criminal proceedings have not culminated, it cannot be said that the security furnished before the Magistrate's Court for interim release of property is sufficient security. Moreover, section 226(4) would apply only when assessment is completed. And even coming to the final disposal of property under section 452 Cr.P.C, there could arise rival claims of title, priority etc. Thus, the security furnished before the Magistrate's Court does not sufficiently secure the possible demand by the department. [Para 14]

■

With regard to the opinion formed by the assessing authority and the approval granted by PCIT for provisional attachment, it is the contention that the document does not reflect the formation of such opinion on tangible material or information. The Apex Court in Radha Krishnan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh [2021] 127 taxmann.com 26 (SC) while considering provisional attachment under the GST Act, 2017, held that provisional attachment of Bank account is draconian in nature and the conditions which are prescribed by the statute for a valid exercise of power must be strictly fulfilled. It was also held that the formation of opinion to order provisional attachment must be on the basis of tangible material that the assessee is likely to defeat the demand, and that the provisional attachment is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue. During the course of arguments both sides submitted that the assessment proceedings have since been completed. In terms of section 281B(2) and the proviso thereto, provisional attachment could be in force for a period of only six months from the date of order, which could be extended for a further period of not exceeding sixty days after the date of assessment or re-assessment. Assessment having been completed, the life of the provisional attachment is short. The assessee submits that an appeal has already been preferred challenging the assessment. The Department has, along with the memo dated 9-1-2025, placed on record the proposal and the approval of the authorities as required under section 281B(1). It is seen that there has been a detailed consideration by the authority while granting approval for provisional attachment. At any rate, at this stage, when assessment has been completed and even an appeal has been filed, the sufficiency or otherwise of the satisfaction arrived at by the authority while provisional attachment was ordered needs not to be delved into. [Para 15]

■

For the reasons stated above, the conclusions arrived at by the Single Judge cannot be agreed with. [Para 16]

HELD: Given the drastic nature of this power, the Parliament has provided that such provisional attachment can only be done consequent to an order of the Commissioner. FACT: ■

After registration of the FIR, the ECIR was recorded by the respondent for having assets disproportionate to known sources of income and thereupon the investigation was conducted. Appellant challenged said order on ground that after the PAO dated 23.12.2020, the order for its confirmation had to be passed within 180 days, otherwise the attachment would lapse as per section 5 of the Act of 2002. The appellant further submitted that attachment order even included five bank accounts including an account where he was getting the pension. The payment for the purchases was disbursed by the petitioner's firm by RTGS/cheque mode to the respective firms/companies into their bank account. Further, the goods and services tax was credited by the aforementioned firms into their GST/R2A and the same is reflected in it. The petitioner stated that the firms/companies had not remitted the amount of GST tax though the tax amount was already credited into their GST/R2A.

The respondent No. 3 had raided the premises of the petitioner firm and informed that there was a huge conspiracy and creation of bogus bills by the firms and, therefore, they were investigating the entire case. The executives of the petitioner's firm were served with the order of provisional attachment of the petitioner's current account whereby the accounts were provisionally attached under the provisions of Gujarat GST Act, 2017 and the transactions of the accounts were completely restrained.

The respondent No. 13 had again raided the premises of the petitioner firm and seized the sales and purchase register and files and Bank/RTGS files.

The writ applicant sought to challenge the order dated 17-6-2019 passed by the respondent No. 4, Commercial Tax Officer, State of Gujarat whereby a demand has been raised of the total amount of Rs. 1,60,79,302 under the provisions of the CGST Act and GGST Act. The writ applicant also sought to challenge the action of blockage of the input tax credit passed whereby the input tax credit of the writ applicant was blocked under the provisions of the GST Act, 2017. The writ applicant also sought to challenge the order of provisional attachment of the stock of goods valued at Rs. 1,60,00,000, dated 27-11-2018 and the order of provisional attachment of the writ applicant's current account. The State Tax Officer had provisionally attached the accounts in exercise of powers under section 83

HELD: The plain reading of section 83 makes it clear that the powers have been conferred by the legislature upon the Commissioner. The subjective satisfaction that for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue, it is necessary that the goods should be provisionally attached should be that of the Commissioner. The Commissioner has been conferred with the power to pass an order in writing for the purpose of attaching provisionally any property including the bank account belonging to the taxable person. Indisputably, in the instant case the order of provisional attachment of the bank account as well as the goods has not been passed by the Commissioner, the same has been passed by the State Tax Officer, i.e., the respondent No.3. [Para 16]

is required to be passed if an objection is filed in terms of rule 159(5). This issue has been answered by the Supreme Court in the affirmative in the case of Radha Krishnan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh [2021] 127 taxmann.com 26/86 GST 665. [Para 6]

Admittedly such an order has not been passed in the case of the assessee pursuant to its representation dated 18-3-2021. As on date the objections filed by the assessee under rule 159(5) have not been disposed of by the Competent Authority by passing a reasoned order, it will be too early for the Writ Court to make an observation that there is no meaning in attaching the bank account further. It is too early for the Court to adjudicate as to whether at all the future receivables, if any, could be attached. The statutory rule 159(5) provides for a procedure, where the person whose bank account has been attached can seek for lifting of such attachment. Thus the assessee, having sought for lifting the attachment by filing representation/objection dated 18-3-2021, ought to have pursued the same. Without pursuing the said objections, a challenge to the provisional attachment order has to be held to be premature. [Para 7]

In view of the aforesaid, the writ appeal is allowed and the order impugned and directions issued in the writ petition are set aside. [Para 8]

It is directed to the assessee to submit fresh objections in terms of rule 159(5) within three days. On such objections being filed, the Competent Authority shall consider the objections and pass a speaking order and communicate the same to the assessee. Thereafter it is open to the assessee to work out its remedy in the manner known to law. [Para 9]

FACT: The appellant manufactures lead according to specific requirements of its clients, and has a factory in Himachal Pradesh. The appellant had been in the same line of business since 2008. Upon introduction of the Goods and Services Tax, the appellant migrated to and was registered under GST.

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with rule 159 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/ Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with rule 159 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority, exercising under section 83, had attached bank accounts of assessee - Assessee filed writ petition seeking relief in this regard - Whether assessee was to be directed to file objections under rule 159(5) against order of attachment before Competent Authority, who would decide such objections as expeditiously as possible - Held, yes [Para 5][In favour of revenue]GST: Where Comptent Authority, exercising under section 83, had attached bank accounts of assessee, assessee was directed to file objections against order of attachment before Competent Authority, who would decide such objections expeditiously

FACT: The Competent Authority, exercising under section 83, had attached the bank accounts of the assessee.

The assessee filed a writ petition seeking relief in this regard.

HELD: When the communication of the Competent Authority itself informs the assessee that he has a remedy against the order of attachment by way of filing objections under sub-rule (5) of rule 159, the Court would be reluctant to entertain the petition under article 226 of the Constitution of India in view of the fact that the assessee has an efficacious alternative remedy before the Competent Authority before whom all the contentions raised in the present petition can be raised. The Court is, therefore, not inclined to entertain the writ petition. [Para 3]

In the above view of the matter, the petition is dismissed as not entertained in the light of the availability of the efficacious alternative remedy under sub-rule (5) of rule 159. [Para 4]

The second significant aspect of sub-rule (5) is the mandatory requirement of furnishing an opportunity of being heard to the person whose property is attached. This is in consonance with the principles of natural justice and ensures that a fair procedure is observed. Sub-rule (5) provides for a post provisional attachment right of:

(i)

Submitting an objection to the attachment;

(ii)

An opportunity of being heard. Sub -rule (5) contains clear language to the effect that a person whose property is attached is entitled to two procedural entitlements: first, the right to submit an objection on the ground that the property was not or is not liable to be attached; and second, an opportunity of being heard to the person filing an objection. This is a clear indicator that in addition the filing of an objection, the person whose property is attached is entitled to an opportunity of being heard. It is not open to the Commissioner, as has been stated in the present case, to hold the view that the only safeguard under sub-rule 5 is to submit an objection without an opportunity of a personal hearing. Such a construction would be plainly contrary to sub-rule 5 which contemplates both the submission of an objection to the attachment and an opportunity of being heard. The opportunity of being heard can be availed of as a matter of right by the person whose property is attached. Both the right to submit an objection and to be afforded an opportunity of being heard are valuable safeguards. The consequence of a provisional attachment is serious. It displaces the person whose property is attached from dealing with the property. Where a bank account is attached, it prevents the person from operating the account. A business entity whose bank account is attached is seriously prejudiced by the inability to utilize the proceeds of the account for the purpose of business. The dual procedural safeguards inserted in sub-rule 5 of rule 159 demand strict compliance.

The Commissioner who hears the objections must pass a reasoned order either accepting or rejecting the objections. To allow the Commissioner to get by without passing a reasoned order will make his decision subjective and defeat the purpose of subjecting it to judicial scrutiny. The Commissioner must deal with the objections and pass a reasoned order indicating whether, and if not, why the objections are not being accepted. Sub-rule 6 of rule 159 allows for the release of a property which either was or is no longer liable for attachment. The form in which such an order has to be passed, namely form GST DRC-23, states that 'now there is no such proceeding pending against the defaulting person which warrants attachment' of the account or as the case may be, the property. Sub -rules 5 and 6 do not expressly contemplate a situation in which the person whose property is attached can object on the ground that the attachment is in excess of the amount likely to be due for which proceedings have been launched under the Act. Nor does it provide for a specific opportunity to the taxable person to offer any alternative form of security in lieu of the attachment. Such an opportunity must be read into the provision to allow for a fair working in practice. Whether any alternative security that is furnished by the taxable person should be accepted and if so, its sufficiency, is a matter for the Commissioner to determine. Undoubtedly, the taxable person may not have a right to demand that only a particular form of security must be accepted. The Commissioner has to decide whether the form of security offered would secure the interest of the revenue. Where the taxable person sets up the plea that the extent of the attachment is excessive or where the taxable person offers an alternative form of security, these are also matters which ought to be determined by the Commissioner in the exercise of powers under rule 159(5). The scope of objection can also extend to the nature of the property which is being provisionally attached. Now, it is in this backdrop that it needs to be determined whether the petition under article 226 was maintainable and if it was, whether Commissioner exercised the powers under section 83 read with rule 159 in accordance with law. [Para 56]

On writ:

HELD: From a careful analysis of section 83 read with sub-rule (1) of rule 159 what is to be noted is that the property including the bank account liable to or which has been provisionally attached must belong to the taxable person. 'Taxable person' has been defined in section 2(107) of the CGST Act to mean a person who is registered or is liable to be registered under section 22 or 24. [Para 19]

The department have explained in their affidavits that the investigation carried out against the petitioner fell within the ambit of sections 67 and 74 and provisional attachment orders were issued in the prescribed format. [Para 20]

Contention of the petitioner that there was violation of the provisions of section 83 and no due process was followed while provisionally attaching the bank accounts and the rebuttal contentions of the respondents that there has been due compliance to the statutory requirement of section 83 read with rule 159 may require a detailed examination. As regards the attachment of the bank accounts from the perspective of the taxable person, from the list of bank accounts, it is seen that the three bank accounts are in the joint names of petitioner's wife and petitioner whereas one bank account is solely in the name of petitioner's wife. It has been clarified that 'M' and 'M' Mandavia is one and the same person and is the wife of the petitioner. On the other hand it was found that other bank accounts are in the joint names of the petitioner and his (minor) son. Prima facie, 'M' and minor son are not the concerned taxpayers in this case. FACT: The petitioner was the proprietor of the Firm running in the name and style of Global Corporation. He was involved in voluminous transactions of several parties and followed the law while conducting his business.

He received an attachment order and realized from the Office of the Principal Commissioner of Central GST, Mumbai that the Central Bank of India on 20-8-2020 freezed his current account with the Rajkot Main Branch and since then, he had not been allowed to operate the account.

The petitioner approached the Bank through its Manager and requested to let him be provided the necessary details for the reason of freezing his account. However, despite his repeated requests, no information was disclosed by the authority concerned as to why the GST authority exercised such powers. He was orally conveyed that because of voluminous transactions with the third party, which was involved in violation of the provisions of the CGST Act, his account has been frozen.

He moved an application under the Right to Information Act, 2005. The Reply received from the bank revealed that the information sought for could not be revealed on account of the fact that same would impede the process of investigation.

On Writ Petition before the High Court:

HELD: In the instant case, there are no proceedings against the present petitioner under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 and 74. There is no reason therefore, to invoke section 83 against the writ applicant and proceedings. Since the proceedings are initiated by the authorities in connection with the third parties, invocation of powers under section 83 are not available with the respondents. Therefore, the order of the provisional attachment in connection with the bank Account No. 3785569992 of Global Corporation be interfered with. It is also necessary to note that despite of due service to the bank, the bank has chosen not to remain present. Under the RTI Act, where information was sought by the petitioner. It has chosen not to divulge on the ground of pending investigation strangely. It is rightly pointed out that this action of freezing account is harsh and to be resorted as provided under the statute. Thus, being a drastic power, the authority concerned cannot be oblivious of the serious consequences of provisional attachment of the bank account. Even if for the purpose of safeguarding the interest of the government revenue, the bank had chosen to follow the directions from the respondents, not to intimate to the petitioner as to why his account was frozen is wholly impermissible. In relation to the third party when such powers are impermissible to be exercised under section 83, the bank ought to have applied its mind and more so when even under the RTI Act, the bank had been requested to furnish the details. A copy of this order was to be sent to the legal department of the bank for the future reference where it is not to be a party to something which the statute does not permit. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demand and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority for recovery of dues of Rs. 14.62 crores had provisionally attached various bank accounts of assessee - Whether since assessee had already reversed input tax credit to tune of Rs. 13.28 crores, interest of revenue was sufficiently secured - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, provisional attachment of bank accounts of assessee was no longer justified - Held, yes - Whether Competent Authority was to be directed to forthwith release provisional attachment over bank accounts of assessee - Held, yes [Para 12][In favour of assessee]GST: Where Competent Authority for recovery of dues of Rs. 14.62 crores had provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee, since assessee had already reversed input tax credit to tune of Rs. 13.28 crores, interest of revenue was sufficiently secured and, therefore, provisional attachment of bank accounts was no longer justified

FACT: The Competent Authority for recovery of GST dues had provisionally attached various bank accounts of the assessee.

The assessee filed a writ petition seeking directions to the Competent Authority to release all bank accounts.

HELD: The impugned order of provisional attachment has been made in exercise of powers under section 83. Section 83 inter alia provides that where during the pendency of any proceedings under section 67 or section 73 or section 74, the Commissioner is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue, it is necessary so to do, he may, by an order in writing attach provisionally any property, including bank account, belonging to the taxable person in such manner as may be prescribed. [Para 9]

At the time when the impugned order under section 83 came to be passed, according to the Competent Authority, an amount of Rs. 14.62 crores would have been due and payable by the assessee. [Para 10]

Under section 83, the Commissioner is empowered to order provisional attachment for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue. In the facts of the instant case, while a liability of Rs. 14.62 crores had been estimated at the time when the order under section 83 came to be passed, the present estimate is Rs. 16.24 crores. Thus the assessee upon conclusion of any proceedings that may be taken pursuant to the proceedings under section 67 or section 73 or section 74 may be liable to pay such amount. Admittedly the assessee has already reversed input tax credit to the tune of Rs. 13.28 crores. Considering the amount paid by reversing input tax credit, the interest of the revenue is sufficiently secured. Therefore, the provisional attachment of the bank accounts of the assessee is no longer justified. [Para 11]

In view of the aforesaid, the Competent Authority was to be directed to forthwith release the provisional attachment over the bank accounts of the assessee. [Para 12]

The contention that this could only mean 'cash' and not money in a bank account may be an attractive argument but not in the context in which the above expression occurs. It is certainly a valuable thing. In other words, a sum in a bank account is not outside the ambit of section 132(1) and can be subject to search and seizure. [Para 53] Thus, a person could be in possession of undisclosed income not only in his or her own account but in someone else's account. In the context of the instant petitions, therefore, when pursuant to the search warrant, the department proceeded to search and seize not only valuable things etc. found in the premises of 'M' but also those in the accounts of the 8 petitioner companies as well as that of VS who was actively involved in the day to day management of various companies controlled by 'M' and worked closely with him, they could do so as long as they were satisfied that what constitutes M's undisclosed income was in the accounts of the 8 companies and VS. [Para 54]

The second proviso to section 132(1) read with section 132(3) permits the department to require the bank in which the account that is subject to search is located to freeze it since it may not be possible 'to take physical possession' immediately of such 'valuable article or thing and remove it to a safe place.' Section 132B deals with the powers of the authorised officer to deal with the valuable thing which has been so seized and the conditions on which the restraint placed may be lifted. [Para 55]

The assertion by petitioners that this is realization of the debt owed by the bank to the petitioners and that the amount therein cannot be transferred to the department is based on an incorrect understanding of the legal position under section 281B. The said provision states that in order to protect the interests of the revenue, it may be necessary to go in for a provisional attachment. Therefore, the direction issued to RBL by the department does not mean that the money is finally taken over by the revenue. It will undoubtedly be kept in a suspense account like a PD Account to await the final orders in the assessment proceedings and the issues raised as a consequence thereof. For this purpose, the argument that this does not constitute 'assets' or 'money' within the meaning of section 132(1) read with section 133 has not merit. [Para 57]

For the aforementioned reasons, both the petitions are dismissed. [Para 60]

The petitioner has filed an additional affidavit pursuant to order of the High Court. In such affidavit, he has stated two things, firstly, that both the flats placed under attachment belong to him. The order of provisional attachment before the assessment order is made, may be justified if the Assessing Authority or any other authority empowered in law is of the opinion that it is necessary to protect the interest of revenue. However, the subjective satisfaction should be based on some credible materials or information and also should be supported by supervening factor. It is not any and every material, howsoever vague and indefinite or distant remote or far fetching, which would warrant the formation of the belief.

(2) The power conferred upon the authority under section 83 for provisional attachment could be termed as a very drastic and far reaching power. Such power should be used sparingly and only on substantive weighty grounds and reasons.

(3)

The power of provisional attachment under section 83 should be exercised by the authority only if there is a reasonable apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand that is likely to be raised on completion of the assessment. It should, therefore, be exercised with extreme care and caution.

(4)

The power under section 83 for provisional attachment should be exercised only if there is sufficient material on record to justify the satisfaction that the assessee is about to dispose of wholly or any part of his/her property with a view to thwarting the ultimate collection of demand and in order to achieve the said objective, the attachment should be of the properties and to that extent, it is required to achieve this objective.

(5)

The power under section 83 should neither be used as a tool to harass the assessee nor should it be used in a manner which may have an irreversible detrimental effect on the business of the assessee.

(6)

The attachment of bank account and trading assets should be resorted to only as a last resort or measure. The provisional attachment under section 83 should not be equated with the attachment in the course of the recovery proceedings.

(7)

The authority before exercising power under section 83 for provisional attachment should take into consideration two things: (i) whether it is a revenue neutral situation (ii) the statement of 'output liability or input credit'. Having regard to the amount paid by reversing the input tax credit if the interest of the revenue is sufficiently secured, then the authority may not be justified in invoking its power under section 83 for the purpose of provisional attachment. [Para 52]

Thus, the respondents have not acted in accordance with law. [Para 53]

However, it is clarified that if the authority wants to proceed against the writ applicant under section 74, then it shall be open for the authority to do so after issuing appropriate show cause notice and give an opportunity of hearing to the writ applicant. [Para 54]

FACT: Proceedings under section 74 had been initiated against the respondent No. 3 As part of the said proceedings, the escrow account which stood in the joint names of respondent No. 3 being the first holder and petitioner No.1 (second holder) was provisionally attached vide order dated 27-9-2019.

Petitioners pleaded that since no proceedings had been contemplated and or initiated under any provisions of the CGST Act against petitioners, the provisional attachment of the escrow account to the extent of 97 per cent of the receipts received in the account belonging to the petitioners was not justified and was exfacie arbitrary.

Thus, petitioners prayed to quash and set aside impugned communication/order to the extent it provisionally attached share of the Petitioner No. 1 in the escrow account and had also prayed that by way of interim relief, bank be directed to transfer 97 per cent of the amount lying in escrow account to the account of the Petitioner No. 1 on such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit.

HELD: Section 83 confers power upon the authority to make provisional attachment in certain cases. [Para 14]

From the above it is discernible that such power can be exercised only if any proceedings under mentioned provisions of the Act have been initiated against the taxable person.

It is an admitted position that proceedings under the provisions of section 74 have been initiated against respondent No. 3 only.[Para 16]

The provisional attachment order states that respondent No. 3 is a registered taxable person under the CGST Act and proceedings have been launched under section 74 to determine the tax and any amount due in order to protect the interest of the revenue. Therefore bank account No. 36030500000014 was provisionally attached under section 83 read with rule 159(1) of the CGST Rules. However it is also imperative to note that account No. 36030500000014 is an escrow account in respect of which standing instruction were given by respondent No. 3 to respondent No. 4 bank on 25-7-2017 that out of the total receipts received in the said account, the share of respondent No. 3 would be 3 per cent only; the balance 97 per cent would have to be transferred to the petitioner No.1's account. [Para 16.1]

The fresh provisional attachment order has been issued on 22-9-2020 since the first provisional attachment order dated 27-9-2019 would cease to operate beyond the period of one year in view of the provision of sub-section (2) of section 83.To this the petitioners have filed their statutory objections dated 9-10-2020 as contemplated under the sub-rule (5) of rule 159 of the CGST Rules. It is pertinent to note that the petitioners were never served with both the attachment orders dated 27-9-2019 and 22-9-2020. Petitioners learnt about the same from respondent No. 4 bank when the share of petitioner No. 1 (97 per cent) was not transferred from the escrow account.[Para 17]
