11. Some Substantive provisions :

Section 3 – Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes

Section 3 of the Ordinance places a blanket ban on Unregulated Deposit Schemes and prohibits deposit taker from promoting, operating, issuing any advertisement soliciting participation or enrolment in or accepting deposits in pursuance of an Unregulated Deposit Scheme.

Section 4 – Fraudulent default in Regulated Deposit Schemes

Section 4 of the Ordinance prohibits deposit taker, while accepting deposits under a Regulated Deposit Scheme, from commission of fraudulent default in the repayment or return of deposit on maturity or in rendering any specified service promised against such deposit.

It may be noted that Section 4 is not applicable to companies (as per proviso to Section 27 of the Ordinance)

Section 5 – Wrongful inducement in relation to Unregulated Deposit Schemes

Section 5 of the Ordinance prohibits any person from knowingly making any statement, promise or forecast which is false, deceptive or misleading in material facts or deliberately conceal any material facts, to induce another person to invest in, or become a member or participant of any Unregulated Deposit Scheme.

Section 6 – Certain scheme to be Unregulated Deposit Scheme

Section 6 of the Ordinance provides that prize chit or a money circulation scheme banned under the provisions of the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Scheme (Banning) Act, 1978 shall be deemed to be an Unregulated Deposit Scheme under this Ordinance.

Section 7 – Provisional Attachment

The power for provisional attachment in cases of contravention of section 3 has been vested with a Competent Authority. This Competent Authority is an officer appointed by appropriate Government who is not below the rank of Secretary to that Government.

As per section 7(3) of the Ordinance, where the Competent Authority, has reason to believe (the reason for such belief to be recorded in writing), on the basis of such information and particulars as may be prescribed that any deposit taker is soliciting deposits in contravention of section 3, he may, by order in writing, provisionally attach the deposits held by the deposit taker and the money or other property acquired either in the name of the deposit taker or in the name of any other person on behalf of the deposit taker.

It is pertinent to mention that section 7(3) of the Ordinance is not properly drafted and does not provide for giving any show cause notice to the deposit taker prior to provisionally attaching deposits. Not providing an opportunity of being heard prior to provisional attachment tantamount a contravention of principles of Natural Justice and vitiates the pre-requisites of a fair trial. As this law will evolve, there is a high possibility that section 7(3) may be read down by the Courts to the extent it fails in providing a show cause notice prior to provisional attachment. It will be tested in future.

Section 14 and 15 – Confirmation of attachment by Designated Court

(i)

Section 14 of the Ordinance requires the Competent Authority to file an application before the Designated Court for making the provisional attachment absolute within a period of 30 days (which may extend upto 60 days) from the date of the order of provisional attachment. This period may be extended up to sixty days, for reasons to be recorded in writing.

(ii)

As per section 15(1) of the Ordinance, the Designated Court shall then issue notice to the deposit taker or any person whose property is attached under section 14, to show cause, within a period of 30 days, as to why the order of attachment should not be made absolute and the properties so attached be sold.

(iii)

As per section 15(2) of the Ordinance, the Designated Court shall issue notice to all other persons represented to it as having or being likely to claim any interest or title in the property to appear on the same date as persons referred to in section 15(1) to raise objections, if they so desire, to the attachment of the property.

(iv)

Undivided Family; (iii) a company; (iv) a trust; (v) a partnership firm; (vi) a limited liability partnership; (vii) an association of persons; (viii) a co-operative society registered under any law for the time being in force relating to co-operative societies; or (ix) every artificial juridical person, not falling within any of the preceding sub-clauses.

Meaning of "Regulated deposit scheme" (RDS) 7. As per section 2(14) of the Ordinance, schemes provided as per column (2) of the First Schedule will be RDS. These schemes are framed under rules and regulations of (i) SEBI, (ii) RBI, (iii) IRDA (a contract of insurance), (iv) State Government or Union Territory Government (such as schemes framed by co-operative societies, Chit Fund schemes sanctioned by the Government, money lending regulated by appropriate enactment), (v) National Housing Bank (such as scheme/arrangement registered under the National Housing Bank Act, 1987), (vi) Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority, (vii) Employees Provident Fund Organisation, (viii) Central Registrar, Multi-State Co- operative Societies, (ix) MCA, Government of India, (x) deposits accepted under any scheme or an arrangement registered with any regulatory body in India constituted or established under a statute; or (xi) any other scheme as may be notified by the Central Government.

Meaning of "Unregulated Deposit Scheme" (UDS)

8. "Unregulated Deposit Scheme" (UDS) means a Scheme or an arrangement under which deposits are accepted or solicited by any "deposit taker" by way of business and which is not a RDS.

Banning of UDS

9. As per section 3 of the Ordinance, on and from the date of commencement of this Ordinance (i.e., 21st February, 2019), (a) the Unregulated Deposit Schemes shall be banned, and (b) no deposit taker shall, directly or indirectly, promote, operate, issue any advertisement soliciting participation or enrolment in or accept deposits in pursuance of an Unregulated Deposit Scheme.

Section 5 of the Ordinance prohibits any person, by whatever name called, to make knowingly, any statement, promise or forecast, which is false, deceptive or misleading in material facts or deliberately conceals any material facts, to induce another person to invest in, or become a member or participant of an UDS.

Section 6 of the Ordinance provides that a prize, chit, or money circulation scheme banned under the provisions of the "Prize Chits and Money circulation scheme (Banning) Act, 1987" shall be deemed to be an UDS.

Controlling fraudulent default on repayment by RDS

10. As per section 4 of the Ordinance, it is provided that no deposit taker, while accepting deposit pursuant to an RDS, shall commit any fraudulent default in the repayment or return of deposit on maturity, or in rendering any specified service promised against such deposit.

Provisional attachment

11. Section 7 provides for provisional attachment of property of the deposit taker in cases of contravention of section 3. This power is vested in a Competent Authority who is an officer appointed by Appropriate Government and is not below the rank of Secretary to that Government. On the basis of information and particulars, as may be prescribed, that any deposit taker is soliciting deposit in contravention of section 3, the Competent Authority, by an order in writing, may provisionally attach the deposits and by the deposit taker, money or other property acquired by the deposit taker in his name or in the name of any other person on behalf of deposit taker.

Confirmation of attachment by Designated Court

12. Sections 14 and 15 provide that Competent Authority shall file an application before the Designated Court for making the provisional attachment absolute within the period of 30 days (which may be extended to 60 days for reasons to be recorded in writing) from the date of the order of provisional attachment. After issuing the notice to the deposit taker within 30 days, why not the provisional attachment be made absolute, the Designated Court may either make the provisional order of attachment absolute or vary the terms of attachment and release a portion of attachment or cancel the provisional order of attachment.

Appeal to the High Court

13. As per section 19, any person (including Competent Authority or deposit taker) aggrieved from the order of Designated Court may appeal to the High Court within the period of 60 days from the date of that order.

Priority of depositor's claim

14. As per section 12, any amount due to the depositor from a deposit taker shall be paid in priority over other debts including taxes and cess.

Priority of attachment under Ordinance

15. As per section 13, provisional attachment u/s 7 shall have priority to the extent of the claim of the depositors over any other attachment by any other Competent Authority in respect of any debt, revenue, taxes, cess, other rates payable to Appropriate Government or local authority. However, claim under SARFAESI and IBC will have priority over claim under this Ordinance.

Provisional attachment - Legal provisions

1. Section 45 of Gujarat Value Added Tax Act (GVAT Act) deals with provisional attachment. As per the said section, if during the pendency of any proceedings of assessment or reassessment of turnover escaping assessment, if Commissioner is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of revenue it is necessary to attach the property of a dealer, he may by order in writing attach provisionally any property belonging to the dealer. Property can be provisionally attached for a maximum period of one year. Rule 41 of Gujarat Value Added Tax Rules, 2005 (GVAT Rules) provides that Commissioner has to pass an order mentioning the details of property that is attached. If the property attached is of immovable nature, he shall send intimation to the land revenue authority to endorse a charge on said property. If the property is of a perishable nature, provisionally attached property shall be immediately released on payment of the market price of said property. If the dealer fails to pay the same, Commissioner shall dispose of such property and adjust the amount realized against the tax liability. Thus only condition required to be satisfied before making provisional attachment is formation of an opinion that in order to protect the interest of revenue, attachment is needed. Let us now look at judicial pronouncements on the same.

PRINCIPLE: Formation of an opinion that to protect the interest of revenue provisional attachment is done is must.

Likelihood of raising heavy demand not a ground for provisional attachment

2. Hon.'ble Andhra Pradesh High Court in case of B.J. Services Company Middle East Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer [2007] 10 VST 597 had an occasion to interpret the provisions contained in Andhra Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2005 with respect to provisional attachment. In this case, department made provisional attachment on the likelihood of raising heavy demands when assessment was made. Hon.'ble High Court held that it is abundantly clear from bare perusal of the provision that an order of attachment can be made where the prescribed authority frames an opinion that such order is necessary to be passed for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Revenue. Likelihood of raising heavy demand cannot be the ground for making provisional attachment.

PRINCIPLE: Likelihood of raising heavy demand cannot be a ground for making provisional attachment

No provisional attachment if no proceedings are pending

3. In case of Carlton Industrial Engineers v. Commercial Tax Officer [2007] 9 VST 77 (AP), Hon.'ble High Court held that provisional attachment can be made only during pendency of any assessment or reassessment proceedings. It cannot be made when order has already been passed. Even u/s 45(1) of GVAT Act, provisional attachment can be done only when proceedings are pending.

Principle: Provisional attachment cannot be made if no proceedings are pending.

Factors to be considered before making provisional attachment

4. In case of Pratik Manhendra Gandhi v. State of Gujarat [2013] 63 VST 178 (Guj.), Hon.'ble Gujarat High Court held that provisional assessment under section 45 of the Act, is a drastic measure. In this case provisional attachment of the bank account as well as stock of the dealer was made by the department on the apprehension that the dealer had purchased goods from suppliers which registration has been cancelled. It was submitted on behalf of petitioners that the purchases were made before the date on which order of cancellation was made. It was submitted that there was no discrepancy in the physical and book stock when department visited the premises of the dealer. Hon.'ble High Court considered the above submissions and opined that making full attachment of the stock will hamper the business of the dealer. Thus it devised a workable formula wherein dealer was required to maintain a minimum level of stock and provisional attachment was ordered to be lifted so that dealer can continue the business. Ratio of the said decision is that interest of trade and business, prima facie merits of the case as well as interest of revenue must all be considered before making a provisional attachment.

PRINCIPLE: Interest of trade, value of immovable property offered as security, merits of the case as well as interest of revenue must be balanced before making provisional attachment.

Time limit of provisional attachment

PRINCIPLE: Attachment can continue only for a maximum period of one year

14 of IBC does not apply to proceedings initiated against promoters of Corporate Debtor: SC

[Anjali Rathi v. Today Homes and Infrastructure (P.) Ltd [2021] 130 taxmann.com 253 (SC)]

In this significant ruling, the Apex Court held that petitioners-home buyers would not be prevented by the moratorium under Section 14 from initiating proceedings against the promoters of the Corporate Debtor in relation to honouring the settlements reached before the court.

Facts The Petitioners/home buyers and developer/corporate debtor entered into a homebuyer agreement which envisaged that delivery of possession in almost all cases was to be in 2014.

The Corporate debtor abandoned the project. As a result, the petitioners instituted proceedings before NCDRC sought a refund of their monies, and NCDRC allowed their claim.

In the meantime, proceedings were initiated against the respondent/developer under section 9 by an operational creditor, and the same was admitted. CoC approved the resolution plan submitted by the consortium of home buyers, and the Adjudicating Authority was yet to decide on the application for approval of the resolution plan.

Petitioners submitted that during the course of instant proceedings, settlements were arrived at, and hence promoters of corporate debtor/ developer should be held liable personally to honour the settlements. Petitioners urged that instant court should direct the personal properties of promoters to be attached in view of provisions contained in the resolution plan.

The Supreme Court's Ruling

The Apex Court held that if the petitioners have any objections to the Resolution Plan, they have to submit them before the Adjudicating Authority. The NCLT was directed to ensure that the application for approval is disposed of expeditiously and preferably within six weeks from the date of receipt of a certified copy of the instant order.

The Court further clarified that the petitioners would not be prevented by the moratorium under Section 14 from initiating proceedings against the promoters of the Corporate Debtor in relation to honouring the settlements reached before an instant court. However, instant Court cannot issue a direction as sought by petitioners relying on a Resolution Plan which is still pending approval before an Adjudicating Authority.

14. Bank account of director cannot be attached merely on the ground of allegation against Co.: Delhi High Court

[Roshni Sana Jaiswal v. Commissioner of Central Taxes GST Delhi (East) [2021] 128 taxmann.com 357 (Delhi)]

In this case, the Honorable High Court of Delhi held that provisional attachment could be ordered against property belonging to taxable person and provisional attachment order of directors' bank accounts on fake Input Tax Credit (ITC) allegations on their company is not valid.

Facts

The petitioner acted as a director on the Board of Directors of a company between 2006 and 2008. The department initiated an investigation against that company, alleging that the company was availing ITC against fake/ineligible invoices. The petitioner was also a shareholder in the company and owned approximately 14.33% equity shares. The department, therefore, initiated proceedings under section 83 against the petitioner and provisionally attached her bank accounts. She filed a writ petition against the same.

The High Court's Ruling

The Honorable High Court observed that there is nothing on record to show material available with the department, linking the petitioner to purported fake invoices. In other words, in the absence of such material, the impugned action concerning provisional attachment of the petitioner's bank accounts, which is otherwise a "draconian" step, was unsustainable. In the zeal to protect the interest of the revenue, the department cannot attach any property, including bank accounts of persons other than the taxable person. Therefore, it was held that provisional attachment orders were liable to be quashed.

15. Section 272 (1)(e) of Cos. Act is not ultra vires Constitution of India: Karnataka High Court

[Devas Employees Mauritius (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2021] 127 taxmann.com 108 (Karnataka)]

In the instant case, the High Court dismissed a petition which sought to quash proceedings initiated against Devas Multimedia Private limited by ISRO arm Antrix Corp. before NCLT.

The petitioner, Devas Employees' Mauritius Pvt. Ltd., a Company incorporated under the laws of the Republic of Mauritius, had presented a writ petition with prayers to:

(a)

declare Section 272(1)(e) of Companies Act, 2013 as ultra vires Constitution of India;

(b)

to declare that the second proviso to Section 272(3) of the Act must be read to apply to the petitions presented by persons falling under Section 272(1)(e) of the Act; and

(c)

to issue a writ of certiorari quashing sanction order and consequently to quash all proceedings before NCLT.

The High Court held that Section 272 (1)(e) is not an ultra vires Constitution of India. As Registrar and 'a person authorised by Central Government' fall into different categories, it does not warrant reading down Section 272(3).

Introduction

Money laundering is a felony, which, per se, is not new to the world. Given its nature, it is essential to have written law in place, which should be amended, time and again, to adequately deal with the on-going changes in the economical environment. In India, the enactment of Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 ('PMLA') was a remarkable and important step towards ensuring the same. Since its initial introduction, the law has undergone various amendments over the years. The Interim Budget for 2019-2020 has made several changes in enactments, which also include changes in PMLA. The amendment is part of the Finance Bill, 20191, and is yet to be notified.

PMLA is a comprehensive law which deals with all the major aspects of money laundering, which includes defining what constitutes as money laundering, the process of attachment and adjudication, management of confiscated properties, obligations on reporting entities like banks and financial institutions, etc.

Background to the amendment

Chapter III of the PMLA deals with "Attachment, Adjudication and Confiscation". Section 5 under the Chapter, gives powers to the Director or Deputy Director (appointed authority under PMLA by the Central Government) to provisionally attach the property in case he has reason to believe that the property is involved in money laundering. This is an interim action which prevents any likelihood of further transfer of/ or launder of property or money. The initial attachment is merely allowed for a period of 90 days.

The aforesaid complaint is transferred to the Adjudicating Authority (AA), which further investigates the matter in accordance with the provisions of section 8 of PMLA. At this stage, it is pertinent to understand the definitions of 'attachment' and 'investigation'; both the expressions are defined as under:

"attachment" means prohibition of transfer, conversion, disposition or movement of property by an order issued under Chapter III.

"investigation" includes all the proceedings under this Act conducted by the Director or by an authority authorised by the Central Government under this Act for the collection of evidence.

While attachment is an act to stop any movement of the property, investigation is a lawful process, which allows collection of evidence of money laundering, leading to punishment and confiscation. If on investigation, the AA concludes that the property is involved in money laundering, it shall confirm the continuation of the provisional attachment, which becomes final after the final order of confiscation is passed by the court.

Post amendment

The amendment has substituted the words 'ninety days' with 'three hundred and sixty five days'. While the amendment seems minor, it actually extends the time period of attachment by a total of 275 days. Resultantly, the attachment shall continue for one year during pendency of proceedings before a criminal court, under PMLA or a corresponding foreign law.

While the provisional attachment period remains unchanged, extending the attachment period before final confiscation, gives the authorities increased time in hand to deal with a given case. With the increased number of cases of money laundering, this is a relief for the authorities investigating matters under PMLA.

Additionally, the amendment inserts explanation to sub-section (3) above; accordingly, the aforesaid period of 365 days shall exclude any period for which the respective investigation is stayed by any court of law. Since investigation is construed to be ineffective while it is stayed, and the number of attachment days is calculated in reference to the investigation, the period of stay should be excluded.

Conclusion

In essence, the amendment adds flexibility to the proceedings under PMLA and gives more time to the authorities, which can be invested into finding relevant evidence and records.

(ii) Is there any threshold limit for invoking attachment provision ? - Neither section 73C nor the Rules lay down any threshold limit for initiating attachment proceedings. However, the CBEC’s Circular No. 103/06/2008-ST, dated July 1, 2008, provides that it should be resorted to only in a case where the service tax or CENVAT credit alleged to be involved is more than Rs. 25 lakh.

(iii) Against whom can the provisions of attachment be invoked ? - As per section 73C, provisional attachment can be ordered in respect of any property belonging to a person on whom a notice has been served under section 73(1) or 73A(3). It may be noted that under section 73(1), a notice can be served on the person chargeable with the service tax which has not been levied or paid or which has been short-levied or short-paid or the person to whom service tax has been erroneously refunded, whereas, a notice under section 73A(3) can be served on - (1) a person liable to pay service tax who has collected any amount in excess of the service tax assessed or determined and paid on any taxable service from the recipient of the taxable service, or (2) any person who has collected any amount as service tax, which is not required to be collected, from any other person.

(iv) Which property can be attached under the provision of service tax ? - As noted in FAQ 3, provisional attachment under section 73C can be ordered in respect of any ‘property’ belonging to the specified person. Rule 2(c) of the Rules defines the term ‘property’ to include immovable property. Further, rule 4(2) of the Rules provides that movable property shall be attached only if the immovable property is not sufficient to protect the interest of revenue.

The CBEC, vide its circular dated July 1, 2008, has clarified that immovable property/properties which is/are used for commercial purpose may be provisionally attached.

(v) Can personal property(ies) of proprietor/partner(s)/ director(s) be also attached ? - As per proviso to rule 3(3) of the Rules, personal property of proprietor or partners or directors, as the case may be, shall not be attached. As per rule 2(d), ‘personal property’ means any movable or immovable property belonging to a proprietor or partner or director, which is not in relation to business activity.

Accordingly, the CBEC in its circular dated July 1, 2008 has also clarified that any movable or immovable property which is in personal use of the sole proprietor/partner/director cannot be attached.

(vi) What shall be the extent of attachment ? - In terms of rule 4(1), the provisional attachment of property shall be to the extent it requires to protect the interest of revenue. In other words, the value of property attached shall be as nearly as may be equivalent to that of the amount of ‘pending revenue’.

The term ‘pending revenue’ is defined under rule 2(b) to mean "any service tax that has not been levied or paid or has been short-levied or paid or erroneously refunded in respect of which a notice has been served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A". Thus, the term ‘pending revenue’ refers to the amount demanded in the proceedings under section 73 or 73A.

(vii) What can be the possible justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary ? - If the Central Excise Officer reasonably believes that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, any of his property(ies) liable to attachment, it can be considered as sufficient justification necessitating attachment of property. The belief must, however, be based on substantial grounds.

(viii) What precautions should the Central Excise Officer take before initiating attachment proceedings ? - Although section 73C and the Provisional Attachment of Property Rules, are both silent in this regard, the CBEC has in its circular dated July 1, 2008, stated emphatically that the remedy of attachment is of extraordinary nature and should be resorted to in the utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution. There should be sufficient justification to hold the view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interests of revenue. The Central Excise Officer should, in his proposal for attachment, clearly state the grounds on which he entertains the reasonable belief that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, the property and the sources of his information, if any.

The circular further states that appropriate disciplinary action shall be initiated against the officers who may be found to have exercised the powers of provisional attachment of property frivolously and without sound reasons.

III. Understanding the Ordinance

1. Applicability

This is a prospective law made applicable from 21st February 2019. It would apply to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir. For all the deposits before 21st February 2019, the regulatory framework at that point of time would continue to apply.

2. Targeting Unregulated Deposit Schemes

UDS contains a substantive banning clause which bans Deposit Takers from promoting, operating, issuing advertisements or accepting deposits in any Deposit Taking Scheme which is not regulated. The principle is crystal clear that this Ordinance bans unregulated deposit taking activities altogether, by making them an offence ex-ante, rather than the existing legislative-cum-regulatory framework which only comes into effect ex-post with considerable time lags.

People of the western regions of the country may not understand and appreciate the importance of this law. But when we see the investment patterns of the households of the southern region of the country and even some eastern parts, the investment in such deposit schemes like chit funds are huge. And these marginal and gullible investors are the real victims of the illicit deposit schemes.

3. Prescribed Offences

The Ordinance broadly prescribes three different types of offences and prescribes severe punishment and heavy pecuniary fines for the same. The offences are –

Running of Unregulated Deposit Schemes;

Wrongful inducement in relation to Unregulated Deposit Schemes; and

Fraudulent default in Regulated Deposit Schemes.

4. Administrative Segment

The Central Government will establish an online database for maintaining records of deposit takers. All the deposit takers pan-India have to provide the information on the database portal regularly. Time and form of reporting has not been prescribed yet. This online portal once made accessible to all, people can verify the genuineness of the deposit takers and substantially reduce the flow of money to illicit deposit schemes. Further, any violation of provisions related to reporting on online database by deposit takers would invite penalty of up to INR 10L.

Deposit takers covered under Regulated Deposit Schemes are allowed to accept and solicit for obtaining deposits. However, any fraudulent default in repayment or servicing of deposits would invite fine of higher of INR 5L; INR 25 cr.; or thrice the amount of profits made on such default. This will be in addition to imprisonment which may extend to 7 years.

Introduction

The Supreme Court's recent judgment in National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL) v. Union of India & Ors (Writ Petition (Civil) No. 995 of 2019) is a landmark in the domain of financial fraud litigation and asset recovery. The decision, delivered on 15 May 2025, addresses the complex interplay between the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (MPID) Act, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), and central statutes such as the SARFAESI Act, Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act (RDB Act), and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

At its core, this decision represents a careful recalibration of the legal hierarchy between secured creditors, government agencies, and public interest protections in cases involving tainted assets.

Background: The NSEL Scam and Legal Tangle

NSEL, a commodity trading platform promoted by 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. The collapse of the National Spot Exchange in 2013 triggered a Rs. 5,600 crore default, affecting about 13,000 traders and investors. The fallout led to multiple FIRs, civil suits, and the attachment of assets by both the Enforcement Directorate (under PMLA) and the State of Maharashtra (under the MPID Act). The NSEL itself secured decrees and arbitral awards worth around Rs. 3,365 crore against defaulting members, but faced significant hurdles in executing them due to overlapping attachments and competing claims from secured creditors (primarily banks) under SARFAESI/RDB Act. IBC proceedings also initiated against several entities.

Genesis of the Supreme Court Committee

To streamline the complex situation, involving execution of multiple decrees and avoid conflicting proceedings, the Supreme Court, invoking Article 142, constituted a high-powered committee chaired by Justice (Retd.). This committee was vested with the powers of a civil court to execute all decrees, orders, and arbitral awards obtained by NSEL, including the authority to sell properties attached under PMLA and MPID Act and oversee distribution to verified claimants. In short, Article 142 was used as a constitutional "safety valve" to harmonize conflicting statutory regimes, centralize execution, and prioritize investor restitution in a manner that ordinary statutory processes could not have achieved efficiently.

Power under Article 142 is extraordinary, discretionary, and unique to the Supreme Court. It allows the Court to:

Fill legal gaps where no statute provides an adequate remedy. It Complements statutory law, but does not override it—cannot be used to violate or contradict existing statutes

Issue binding directions, even if not strictly aligned with procedural law. Curative in nature—used to resolve issues when ordinary law falls short or causes injustice

Craft equitable solutions, especially in complex, multi-party, or sensitive matters.

However, Article 142 cannot be used to create a new law or override substantive rights conferred by legislation. It must be used judiciously and only when regular statutory or procedural remedies are inadequate or unjust. Article 142 cannot be used to achieve something indirectly what cannot be achieved directly.

While initially hailed as a pragmatic consolidation, the order's breadth brought it into direct strain with key statutory provisions of PMLA, SARFAESI, RDB Act, and IBC—particularly regarding the priority of secured creditors and the moratorium under insolvency law.

Key Legal Questions before the Supreme Court

Two main issues crystallized before the Court in the later stages of the litigation:

1.

Do secured creditors have priority over assets attached under the PMLA and MPID Act by virtue of SARFAESI and RDB Act?

2.

Are properties attached under the MPID Act immune from the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC?

These questions weren't just technical—they strike at the heart of India's recovery framework, challenging the hierarchy of creditor rights in fraud scenarios.

Supreme Court's Ruling on Secured Creditors' Priority

The Court held that the MPID Act and PMLA take precedence over the SARFAESI Act and RDB Act when it comes to assets attached as "proceeds of crime" or for the protection of depositors. The rationale is rooted in constitutional law: the MPID Act is a state law enacted to maintain public order and protect depositors, while SARFAESI and RDB Act are central laws focusing on banking and secured creditors' rights. Since these statutes operate in distinct legislative fields, the doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254 does not apply.

However, as per CBEC’s circular any property which is exempted from attachment and sale for execution of a decree of a civil court in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, shall also be exempt from provisional attachment in terms of section 73C. Further, as regards what property is entitled to exemption, the decision of the Commissioner of Central Excise shall be final.

Conclusion

3. It is astonishing to note that the Provisional Attachment of Property Rules, notified after more than two years of the basic provision of section 73C coming into force, appear to have been drafted hastily, leaving a number of issues unanswered. The CBEC has, however, endeavoured to fill the gaps simultaneously by issuing the circular on the same date. Most obviously, these gaps had already been reckoned by the CBEC. It would have been better if the issues answered by the circular were also incorporated in the Rules making them comprehensive and complete. Departmental circulars being administrative instructions do not get legislative ratification as in case of Rules.

21. Money in bank accounts is a property liable for provisional attachment under Section 281B: HC

Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax v. Mohammed Salih [2025] 171 taxmann.com 23 (Kerala)

The police seized a huge amount of cash from a car in which the assessee was riding. After recording reason to believe that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment, proceedings were initiated in relation to the same by the issuance of notice under Section 148.

The expected demand on assessment, including penalty, would be a substantial amount exceeding two crores. The competent authority of the Department ordered provisional attachment of the Bank accounts of the assessee under section 281B.

The matter reached the Kerala High Court.

The High Court held that the word 'property' is a word of very wide connotation. It is relevant to note that section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of 'any property'. The prefix 'any' to the word 'property' has much significance. It indicates that the word 'property' occurring therein is not to be comprehended in a restricted sense.

Therefore, 'any property' mentioned in section 281B(1) would take within its sweep, money lying in the bank account also. Section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of any property belonging to the assessee in the manner provided in the Second Schedule to the Act. The Second Schedule to the Act is titled, 'Procedure for Recovery of Tax'. Evidently, except for the property exempted from attachment under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), other properties are liable to attachment.

Section 60 CPC provides the property liable to attachment. Noticeably, section 60(1) CPC specifically states that money is an attachable property. Properties that are not liable to attachment have been specified in the proviso to the section. Therefore, money in a bank account is property liable to attachment.

There could be instances where the assessee does not own immovable property sufficient enough to secure the likely demand, but there are sufficient funds in the bank account. The power for provisional attachment is provided to protect the interest of the revenue. There is no warrant to hold that money lying in a bank account is not liable to attachment.

1. Section 73C of the Finance Act, 1994 provides for provisional attachment of property of an assessee. It reads as follows:

"73C. Provisional attachment to protect revenue in certain cases.—(1) Where, during the pendency of any proceeding under section 73 or section 73A, the Central Excise Officer is of opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interests of revenue, it is necessary so to do, he may, with the previous approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise, by order in writing, attach provisionally any property belonging to the person on whom notice is served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A, as the case may be, in such manner as may be prescribed." [Emphasis supplied]

An analysis of the above section makes it clear that the following ingredients are essential for issuance of an order of attachment thereunder:

(i)

The attachment should be during the pendency of any proceeding under section 73 or section 73A;

(ii)

notice should have been served on the assessee under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A;

(iii)

the Central Excise Officer before whom proceedings are pending is of opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interests of revenue, it is necessary to attach the assessee's property;

(iv)

previous approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise is necessary for the attachment;

(v)

the attachment order should be in writing; and

(vi)

the attachment is provisional.

1. Discharge rightly denied where accused aided co-accused in bank forms and cheques, knowing link to proceeds of crime: SC

K. Murali Krishna v. Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement [2025] 180 taxmann.com 462 (SC)

In the present case, the question before the Supreme Court was whether the petitioner was entitled to discharge under section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, in a prosecution for the offence of money laundering under section 3 read with section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.

The Supreme Court observed that, at the stage of considering a discharge application, the court is not expected to examine the truthfulness or sufficiency of the allegations, as such an exercise falls within the domain of trial. It was further noted that the scope of section 3 of the PMLA cannot be narrowly construed for the purpose of discharging an accused at the threshold.

The Court noted that the allegations against the petitioner indicated that he had indirectly assisted the main accused in filling up bank account opening forms and handling cheque leaves and was, therefore, alleged to be knowingly a party to activities connected with the proceeds of crime.

The Supreme Court held that since these allegations required appreciation of evidence and adjudication during trial, they could not be examined at the initial stage of discharge. Accordingly, it was held that there was no valid ground to interfere with the order of the High Court confirming rejection of the discharge application.

2. Attachment order under PMLA can be made without prior communication under Section 66(2): HC

Directorate of Enforcement v. Prakash Industries Ltd. [2025] 180 taxmann.com 189 (Delhi)

In the present case, the Supreme Court was called upon to examine the interplay between Section 3 read with Section 24 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002(offence of money laundering) and Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (discharge of accused).

The petitioner had filed an application under Section 227 Cr.P.C. before the Trial Court seeking discharge on the ground that he was not connected with the banking transactions underpinning the alleged money-laundering offence and had merely assisted Accused in filling bank account forms without knowledge of Accused's identity, contending he was wrongly implicated.

The Trial Court rejected this application. The High Court, in the impugned order, upheld that the scope of Section 3 of the PMLA is wide and cannot be narrowly circumscribed at the discharge stage.

The court further retreated that at the discharge stage under Section 227 Cr.P.C. is not to assess the truthfulness of allegations but only to determine whether prima facie a case is made out, leaving detailed factual inquiries for trial. It observed that, as per the complaint under Sections 44 and 45 of the PMLA, the petitioner was alleged to have "indirectly assisted" in filling account and cheque forms and was knowingly a party to activities connected with proceeds of crime — allegations which, if accepted, fall within the ambit of the offence under Section 3 read with the statutory presumption under Section 24 of the PMLA.

Therefore constituted prima facie material for trial, not a fit case for discharge. On this basis, the High Court confirmed the Trial Court's order, and the Supreme Court found no valid ground to interfere with the impugned order.

3. Once Recovery Certificate becomes final, Recovery Officer is bound to proceed in accordance with same: HC

Maharaji Educational Trust v. Housing and Urban Development Corporation Ltd. HUDCO

In the present case, the Delhi High Court examined whether the Recovery Officer could travel beyond a revised Recovery Certificate issued under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993, in recovery proceedings initiated by HUDCO against Maharaji Educational Trust.

In the wake of the rising non-performing assets crisis, the Indian legal system seems to be grappling with major challenges than before. While turnaround of debt remains a problem, wilful default of debt adds to this menace. As banks and the government are dead beat trying to prosecute Mr. Vijay Mallya for wilful default of loans and Mr. Karti Chidambaram on money laundering charges, they continue to evade law by residing out of India. The Fugitive Economic Offenders Bill, 2017 (the "Bill") seems to be a knee-jerk reaction which attempts to remedy such regulatory fiascos. The Bill was put in public domain on May 19, 2017 for comments.

Background

To state that the existing legal framework to deal with high value multi-jurisdictional economic offences is inadequate would be an understatement. The RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters (July 01, 2015) provides for barring a wilful defaulter from (a) raising any loans from banks, financial institutions and non-banking companies; and (b) floating a new venture. The other remedies available to banks and financial institutions are contained in the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 and the Recovery of Debt due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 which are time consuming since they involve prolonged litigation.

Moreover, even though the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 aims to provide for a speedy bankruptcy process, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal by holding that the timelines prescribed in Section 7, 9 and 10 of the Code are directory in nature1 has reduced its effectiveness to an extent. Further, liquidation/ bankruptcy process is not a sufficient deterrent in case of high value economic offences. The provisions of civil law in India do not address the issue of high value multi-jurisdictional fugitive economic offenders whereas the process prescribed under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is time consuming and hence inefficient.

The Explanatory Note appended to the Bill states that fleeing of economic offenders leads to several "deleterious" consequences such as (a) hampering investigation in criminal matters; (b) wasting the precious time of the court; (c) undermining the rule of law; and (d) cases which involve non-payment of bank loans cause strain on the banking system. The Bill is aimed to deter a fugitive economic offenders by providing for confiscation of all properties of a wilful defaulter prior to conviction.

Key features

The key features of the Bill are as follows:

1.

Definition of Fugitive Economic Offenders : The Bill defines a "Fugitive Economic Offender" as any individual against whom a warrant for arrest in relation to a scheduled offence2 has been issued by any court in India who (a) leaves or has left India so as to avoid criminal prosecution; or (b) refuses to return to India to face criminal prosecution. Further, in order to ensure that the courts are not overburdened with such cases, only such cases where the total value involved is INR 100 crores or more shall be within the purview of the Bill. This is a higher threshold and must be reduced.

2.

Applicability: The provisions of the Bill shall apply to any individual who is, or becomes, a Fugitive Economic Offender on or after the date of coming into force of this law. It may be argued that the Bill (when becomes law) will be an ex post facto law i.e. it will impose penalties retroactively3. It may appear that such a provision shall the violate Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India. In case this line of argument is upheld by the court, by application of doctrine of severability, the remainder of the Bill may survive as good law which means that those individuals who fall within the definition of a "Fugitive Economic Offender" on the date of enactment of the Bill may be excluded from penalties under the Bill4.

3.

Process : The Director5 or any authorised officer shall make an application to the Special Court6 for declaring an individual as a Fugitive Economic Offender. The Director or any authorised officer may pass an order attaching the properties as described in the application. Such attachment shall be valid for a period of 180 days from the date of the order.

The Special Court shall serve notice and call upon the said individual to present himself before the Special Court within a stipulated time period. The Special Court may terminate such proceedings if the said individual appears in person within the specified time. However, prescribed time may be provided by the Special Court if the individual seeks to be represented by a counsel. If the Special Court concludes that the individual is a Fugitive Economic Offender, the Special Court is required to record the reasons in writing.

6. Section 73C has been newly introduced by the Finance Act, 2006 and according to it where a proceeding is pending under section 73 or 73A then to protect the interest of the revenue the Central Excise Office can attach the property of the person to whom notice under section 73 or 73A is issued.

Since this is very delicate provision, the Central Excise Officer has to get approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise.

Here it should be noted that section 73 is related to the recovery of service tax and other sum due from any person under the service tax law on account of recovery of service tax not levied or short-levied or short-paid or erroneously refunded.

Section 73A is also newly introduced by, Finance Act, 2006 and is related to recovery of service tax collected by a person when it is not required to be collected or there is excess service tax collection by any person from the recipient of the service.

If the amount due under section 73 or 73A is not paid by the person who is required to pay the same to the Central Government, then the Central Excise Office is empowered to issue a notice to such person; and if during the pendency of proceedings under both these sections, Central Excise Office is of the opinion that to protect the interest of the revenue it is necessary to attach the property of such person, then he can provisionally attach the property of such person with the previous approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise.

How long the provisional attachment will be effective and on which type of property it can be issued ?

7. The provisional attachment can be made of each and every type of property of the person subject to such attachment and it will include all the movable and immovable property of the person subject to such attachment.

Once issued, the attachment order is valid only for the period of 6 months from the date on which is it issued. Though the Chief Commissioner of Central Excise, after recording the reasons in writing of doing so, has the power to extend this period further, and this extension can not go beyond the period to make overall validity of the original attachment order more than 2 years.

Hence, the original provisional attachment order is valid for 6 months from the date of its issuance and the Chief Commissioner can further extend it for 1 year and 6 months so as to make total validity for 2 years.

Brief Introduction

As in case of any new law, emerge new issues and propositions which are ironed out either by legislature through amendments in the statue or through judicial pronouncements. Such an issue was recently faced in respect of cases undergoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) and Liquidation Processes under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC or Code) pertaining to attachment orders passed by the Regulatory Authorities on the assets of Corporate Debtor.

Though Section 238 of the

through multiple orders passed by various benches of Adjudicating Authorities including Appellate Authority (National Company Law Appellate Tribunal) and also by way of amendments in the laws, the Regulatory Authorities still continue to pass provisional or final orders for attachment of the assets of the Corporate Debtor. IPs are then left with the only option to file an application under Section 35(1)(n) of the Code before Adjudicating Authority for seeking necessary direction to get these attached assets released. Bhushan Power and Steel Limited (BPSL) has been among one of the initial twelve cases referred for initiation of CIRP under IBC which has been subject to various litigation due to which the entire resolution process has come to a standstill. The topmost litigation being the attachment of the BPSL assets amounting to Rs. 4025 Crores by Enforcement Directorate (ED) in connection with money laundering investigation initiated under PMLA. The Appellate Authority vide its order dated 14 October 2019 directed ED to immediately release the confiscated assets of BPSL in favour of the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor.

Another plea taken by ED in BPSL case is that Section 32A is prospective and hence, shall not be applicable where the plan is already approved by committee of creditors and Adjudicating Authority prior to the said amendment in the Code. Accordingly, ED again filed an application with Appellate Authority against approval of resolution plan of JSW Steel Limited in BPSL where Appellate Authority in its order dated 17 February 2020 took note of the newly introduced Section 32A and set aside the attachment order passed by ED and granted immunity from prosecution by the ED.

It is rather remarkably interesting to note that by taking this plea of "prospective law" ED is contradicting one of its stands which it adopts in every single case. ED normally pleads that even if an asset is procured before the PMLA Act came into force, the same can still be attached, as it might have been used for laundering the money, i.e. the asset could be a part of the conspiracy for committing the scheduled offence and thus their cannot be an argument or dispute on retrospective or prospective effect.

Although the issue of attachment by the ED has been discussed at length and some clarity already given vide the judgment in Directorate of Enforcement v. Axis Bank, 2019, still the ambiguity remains as even this judgements lays stress on approaching the respective authority for the detachment.

Introduction of Section 32A of the Code

Seeing such anomaly and difficulties in resolving stressed units, Section 32A of the Code was inter-alia introduced by way of an amendment dated 28 December 2019. Section 32A was introduced with the purpose to provide immunity to Corporate Debtor against any offence committed prior to initiation of insolvency proceedings for the Corporate Debtor and to give protection to New Resolution Applicant against any coercive action that could have been taken by the Regulatory Authority in pre-existing scenario. This shall surely induce the Resolution Applicants who were previously targeting the assets of such companies but were afraid to buy-out through resolution process considering legal complexities. This would certainly change the valuation profile of such companies and would benefit the lenders in the long run. It would enable the banks to recover the maximum public money stuck in such companies facing insolvency or liquidation proceedings.

However, despite the amendment in the Code, an air of uncertainty still exists due to which the benefit of Section 32A does not get passed to insolvency process or being availed in scheme for compromise or arrangement as provided under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013. The ED attachment on assets have posed a challenge for the IPs to manage the companies as going concern and liquidate the assets within a reasonable time as per law, especially in absence of any clarity available on the issue. This aggravates the situation further when the bank accounts of the Corporate Debtor are also attached by ED, leaving no cash flows with the IPs to manage the business operations, ultimately resulting in closure of business and deterioration/complete erosion of value of assets. Companies (specifically that are having operations) that undergo liquidation are already facing the liquidity crunch and the IPs make every effort to ensure the Corporate Debtor continues to sustain till it is transferred to a potential applicant at a reasonable value. All the efforts made by the IPs are in consonance with the intent of the Code to revive the Corporate Debtor or to liquidate it through sale of assets lest the delays start affecting business leading to erosion in value.

Adjudicating Authority through its recent judgement in the matter of Varrsana Ispat Limited and REI Agro Limited have provided a wave of relief wherein the Adjudicating Authority allowed the benefit of newly introduced Section 32A of the Code to the liquidator of these companies and allowed him to liquidate the assets. However, at the same time, the order does not vacate the attachment order and instead states that the successful applicant can approach the relevant authority for releasing the assets. Buyers, in most of these cases, don't prefer to indulge in any litigation and that too with ED and want the property title free of such encumbrances.

4. The new section 73C empowers a Central Excise Officer to provisionally attach the property during the pendency of recovery proceedings with prior permission of the Commissioner. The property may be either movable or immovable; the implication of the same is that the assessee cannot dispose of or mortgage or otherwise transfer the property. Section 73D proposes to provide that name of any person and particulars of any proceedings under Chapter V of the Act in relation to such person can be published in public interest. The Act does not spell under what circumstances this power can be exercised. The rules to be framed under section 73D(1) will probably contain such details.

Sub-section (2) of section 73 provides that no publication under this section shall be made in relation to any penalty imposed under this Chapter until the time for presenting an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 85 or the Tribunal under section 86, as the case may be, has expired without an appeal having been presented or the appeal, if presented, has been disposed of.

Section 73(2) provides that a provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of a period of six months though it may be extended up to 2 years by the Chief Commissioner of Central Excise.

This amendment is a departure from the liberal approach, which was practiced so far. On the one hand, the Government wants to promote voluntary compliance and on the other hand it seeks to enact the law of provisional attachment even before the completion of adjudication proceedings. The only silver lining is that the order of attachment has to be approved by highest authorities, i.e., Commissioner or Chief Commissioner, as the case may be. Similarly provisions are already there in other legislation, e.g., section 281B of Income-tax Act, 1961. One only hopes that such provisions will be used sparingly and in extreme cases.

Penalty provisions

The existing section 76 provides that if a person liable to pay service tax fails to pay such tax, he shall be liable, in addition to such tax and interest thereon in accordance with the provision of section 75, to pay a penalty which shall not be less than Rs. 100 for every day during which such failure continues but which may extend to Rs. 200 for every day during which such failure continues subject to maximum of service tax not paid.

In ETA Engg. Ltd. v. CCE, Chennai [1994-2006] STT 613 (Delhi - Cestat), the Larger Bench of the Appellate Tribunal has held that in case of failure to pay service tax, penalty of Rs. 100 per day is to be imposed for every day after the due date as under said section (as was in existence prior to September 10, 2004), words ‘for every day during which such failure continues’ qualify words ‘not less than one hundred rupees but which may extend to two hundred rupees’. The Tribunal further held that if the intention of the Legislature were to impose a penalty of only Rs. 100, then there would have been a comma after words ‘rupees one hundred’.

The Finance Act, 2006 has substituted the existing section 76 with a new section. of a notice on the assessee for provisional attachment. It is pertinent to note that mere issuance of a notice is not a satisfactory performance and the notice must be served on the person for provisional attachment. The notice would provide the name, description, etc., of the property proposed to be attached provisionally and would also make a mention that till the disposal of the proceedings of provisional attachment, the assessee or his authorized agent should not cause the transfer of title or debase the title of such property. u Moreover, the revenue authorities have to comply with all the principles of natural justice before passing an order of attachment even when some of the principles have not been provided specifically by the Act or the Rules. In the case of S.K. Modi v. Union of India 2002 (144) ELT 59 (Delhi), the Hon’ble High Court had held that the principles of natural justice have to be complied with before order of attachment against petitioner could be passed.

u The notice would require the person to make submission as to why his property must not be attached. Such submission would be required to be made within fifteen days of service of such notice.

u The Commissioner would then pass the orders for or against the attachment of the property after considering the submission of the assessee.

u The circular provides certain offences which may be considered for provisional attachment of property. Among others, offences like evasion of tax, short payment of service tax, claiming fraudulent refund or Cenvat credit, etc., have been mentioned.

u The circular also mentions that no proceedings under the Attachment Rules would be initiated in the cases where the service tax or Cenvat credit alleged is less than Rs. 25 Lakhs.

u On receipt of such orders, the Central Excise Officer would proceed with the provisional attachment of the property. It has been specifically mentioned that personal property of the assessee/partners/directors could not be provisionally attached. However, the circular provides that the immovable property used for commercial purpose may be provisionally attached. Thus, if the property is being commercially used (whatever purpose) and not necessarily for the provision of services only, the same could be attached. Thus, in case the service provider has rented out his house or he is carrying on his business from the said property, the Central Excise Officer is free to attach the said property under the Attachment Rules as the same are being commercially used.

u The attachment of the immovable property (where available) must precede the attachment of any movable property. Also, the value of property attached must correspond as nearly as possible to the amount of pending revenue against the assessee. The valuation of properties like land, gold and securities would always be a matter of dispute since their values variate over a period of time.

u The assessee whose property has been provisionally attached should not cause to transfer the title or create a lien of a third party over such property. Having said this, it is important to mention that as is the case in Excise and Customs, in service tax also the secured creditor is entitled to preference over claim of revenue. The same has been upheld in the matter of UTI Bank Ltd. v. Dy. CCE [W.P. No. 39536 of 2005, dated 20-12-2006]. However, contrary to this, the circular provides that in case of provisional attachment, any debts, claims, etc., against the provisional attachment would be void. Thus, on a harmonious reading of both the provisions, it can be construed that any mortgage or any other charge created after the provisional attachment of the property would only be void against such provisional attachment.

u The circular also provides that the provisional attachment should not hamper the business of the assessee. Also, properties as is exempted by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, would also be exempt from provisional attachment under the Attachment Rules.

u Last but not the least, the property remains provisionally attached for a period of six months from the date of service of notice. Post which, an extension must be given for such attachment by the Chief Commissioner of Central Excise (‘Chief Commissioner’). However, the total period of extension by the Chief Commissioner cannot exceed two years.

u The Attachment Rules provide for automatic release of the attached property if the assessee pays the dues with interest.

Thus, though the Attachment Rules empower the Central Excise Officer in relation to provisional attachment of property of an assessee, yet these provisions are not arbitrary and subjective. These provisions must be used only to safeguard the interest of the revenue and are to be enforced in a manner which is rational and not based on mere surmises or suspicion. The Circular has clearly spelt out that with more powers (to Central Excise Officer) comes more responsibility.

The introduction of Section 32A to the IBC has significantly altered the legal landscape by providing statutory immunity to the Corporate Debtor and its assets from prosecution and attachment for prior offences, provided the resolution plan has been approved and management has changed hands.

Some of the below judgments have given paramount importance to section 32A and 238 of the IBC' act- LANDMARK 2025: THE SUPREME COURT'S MANDATE

5.1 Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power & Steel (September 2025)

The Bhushan Power case is perhaps the most significant in IBC history. After JSW Steel acquired BPSL, the ED attached assets worth Rs. 19,000 crores. In 2025, the Supreme Court ruled:

Section 32A is Absolute: Once a resolution plan is approved and the management changes to an unrelated party, the liability of the Corporate Debtor for pre-CIRP offences ceases.

Immunity of Assets: The protection extends to the assets themselves. The ED cannot continue attachments once the NCLT approves a plan.

Jurisdictional Boundary: The Court clarified that while the NCLT cannot "quash" an ED attachment (as it is a criminal law function), the attachment ceases to operate by operation of law upon plan approval

5.2 Directorate of Enforcement v. V Hotels Ltd. (November 2025)-

In this crucial update, the Supreme Court confirmed the setting aside of a Provisional Attachment Order (PAO) after the successful resolution of V Hotels. The Court held that the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA), who steps into the shoes of the debtor as a "clean" entity, cannot have their properties liened by the ED for the sins of the erstwhile management.

Hon'ble Supreme Court held that- "In view of Section 32A of the IBC, the name of the Corporate Debtor shall be deleted from the array of accused in Supplementary Prosecution Complaint dated 12.07.2024 in Spl. Case, while continuing with the prosecution of the erstwhile directors and/or persons in control or conspirators or abettors and confiscation of their attached/restrained properties/entitlements, if any.

Needless to state, the benefit of Section 32A of IBC is subject to the condition that the SRA is neither connected with the erstwhile Directors of the Corporate Debtor nor is the SRA a beneficiary of proceeds of crime derived from the alleged scheduled offence. If this foundation is eroded in the ongoing investigation, the Directorate of Enforcement shall be at liberty to take appropriate steps in accordance with law, including questioning the resolution plan.

In view of the above, any challenge of the Directorate of Enforcement to the approval of the Resolution Plan by the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai, shall stand closed, and accordingly the Directorate of Enforcement shall have no right or lien either on the properties of the Corporate Debtor attached under Provisional Attachment Order."

5.3. Udaipur Entertainment World Private Limited v. Union of India (October' 2025)

The same issue was dealt by the Hon'ble Supreme Court pertaining to restoration of the assets of the corporate debtor with Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) who stepped into the shoes of the Corporate Debtor.

It was held that- "Provisional Attachment passed against the Corporate Debtor is partially set aside and the attached properties are directed to be restored to the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) who stepped into the shoes of the Corporate Debtor solely for the benefit of genuine and innocent home-buyers who subsequently acquired the attached units.

The proposal for confiscation of the properties of the Corporate Debtor shall be substituted with a prayer for confiscation of only those 11 units stated in the additional affidavit dated 7.10.2025 by the DoE, while continuing with prosecution of the erstwhile directors and/or persons in control or conspirators or abettors and confiscation of their attached properties/entitlement, if any."

In the said appeal before NCLAT, following questions were rose pertaining to supremacy of IBC on provisional attachment by PMLA -

ISSUE I: Whether the provisional attachment of assets by the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) under the PMLA violates the moratorium imposed under Section 14 of the IBC?

It was held by the NCLAT that if the property is alleged to be "proceeds of crime" and is already under adjudication by competent authority under a penal statute, such property cannot be deemed to be part of the freely available resolution estate. The PMLA provides its own adjudicatory process and remedy for challenging attachments, which is separate from the IBC. Therefore, the issuance of the PAO by ED under the PMLA does not violate the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC.

ISSUE II: WHETHER THE IBC, BY VIRTUE OF SECTION 238, OVERRIDES THE PMLA IN CASE OF INCONSISTENCY, PARTICULARLY IN THE CONTEXT OF RESOLUTION PROCESSES INVOLVING TAINTED ASSETS

NCLAT held that Crux of this issue lies in a potential conflict between two central legislations viz. the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA). The IBC is a commercial legislation aimed at facilitating time-bound insolvency resolution of financially distressed companies. On the other hand, the PMLA is a penal statute that seeks to identify, attach, and confiscate properties derived from criminal activities such as money laundering.

Section 238 of the IBC is intended to ensure that the objects of the Code are not frustrated by competing statutory provisions. In 'Innoventive Industries Ltd. (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that: Section 238 overrides all other laws, including company law provisions, to the extent of inconsistency. This ensures that once IBC applies, other statutes cannot interfere.

In the present factual matrix, the IBC cannot be said to override the PMLA merely because the ED's attachment interferes with the CIRP. The ED does not act as a creditor, but as a public enforcement agency.

Hon'ble SC in its judgment in Kalyani Transco's case (supra) discussed the powers of NCLAT vis a vis provisions under PMLA 2002.

11. State is a secured creditor for tax purposes under GVAT Act; Section 53 of IBC doesn't override Section 48 of GVAT Act: SC

IBC | State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 157/174 SCL 250 (SC)

In the landmark ruling, the Supreme Court held that the State is a secured creditor for tax purposes under GVAT Act, and Section 53 of IBC doesnot override Section 48 of the GVAT Act.

In the instant case, the following questions were placed before the Supreme Court:

(a)

Is State a secured creditor under IBC for tax purposes under Gujarat VAT (GVAT Act)?

(b)

Whether Section 53 of IBC overrides Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT (GVAT Act) or not?

The Apex Court held that the State is a secured creditor under the GVAT Act. Section 3(30) of the IBC defines the secured creditor as "a creditor in favour of whom security interest is created".

The court further held that such security interest could be created by the operation of law. The definition of a secured creditor in the IBC does not exclude any Government or Governmental Authority. Therefore, the State will be treated as the secured creditor under IBC for tax purposes.

In view of the above, the Supreme Court concluded that State is a secured creditor for VAT under GVAT Act, and Section 53 of IBC doesnot override Section 48 of the GVAT Act.

With regard to the overriding effect of Section 53 of the IBC, it was held that Section 48 of the GVAT Act is not contrary to or inconsistent with Section 53 or any other provisions of the IBC. Section 53 of the IBC deals with the distributions of the asset. As per Section 53, proceeds from the sale of the liquidation assets shall be distributed in the order of priority and within such period as prescribed in the provision.

Under Section 53(1)(b)(ii), the debts owed to a secured creditor, which would include the State under the GVAT Act, shall rank equally with other specified debts, including debts on account of workman's dues for 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date.

The term "Secured Creditor", as defined under the IBC, is comprehensive and wide enough to cover all types of security interests, namely, the right, title, interest or a claim to the property created in favour of or provided for a secured creditor by a transaction, which secures payment or performance of an obligation and includes mortgage, charge, hypothecation, assignment and encumbrance or any other agreement or arrangement securing payment or performance of any obligation of any person.

In view of the statutory charge in terms of Section 48 of the GVAT Act, the claim of the tax department of the State squarely falls within the definition of "Security Interest" under Section 3(31) of the IBC, and the State becomes a secured creditor under Section 3(30) of the Code.

In the above case the High Court examined the issue of attachment of properties under PMLA which were purchased by accused out of the loans extended by nationalized banks. The High Court noted that PMLA seeks to punish the offenders as well as victims., as the wordings in Sec. 8 (6) and Sec. 9 which seeks to punish the victims of crime along with the accused. 5.3 By virtue of Sec. 8(8) inserted under the Finance Act, 2015 with effect from 14th May 2015 the Special Court is empowered to direct the Central Government to restore the property/part thereof confiscated, to a claimant who has legitimate interest in the property and who has suffered a quantifiable loss as a result of money laundering. However such restoration is subject to satisfaction of Special Court that the Claimant has acted in good faith and not involved in money laundering. As per 2nd proviso to Sec. 8(8) inserted w.e.f 19.4.2018 such restoration can also be claimed before Special Court during trial. After the judgment of the Hon'ble Madras High Court in the Indian Bank case supra, (rendered in July 2012) sufficient safeguards have been brought into the statute to protect innocent/bonafide parties such as bankers who had given loan on the mortgaged properties which were alleged to be involved in money laundering and treated as proceeds of crime.

6. Conclusion

6.1 In terms of the decision of Hon'ble Delhi High Court, the secured creditors such as Bankers cannot seek release of attached properties on the ground that the same would fall under the sweep of " proceeds of crime". In the proceedings relating to provisional attachment it is left open for the Defendants to raise other factual issues, on case to case basis, to defend that that properties attached are not proceeds of crime.. Also, the relief for the bankers/secured creditors against confirmation of provisional attachment is not before the Adjudicating Authority or under Sec. 26 before the Appellate Tribunal, but before the Special Court in terms of provisions contained under Sec.8 (8).

6.2 Though the victims of crime (such as bankers) whose interest is to be protected on one hand, the intention of PMLA is to confiscate the proceeds of crime arising out of scheduled crime. If the properties acquired out of loan from bank are not treated as proceeds of crime, it would facilitate the gullible offenders/launderers to mortgage the properties derived out of proceeds of scheduled offence with banks/financial institutions, to avoid confiscation. In the money laundering process of layering and integration, proceeds of crime are often intermingled with immovable properties by undervaluing the transaction, and diverting a portion of the proceeds of crime

of section 29A7.

Conflicting interests other regulatory and statutory authorities.

6. The statutory bodies find themselves at the bottom of the waterfall mechanism when it comes to recovering their share of the pie. More often than not, there have been instances where either the bank accounts or the tangible assets of Corporate Debtor are seized prior to commencement of CIRP and they refuse to release upon requests of the RP. In such cases, it makes things worse for the RP to find a prospective bidder. Although Section 31 of the Code, make it clear the resolution plan is binding on all stakeholders, it's not a welcomed by tax authorities, PF authorities etc., since they interested for recovery of their dues under the powers vested under their respective statutes.

In a recent judgment dated 26 July 2018 passed by Division Bench of the Hyderabad High Court in case of A WP bearing no. 8560 of 2018, filed by Leo Edibles & Fats Limited against the Tax Recovery Officer (Central), Income Tax Department, Hyderabad, with regard to the action of the Sub-Registrar, refusing to register its purchase of immovable property due to the attachment, in the liquidation proceedings relating to VNR Infrastructures Limited.

The Court held that

"Tax Recovery Officer cannot claim any priority merely because of the fact that the order of attachment was issued by him was long prior to the initiation of liquidation proceedings under the Code against VNR Infrastructures Limited, Hyderabad. It may be noted that Section 36(3)(b) of the Code indicates in no uncertain terms that the liquidation estate assets may or may not be in possession of the corporate debtor, including but not limited to encumbered assets. Therefore, even if the order of attachment constitutes an encumbrance on the property, it still does not have the effect of taking it out of the purview of Section 36(3)(b) of the Code. The said order of attachment therefore cannot be taken to be a bar for completion of the sale and the Tax Officer to submit claim before Liquidator as and when the distribution of the assets, in terms of Section 53(1) of the Code, is taken up…".

IBBI ought to consider this practical aspect and we should soon expect a clear notification asking all the statutory bodies to release its attachment/freeze orders over the assets of the CD once the CIRP commences and file their claims with the RP as per the provisions of the Code rather than creating hindrances while the RP is running against time to resolve the financial crisis.

Conclusion

7. Apart from enactment of IBC Code and amendments which follow, the Government is constantly putting its best efforts to resolve the NPA situation of the country, starting with RBI's circular of February this year that mandated the banks to report a bad loan to RBI even for a single day default. The recent Inter-Creditor Agreement, a part of Project Sashakt, recommended by Sunil Mehta-led committee, would also help to resolve stressed assets situation by adopting a fast track approach, if 66 per cent of the lenders in a consortium, for loans of Rs. 50-500 crore, agree to implementation of Resolution Plan for a stressed account within 180 days even before it hits the doors of NCLT. Such reforms would provide a breather to both banks and promoters from the tough bankruptcy code.

Finally, a clear message that emanates from the fact that India jumped 30 places in the list of "Ease of Doing Business" due to the introduction of IBC. We foresee funds being freed for the lenders for fresh infusion in markets which would eventually lead to growth in GDP. It is expected to lead to better financial environment for businesses to revive and thrive under the wings of new management with fresh aims and financial support to reach them.
