What emerges from the record is that there is admitted liability of approximately of Rs.50 lakhs of tax by the assessee. Admittedly no returns are filed, nor such tax is paid. At least, such amount, the assessee must deposit with the authorities immediately only then the assessee can seek any discretionary relief from the Court. [Para 2]

Considering the facts and circumstances, the attachment of the assessee's bank accounts required to be lifted subject to deposit of a sum of Rs. 50 lakhs towards possible tax and penalty. The assessee was also directed to file an undertaking as provided in the judgment. [Para 3]

The property that can be attached

4. (1) The provisional attachment of property shall be to the extent it requires to protect the interest of revenue, that is to say, the value of property attached shall be of value as nearly as may be equivalent to that of the amount of pending revenue against such person.

(2) The movable property belonging to such person shall be attached only if the immovable property available for attachment is not sufficient to protect the interest of revenue.

The only question that falls for consideration is whether the Competent Authority was justified in invoking section 83 for the purpose of passing an order of attachment of the bank accounts. [Para 22]

Without entering into any other controversy, the Court is inclined to allow the writ application on the short ground that during the period between July, 2017 and May, 2019, the total input tax credit availed by the assessee aggregates to Rs. 59.49 crores; whereas the total tax paid during this period aggregates to Rs. 63.62 crores. The same is indicative of the fact that against the availment of credit of Rs. 59.49 crores, an amount of Rs. 63.62 crores came to be paid by way of tax. It appears that an amount of Rs. 4.13 crores has been paid in excess than the amount of credit availed. In such circumstances, it cannot be said that the interest of the Government revenue is at a stake. [Para 23]

Even if it is assumed that the allegation as levelled by the Competent Authority is correct and the credits though not available were wrongly availed of. Since the tax had been paid, though it was not payable having regard to the fact that there was no supply of goods, the availment of credits could be said to be justified on two counts: (1) it is a revenue neutral satisfaction, and (2) payment of tax although not payable yet is to be treated if unavailable credits are reversed if they were wrongly paid. [Para 24]

Section 83 empowers the Competent Authority to make a provisional attachment of any property of the assessee during the pendency of any proceeding for the assessment or reassessment of any turnover, even though there is no demand outstanding against the assessee, if he is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so to protect the interest of the revenue. This proivsion has been made in order to protect the interest of the revenue in cases where the raising of demand is likely to take time because of the investigations and there is apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand. In other words, section 83 gives a power to be exercised during the pendency of any proceeding for assessment or reassessment, so that the assessee may not fitter away or secrete his resources out of the reach of the department when the assessment or reassessment is completed.

The expression 'for the purpose of protecting the interest of the revenue' occuring in section 83 is very wide in its meaning. Further the orders of provisional attachment must be in writing. There must be some material on record to indicate that the Competent Authority had formed an opinion on the basis thereof that it was necessary to attach the property in order to protect the interest of the revenue. The provisional attachment provided under section 83 is more like an attachment before judgment under the Code of Civil Procedure. It is a liabiilty on the property. However, the power conferred upon the Competent Authority under section 83 is very drastic far-reaching power and that power has to be used sparingly and only on substantive weighty grounds and for valid reasons. To ensure that this power is not miused, no safeguards have been provideed in section 83. One thing is clear that this power should be exercised by the Authority only if there is a reasonable apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand that is likely to be raised on completion of the assessment. It should, therefore, be exercised with extreme care and circumspection. It should not be exercised unless there is sufficient material on record to justify the satisfaction that the assessee is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property with a view to thwarting the ultimate collection of the demand. Moreover attachment should be made of the properties and to the extent it is required to achieve the above object. It should neither be used as a tool to harass the assessee nor should it be used in a manner which may have an irreversible determinetal effect on the business of the assessee. [Para 28]

In view of the aforesaid, the order of provisional attachment of the bank accounts of the assessee required to be quashed and set aside. [Para 30]

With respect to the collection of three cheques, the action of the department cannot be countenanced. It has been held by the Court and other High Courts of the country that the practice of collecting post-dated cheques under coercion during raid is not permissible means of collection of revenue particularly, when no tax demand has been confirmed or crystallized. [Para 7]

In the instant case, there does not appear to be any justification of the departmental authorities to collect and the petitioners to voluntarily give cheques for the said amount. Therefore, the department is directed to return such cheques. [Para 8]

Chapter XV of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act pertains to demands and recovery. Section 73 contained in the said chapter pertains to the determination of tax unpaid or short paid or erroneously refunded or input tax credit wrongly availed or utilized for any reason other than fraud or wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. This section, thus, provides the procedure for determination of tax which has remained unpaid on the ground other than fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Section 74 on the other hand, pertains to determination of tax unpaid or short paid or erroneously refunded or input tax credit wrongly availed or utilized by reason of fraud or any wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. [Para 10]

In clear terms, powers under sub-section (3) of section 74 would be available where notice has already been issued against the person chargeable with tax under sub-section (1) and the statement referred to in sub-section (3) of section 74 would be containing the details of tax unpaid, short paid etc. for purpose other than those covered under sub-section (1). In other words, powers under sub-section (3) of section 74 cannot be exercised for expanding or enlarging the liability arising out of show-cause notice under sub-section (1) from the same period. Essentially, sub-sections (1) and (3)of section 74 are envisaged to cover separate periods. [Para 11]

In that view of the matter, the respondents are wholly incorrect in issuing a fresh show-cause notice for the same period of July 2017 to 20-02-2018, which notice was already issued under sub-section (1) of section 74 purportedly under exercising powers to suggest that once a notice has been issued under sub-section (1) of section 74, if the authorities find that the liability of tax, interest or penalty larger than one indicated in the statement referred to in sub-section (1) is likely to arise, the competent authority is remedy-less. However, his remedy does not lie in issuing second notice under sub-section (3) of section 74. The impugned notice dated 19-3-2018 therefore, shall have to be quashed. [Para 12]

As regards last surviving question of attachment of bank accounts, as per the departmental authorities, the petitioners had not paid GSTs on branded goods. The tax liability would be Rs. 36,88,706. There could be possible interest and penalty liability on such tax amount. It prima facie appears that the department had issued second show-cause notice dated 19-03-2017 (which is proposed to be quashed) including even the unbranded goods for recovery of GSTs. Having perused the relevant literature, even otherwise it is found that GSTs on unbranded goods has been specifically exempted. As of now, thus, only notice for recovery of tax that survives is one seeking to recover GSTs of Rs. 30 lacs approximately with interest and penalty. At the same time, one must also realize that if the petitioners are not correct in contending that no service tax can be levied on branded goods because the brand belongs to the directors of the company, such liability may eventually arise with interest and matching penalty. [Para 13]

Under sub-section (1) of section 83, the competent authority has power of provisional attachment, where during pendency of any proceedings under the Act he is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of government revenue, it is necessary so to do. Such provisional attachment could be of any property including the bank account of the taxable person. Sub-section (2) of section 83, however, provided that every such provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of a period of one year from the date of which such order has been made. [Para 15]

In the instant case, nothing is demonstrated by the department either in the orders of attachment or in the affidavit filed. The reason why exercise of such drastic power of attachment of bank accounts was necessary. Therefore, such attachments are set aside. At the same time, some security is provided so that eventually, if the tax liability is confirmed, the department is not left with no means to recover the same. [Para 16]

Mere apprehension on the part of the revenue authorities that huge tax demands are likely to be raised on completion of assessment is not sufficient for the purpose of passing a provisional order of attachment. Apart from the fact that a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution of India challenging the provisional attachment order was maintainable, having regard to the fact that the provisional attachment order of a property of a taxable person including the bank account of such person is draconian in nature and the conditions which are prescribed by the statute for the valid exercise of power must be strictly fulfilled. The exercise of power for order of provisional attachment must necessarily be preceded by formation of an opinion by the authorities that it is necessary to do so for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue. Before the order of provisional attachment, the commissioner must form an opinion on the basis of tangible material available for attachment that the assessee is not likely to fulfil the demand payment of tax and it is therefore necessary to do so for the purpose of protecting the Government revenue. [Para 8]

In the instant case, except for merely stating that since there is likelihood of huge tax payments to be raised on completion of assessment and that for the purpose of protecting the revenue, other mandatory requirements and pre-condition have neither been complied with nor fulfilled or followed prior to passing the order. It is apparent that the impugned provisional attachment orders do not satisfy the legal requirements and, consequently, in view of the fact that the impugned provisional orders are cryptic, unreasoned, non-speaking and laconic same deserve to be quashed. [Para 9]

In the light of the undisputed fact that the proceedings under section 153A have already been initiated coupled with the fact that section 281 contemplates that any alienation of any property belonging to the petitioners would be null and void, in addition to the specific assertion made by the petitioner that they own and possess immovable property to the tune of more than Rs. 300 crores, the apprehension of the revenue that in the event huge tax payments are to be raised as against the petitioners-assessee, the assessee may not make payment of the same causing loss to the revenue, is clearly unfounded and without any basis and consequently the said apprehension of the respondents cannot be accepted. [Para 10]

Writ petition of assessee is allowed and provisional attachment order by revenue under section 281B are quashed [Para 11]

On a bare perusal of the CGST Act, 2017, it is absolutely clear that Section 3 equates the 'Principal Commissioner of Central Tax' as the "Principal Additional Director of Central Tax' and the "Commissioner of Central Tax' as the 'Additional Director General of Central Tax'. One need not quibble with the wording as the meaning is plain and unambiguous. Furthermore, the fresh orders of provisional attachment has been passed by 'Principal Additional Director of Central Tax' who is the superior officer and therefore, as per Section 5(2) of the CGST Act, 2017 she possesses the power to pass the provisional attachment orders under Section 83. (Para 7)

As regards the issue of attachment of bank accounts of petitioners it is held that the authorities have acted in a blatantly highhanded and illegal manner by keeping the provisional attachments in a state of continuance for the period from 5-6- 2019 (when the first order of provisional attachment ceases to operate) till 3-10-2019 (when fresh order for provisional attachment was passed). Section 83(2) is crystal clear that the provisional attachment shall cease upon expiry of one year. It was ,therefore, incumbent on the authorities to either release the provisional attachment by informing the bank or by issuing a fresh order of provisional attachment, if the law so allowed. The failure to do the above is nothing short of being an act of highhandedness. Such actions of the authorities is an obloquy and reprehensible. No explanation has been provided for the same either in the affidavits filed in the earlier writ petitions or by the respondent authorities during hearing of arguments. Such action is clearly in violation of the petitioners' rights for carrying on business under Article 19(1) of the Constitution of India and under Article 300A of the Constitution of India wherein the petitioners have been deprived of their property without authority of law. The Revenue in acting in contravention of Section 83(2) is condemnable, and accordingly costs are required to be imposed. In light of the same, the concerned respondent authorities are directed to pay costs of Rs. 5 Lakhs to each of the three petitioner companies. These amounts should be deposited in the current account that are provisionally attached. (Para 11)

The interpretation of Section 83 of the CGST Act, 2017 is not based on the facts that have been presented by the respondents in their affidavits, but on the legal principles of interpretation of fiscal statutes and examination of the precedents cited by parties. It is opined that the powers conferred under Section 83 are drastic and extraordinary in nature. The Court also believes that the powers under this section should not be invoked routinely and must be exercised with due caution, circumspection and deliberation. (Para 28)

It is to be noted that Section 83 does not have a provision for extension of an order for provisional attachment. The contention in instant case is with respect to issue of fresh order of provisional attachment and not extension of the same. (Para 30)

Section 83 has to be construed literally and strictly. On a perusal of Section 83, it is evident that Section 83 does not provide for an extension of an order for provisional attachment and any such extension shall be dehors the statute. Section 83 empowers the competent authority to issue an order for provisional attachment of property including bank accounts if it is of the opinion that such a step is necessary for protecting the interest of government revenue. It is palpably clear that Section 83(2) permits continuation of a provisional attachment order for a period of one year from the date of order after which it ceases to remain in effect. However, there is nothing in the section which indicates that upon completion of the prescribed period, a fresh order cannot be issued. To say this would amount to supplying such requirements into the section which would go against the well-established principles of interpretation of statutes. In the view point of the Court, after the expiry of the time period, the appropriate authority may be of the opinion that such an attachment is further required to protect the interest of government revenue, and may therefore, issue a fresh order upon compliance of the formalities in Section 83(1). (Para 31)

Introduction

Money laundering is a felony, which, per se, is not new to the world. Given its nature, it is essential to have written law in place, which should be amended, time and again, to adequately deal with the on-going changes in the economical environment. In India, the enactment of Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 ('PMLA') was a remarkable and important step towards ensuring the same. Since its initial introduction, the law has undergone various amendments over the years. The Interim Budget for 2019-2020 has made several changes in enactments, which also include changes in PMLA. The amendment is part of the Finance Bill, 20191, and is yet to be notified.

PMLA is a comprehensive law which deals with all the major aspects of money laundering, which includes defining what constitutes as money laundering, the process of attachment and adjudication, management of confiscated properties, obligations on reporting entities like banks and financial institutions, etc.

Background to the amendment

Chapter III of the PMLA deals with "Attachment, Adjudication and Confiscation". Section 5 under the Chapter, gives powers to the Director or Deputy Director (appointed authority under PMLA by the Central Government) to provisionally attach the property in case he has reason to believe that the property is involved in money laundering. This is an interim action which prevents any likelihood of further transfer of/ or launder of property or money. The initial attachment is merely allowed for a period of 90 days.

The aforesaid complaint is transferred to the Adjudicating Authority (AA), which further investigates the matter in accordance with the provisions of section 8 of PMLA. At this stage, it is pertinent to understand the definitions of 'attachment' and 'investigation'; both the expressions are defined as under:

"attachment" means prohibition of transfer, conversion, disposition or movement of property by an order issued under Chapter III.

"investigation" includes all the proceedings under this Act conducted by the Director or by an authority authorised by the Central Government under this Act for the collection of evidence.

While attachment is an act to stop any movement of the property, investigation is a lawful process, which allows collection of evidence of money laundering, leading to punishment and confiscation. If on investigation, the AA concludes that the property is involved in money laundering, it shall confirm the continuation of the provisional attachment, which becomes final after the final order of confiscation is passed by the court.

Text prior to amendment

Section 8(3)(a)

(3) Where the Adjudicating Authority decides under sub-section (2) that any property is involved in money-laundering, he shall, by an order in writing, confirm the attachment of the property made under sub-section (1) of section 5 or retention of property or [record seized or frozen under section 17 or section 18 and record a finding to that effect, whereupon such attachment or retention or freezing of the seized or frozen property] or record shall—

(a)

continue during investigation for a period not exceeding ninety days or the pendency of the proceedings relating to any offence under this Act before a court or under the corresponding law of any other country, before the competent court of criminal jurisdiction outside India, as the case may be; and

(b)

become final after an order of confiscation is passed under sub-section (5) or sub-section (7) of section 8 or section 58B or sub-section (2A) of section 60 by the Special Court.

Post amendment

The amendment has substituted the words 'ninety days' with 'three hundred and sixty five days'. While the amendment seems minor, it actually extends the time period of attachment by a total of 275 days. Resultantly, the attachment shall continue for one year during pendency of proceedings before a criminal court, under PMLA or a corresponding foreign law.

While the provisional attachment period remains unchanged, extending the attachment period before final confiscation, gives the authorities increased time in hand to deal with a given case. With the increased number of cases of money laundering, this is a relief for the authorities investigating matters under PMLA.

Additionally, the amendment inserts explanation to sub-section (3) above; accordingly, the aforesaid period of 365 days shall exclude any period for which the respective investigation is stayed by any court of law. Since investigation is construed to be ineffective while it is stayed, and the number of attachment days is calculated in reference to the investigation, the period of stay should be excluded.

Conclusion

In essence, the amendment adds flexibility to the proceedings under PMLA and gives more time to the authorities, which can be invested into finding relevant evidence and records.

the issue arises whether cash for cash will be consideration for each other. The answer is yes. For example, one is giving high value denomination currency notes to another to get currency notes of small denomination; giving cash to another to keep it in safe custody for some particular period (under apprehension of raid or anything) and to return on demand; to change the demonetized currency notes to new currency notes; loan with or without interest etc. The commission or service charge for such transactions is immaterial . Therefore, where cash is involved, one cannot segregate the word 'consideration' in the form of cash, from the word 'property' in the form of cash. Hence, under this situation both the words consideration and property stand merged with each other and are interchangeable. In the present case, the cash was provided by the appellant to Vikramjeet Ram. Even otherwise, said cash was deposited by the benamidar Vikramjeet in his bank accounts which was given by the appellant company and at this stage of transition, the cash of appellant becomes consideration and the amount held in the bank account of the benamidar Vikramjeet Ram becomes the property. Therefore, both the parts of clause (a) are discernible. Now, coming to clause (b), which is also covered in the present case, as the said amount from the bank account of benamidar was later-on transferred to the account of appellant company, on different dates. It is immaterial whether the said property is held for a sufficient long period or immediately transferred after serving the purpose. The fact that property is re-transferred to the beneficial owner after completion of the purpose for which it was given to benamidar, the provisions of the PBPT Act are clearly attracted and it does not exonerate any party to the benami transaction. As the value of the Benami Transaction was for the sum of Rs. 85.19 lakhs, the respondent can attach the account for the said sum, irrespective of the available balance on the date of passing the attachment order. In view of the above discussion, issue no (iv) to (vi) are decided against the appellant and in favour of respondent. [Para 9]

The argument raised by the assessee is meritorious. The bank accounts of an assessee are provisionally attached to secure the interest of the revenue pending assessment proceedings to meet the eventuality of demand of tax to be raised against such assessee. Once the assessment has been completed, the revenue would be justified to attach the account to the extent of demand raised against an assessee and not the entire amount standing to the credit of the assessee. The action of the revenue in extending the period of attachment in respect of all the bank accounts of the assessee is wholly unjustified and illegal. [Para 4]

Consequently, the present writ petition is allowed and the respondents are directed to release provisional attachment except to the extent of tax demand raised against the assessee. Such tax demand shall not be realized till such time, the appeal filed by the assessee is not decided by the competent authority. [Para 5]

The above acts/omissions shall entail proceedings under section 73 or 73A which may be followed by attachment of property under section 73C. (ii) Is there any threshold limit for invoking attachment provision ? - Neither section 73C nor the Rules lay down any threshold limit for initiating attachment proceedings. However, the CBEC’s Circular No. 103/06/2008-ST, dated July 1, 2008, provides that it should be resorted to only in a case where the service tax or CENVAT credit alleged to be involved is more than Rs. 25 lakh.

(iii) Against whom can the provisions of attachment be invoked ? - As per section 73C, provisional attachment can be ordered in respect of any property belonging to a person on whom a notice has been served under section 73(1) or 73A(3). It may be noted that under section 73(1), a notice can be served on the person chargeable with the service tax which has not been levied or paid or which has been short-levied or short-paid or the person to whom service tax has been erroneously refunded, whereas, a notice under section 73A(3) can be served on - (1) a person liable to pay service tax who has collected any amount in excess of the service tax assessed or determined and paid on any taxable service from the recipient of the taxable service, or (2) any person who has collected any amount as service tax, which is not required to be collected, from any other person.

(iv) Which property can be attached under the provision of service tax ? - As noted in FAQ 3, provisional attachment under section 73C can be ordered in respect of any ‘property’ belonging to the specified person. Rule 2(c) of the Rules defines the term ‘property’ to include immovable property. Further, rule 4(2) of the Rules provides that movable property shall be attached only if the immovable property is not sufficient to protect the interest of revenue.

The CBEC, vide its circular dated July 1, 2008, has clarified that immovable property/properties which is/are used for commercial purpose may be provisionally attached.

(v) Can personal property(ies) of proprietor/partner(s)/ director(s) be also attached ? - As per proviso to rule 3(3) of the Rules, personal property of proprietor or partners or directors, as the case may be, shall not be attached. As per rule 2(d), ‘personal property’ means any movable or immovable property belonging to a proprietor or partner or director, which is not in relation to business activity.

Accordingly, the CBEC in its circular dated July 1, 2008 has also clarified that any movable or immovable property which is in personal use of the sole proprietor/partner/director cannot be attached.

(vi) What shall be the extent of attachment ? - In terms of rule 4(1), the provisional attachment of property shall be to the extent it requires to protect the interest of revenue. In other words, the value of property attached shall be as nearly as may be equivalent to that of the amount of ‘pending revenue’.

The term ‘pending revenue’ is defined under rule 2(b) to mean "any service tax that has not been levied or paid or has been short-levied or paid or erroneously refunded in respect of which a notice has been served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A". Thus, the term ‘pending revenue’ refers to the amount demanded in the proceedings under section 73 or 73A.

(vii) What can be the possible justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary ? - If the Central Excise Officer reasonably believes that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, any of his property(ies) liable to attachment, it can be considered as sufficient justification necessitating attachment of property. The belief must, however, be based on substantial grounds.

(viii) What precautions should the Central Excise Officer take before initiating attachment proceedings ? - Although section 73C and the Provisional Attachment of Property Rules, are both silent in this regard, the CBEC has in its circular dated July 1, 2008, stated emphatically that the remedy of attachment is of extraordinary nature and should be resorted to in the utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution. There should be sufficient justification to hold the view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interests of revenue. The Central Excise Officer should, in his proposal for attachment, clearly state the grounds on which he entertains the reasonable belief that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, the property and the sources of his information, if any.

The circular further states that appropriate disciplinary action shall be initiated against the officers who may be found to have exercised the powers of provisional attachment of property frivolously and without sound reasons.

The order revoking the provisional attachment shall be made within the following time limit : 11.5-1 Circumstances in which the guarantee may be invoked

The AO may invoke the guarantee in following situations:

(a)

Where a notice of demand specifying a sum payable is served upon the assessee and the assessee fails to pay that sum within the time specified in the notice of demand, the AO may invoke the guarantee, wholly or in part, to recover the amount.

(b)

If the assessee fails to renew the guarantee, the AO shall in the interest of the revenue invoke the bank guarantee. He shall invoke it 15 days before the expiry of the guarantee.

(c)

If the assessee fails to furnish a new guarantee from a scheduled bank for an equal amount, the AO shall, in the interest of the revenue invoke the bank guarantee 15 days before the expiry of the guarantee.

11.5-2 Utilisation of the amount realised by invoking the guarantee

The amount realised by invoking the guarantee shall be first adjusted against the existing demand which is payable by the assessee.

The balance amount if any shall be deposited in the personal deposit account of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner in the branch of any of the following banks:

(a)

RBI;

(b)

SBI;

(c)

Any subsidiary of SBI;

(d)

Any bank as may be appointed by RBI as its agent under section 45(1) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

Such account shall be at the place where the office of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner is situate.

11.5-3 Release of guarantee

Where the AO is satisfied that the guarantee is not required anymore to protect the interests of the revenue, he shall release that guarantee forthwith.

11.5-4 Acceptance of guarantee is mandatory

Once the assessee furnishes the guarantee satisfying the aforesaid conditions the AO is bound to revoke the attachment. This is because section 281B(3) provides that the AO 'shall' by an order in writing revoke such attachment.

11.5-5 Satisfied

The AO has to be 'satisfied' that the guarantee for an amount lower than the FMV is sufficient.

The term 'satisfied' has been explained as follows:

It is not the personal whim, wish, view or opinion or the ipse dixit of the President de hors the material but a legitimate inference drawn from the material placed before him which is relevant for the purpose. In other words, the President has to be convinced of or has to have sufficient proof of information with regard to or has to be free from doubt or uncertainty about the state of things indicating that the situation in question has arisen [S. R. Bommai v. UOI AIR 1994 SC 1918/[1994] 1 SCC 3 (SC)].

However, once he is satisfied it appears that he has no discretion not to reduce the amount of guarantee.

11.5-6 Opportunity of being heard

The section does not provide for any opportunity of being heard to the assessee before the guarantee is invoked. In this connection the observations of the Supreme Court in Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 300 ITR 403/169 Taxman 328 are apposite :

"If the statute conferring the power is silent with regard to the giving of a pre-decisional hearing to the person affected and the administrative decision taken by the authority involves civil consequences of a grave nature, and no full review or appeal on merits against that decision is provided, courts will be extremely reluctant to construe such a statute as excluding the duty of affording even a minimal hearing, shorn of all its formal trappings and dilatory features at the pre-decisional stage, unless, viewed pragmatically, it would paralyse the administrative process or frustrate the need for utmost promptitude. In short, this rule of fair play must not be jettisoned save in very exceptional circumstances where compulsive necessity so demands. The court must make every effort to salvage this cardinal rule to the maximum extent possible, with situational modifications. But, the core of it must, however, remain, namely, that the person affected must have reasonable opportunity of being heard and the hearing must be a genuine hearing and not an empty public relations exercise." (p. 666).

It is a moot point whether the aforesaid observations would be applicable before the invocation of the guarantee.

11.5-7 Direct acceptance of guarantee is not possible

The section envisages the situation where the assets are first attached and then a guarantee is accepted in lieu of the assets attached. It does not envisage a situation of acceptance of bank guarantee at the first stage itself without attachment of assets.

In P. Ezhilpandian v. K. Vikash, DCIT [2018] 100 taxmann.com 182 (PBPTA - AT), the facts of the case were that the appellant was an employee and was acting as librarian and sports coordinator of a college run by a Trust. In course of search of the Trust, it was found that the Chairman has given Rs. 15 lakhs in cash to the appellant to organize a football match. Accordingly, the same amount was handed over to Foot Ball Association. This amount was given during demonetization period. At the instance of the department the said amount was collected back and handed over to the department. The IO assumed that the said amount was given to the appellant in the guise of a loan in demonetized currency and to pay the same back subsequently in new currency. Accordingly, IO issued notice under section 24(1) despite the fact that the Trust confirmed that the amount was given to employee to handover same to Football Association for organizing a match. The IO disbelieved the same and issued provisional attachment notice under section 24(3) attaching the bank account of the employee. On basis of these facts, the Appellate Tribunal held as under:-

The appellant was only a facilitator to carry the cash to be handed over to the Football Association.

He was never the owner of the cash as a benamidar.

He had not deposited the cash in the bank which was provisionally attached by the IO without taking into account the facts of the case.

In fact, while attaching the bank account, no property existed which the appellant can alienate.

It was observed that there was no reason to believe by application of mind to the facts of the case while attaching the bank account. Notice was issued in a mechanical manner.

It was observed that every cash transaction cannot be termed as a benami transaction unless the transaction squarely falls under the stipulations of section 2(9)(A), satisfying the twin conditions: firstly, the property being held by a person who has not provided the consideration; secondly, the property is held by that person for the immediate or future benefit, direct or indirect of the person who has provided the said consideration.

The burden of proof of existence of a benami transaction lies on the authorities i.e. the person who alleges that transaction is benami as held in the case of Sitaram Agarwal v. Subrata Chandra [2008] 7 SCC 716.

The order of Adjudicating Authority confirming the order of the IO was set aside.

"We are informed that under administrative circulars, amounts which were not to be appropriated to the revenue are held in personal deposit account to be kept in the name of certain officers, including TRO. ATTACHMENT AND CONFISCATION

Attachment of property is one of the modes of execution of a decree in a civil suit. Failure to pay the decretal amount in the execution of its decree, the Court may resort to attachment of the movable and immovable property and recover the amount which is due to the decree-holder by the disposal of attached assets. It is a measure of safe guarding the interest of the decree holder. Sections 60 to Section 64 and Rules 41-57 of Order 21 of CPC 1908, deals with the procedure of attachment of property. Under Section 2(5) of PBPT Act, 1988 "attachment" means the prohibition of transfer, conversion, disposition or movement of property, by an order issued under the Act. This power of confiscation is vested the Adjudicating Authority under section 27(1). The distinction between the two is that a provisional attachment can be made by the Competent Authorities under benami law in anticipation that the benamidar may alienate the benami property before finalization of the proceeding. Provisional attachment and subsequent confiscation are limited to benami property only. It does not amount to disposition of a property till final order under section 27(1) is passed in a benami proceeding, subject to order of Appellate Tribunal. On the other hand, confiscation relates to a legal form of seizure of the benami property by the State without payment of any compensation. It is a measure of penalty. Under benami law, confiscation follows provisional attachment and final adjudication.

1. Applicability

This is a prospective law made applicable from 21st February 2019. It would apply to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir. For all the deposits before 21st February 2019, the regulatory framework at that point of time would continue to apply.

2. Targeting Unregulated Deposit Schemes

UDS contains a substantive banning clause which bans Deposit Takers from promoting, operating, issuing advertisements or accepting deposits in any Deposit Taking Scheme which is not regulated. The principle is crystal clear that this Ordinance bans unregulated deposit taking activities altogether, by making them an offence ex-ante, rather than the existing legislative-cum-regulatory framework which only comes into effect ex-post with considerable time lags.

People of the western regions of the country may not understand and appreciate the importance of this law. But when we see the investment patterns of the households of the southern region of the country and even some eastern parts, the investment in such deposit schemes like chit funds are huge. And these marginal and gullible investors are the real victims of the illicit deposit schemes.

3. Prescribed Offences

The Ordinance broadly prescribes three different types of offences and prescribes severe punishment and heavy pecuniary fines for the same. The offences are –

Running of Unregulated Deposit Schemes;

Wrongful inducement in relation to Unregulated Deposit Schemes; and

Fraudulent default in Regulated Deposit Schemes.

4. Administrative Segment

The Central Government will establish an online database for maintaining records of deposit takers. All the deposit takers pan-India have to provide the information on the database portal regularly. Time and form of reporting has not been prescribed yet. This online portal once made accessible to all, people can verify the genuineness of the deposit takers and substantially reduce the flow of money to illicit deposit schemes. Further, any violation of provisions related to reporting on online database by deposit takers would invite penalty of up to INR 10L.

Deposit takers covered under Regulated Deposit Schemes are allowed to accept and solicit for obtaining deposits. However, any fraudulent default in repayment or servicing of deposits would invite fine of higher of INR 5L; INR 25 cr.; or thrice the amount of profits made on such default. This will be in addition to imprisonment which may extend to 7 years.

Unregulated Deposits have been declared an offence ex-ante. In case where unregulated deposits vide any schemes are still raised, the law provides for attachment of assets and subsequent realisation of assets for repayment to depositors. Introduction

The Supreme Court's recent judgment in National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL) v. Union of India & Ors (Writ Petition (Civil) No. 995 of 2019) is a landmark in the domain of financial fraud litigation and asset recovery. The decision, delivered on 15 May 2025, addresses the complex interplay between the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (MPID) Act, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), and central statutes such as the SARFAESI Act, Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act (RDB Act), and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

At its core, this decision represents a careful recalibration of the legal hierarchy between secured creditors, government agencies, and public interest protections in cases involving tainted assets.

Background: The NSEL Scam and Legal Tangle

NSEL, a commodity trading platform promoted by 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. The collapse of the National Spot Exchange in 2013 triggered a Rs. 5,600 crore default, affecting about 13,000 traders and investors. The fallout led to multiple FIRs, civil suits, and the attachment of assets by both the Enforcement Directorate (under PMLA) and the State of Maharashtra (under the MPID Act). The NSEL itself secured decrees and arbitral awards worth around Rs. 3,365 crore against defaulting members, but faced significant hurdles in executing them due to overlapping attachments and competing claims from secured creditors (primarily banks) under SARFAESI/RDB Act. IBC proceedings also initiated against several entities.

Genesis of the Supreme Court Committee

To streamline the complex situation, involving execution of multiple decrees and avoid conflicting proceedings, the Supreme Court, invoking Article 142, constituted a high-powered committee chaired by Justice (Retd.). This committee was vested with the powers of a civil court to execute all decrees, orders, and arbitral awards obtained by NSEL, including the authority to sell properties attached under PMLA and MPID Act and oversee distribution to verified claimants. In short, Article 142 was used as a constitutional "safety valve" to harmonize conflicting statutory regimes, centralize execution, and prioritize investor restitution in a manner that ordinary statutory processes could not have achieved efficiently.

Power under Article 142 is extraordinary, discretionary, and unique to the Supreme Court. It allows the Court to:

Fill legal gaps where no statute provides an adequate remedy. It Complements statutory law, but does not override it—cannot be used to violate or contradict existing statutes

Issue binding directions, even if not strictly aligned with procedural law. Curative in nature—used to resolve issues when ordinary law falls short or causes injustice

Craft equitable solutions, especially in complex, multi-party, or sensitive matters.

However, Article 142 cannot be used to create a new law or override substantive rights conferred by legislation. It must be used judiciously and only when regular statutory or procedural remedies are inadequate or unjust. Article 142 cannot be used to achieve something indirectly what cannot be achieved directly.

While initially hailed as a pragmatic consolidation, the order's breadth brought it into direct strain with key statutory provisions of PMLA, SARFAESI, RDB Act, and IBC—particularly regarding the priority of secured creditors and the moratorium under insolvency law.

Key Legal Questions before the Supreme Court

Two main issues crystallized before the Court in the later stages of the litigation:

1.

Do secured creditors have priority over assets attached under the PMLA and MPID Act by virtue of SARFAESI and RDB Act?

2.

Are properties attached under the MPID Act immune from the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC?

These questions weren't just technical—they strike at the heart of India's recovery framework, challenging the hierarchy of creditor rights in fraud scenarios.

Supreme Court's Ruling on Secured Creditors' Priority

The Court held that the MPID Act and PMLA take precedence over the SARFAESI Act and RDB Act when it comes to assets attached as "proceeds of crime" or for the protection of depositors. The rationale is rooted in constitutional law: the MPID Act is a state law enacted to maintain public order and protect depositors, while SARFAESI and RDB Act are central laws focusing on banking and secured creditors' rights. Since these statutes operate in distinct legislative fields, the doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254 does not apply.

INTRODUCTION

This is the most important section in a benami proceeding. The provisions of this section triggers the process of provisional attachment leading to confiscation of the benami property. This section deals with provisional attachment of benami property by the Initiating Officer. The attachment process commences with issue of notice under section 24(1) of the PBPT Act,1988. It is the first step in action to initiate a proceeding for 'Attachment, Adjudication and Confiscation'. Hence, the foundation for initiation of proceeding under section 24(1) should be in conformity with legal parameters as stipulated in this section. If the initiation of proceeding under section 24(1) is bad in law from the beginning and lacks jurisdictional foundation, all other consequential actions which follow the same, would also be bad in law. In this regard, reference may be made to the decisions in the case of CIT v. Kelvinator of India Ltd. [2002] 123 Taxman 433 (Delhi) affirmed by Supreme Court in [2010] 87 Taxman 312. The decisions in cases of Rawatmal Harakchand v. CIT [1981] 129 ITR 346 (Cal) and P.V. Doshi v. CIT [1976] 113 ITR 22 (Guj.). Hence, the need for proper initiation of proceedings by application of mind.

3. As per rule 3(1), if the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise is satisfied that it is necessary for the purpose of protecting the interest of revenue during the pendency of proceedings to attach provisionally the property, he shall send a proposal for provisional attachment of property of such person to the Commissioner in the format attached in the rule. The format attached to the Rules inter alia requires the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner to give reasons as to why he feels that the property should be provisionally attached. The basis of his fear of non-recovery of service tax subsequently shall be clearly spelt out in the reasons for provisional attachment. The instruction issued vide the Circular dated July 1, 2008 in para 2.3, reproduced below, clearly provides that there should be sufficient justification that the provisional attachment is necessary. The attachment should not be resorted in routine manner.

"(iii)It is important to note that there should be sufficient justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interests of revenue. The remedy of attachment being, by its very nature, extraordinary, has to be resorted to in the utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution. The grounds on which the Central Excise Officer entertains the reasonable belief that the notice would dispose of, or remove, the property and the sources of his information, if any, should be clearly stated while seeking the approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise. Normally, the proposal should be forwarded within one month’s period of the issue of show-cause notice. It may also be noted that appropriate disciplinary action shall be initiated against the officers who may be found to exercise the powers of provisional attachment of property frivolously and without sound reasons."

In case the show-cause notice is answerable to the Commissioner, he shall himself make the proposal.

The Commissioner of Central Excise shall serve the show-cause notice on such person for provisional attachment giving reasons for initiating the provisional attachment.

After considering the reply of the assessee, the Commissioner shall pass the order of provisional attachment of the property. However, no such order shall be issued to attach the personal property of partner, proprietor or director, as the case may be.

It will, thus, be seen that enough safeguard has been inbuilt before exercising such power by the Commissioner. 21. Money in bank accounts is a property liable for provisional attachment under Section 281B: HC

Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax v. Mohammed Salih [2025] 171 taxmann.com 23 (Kerala)

The police seized a huge amount of cash from a car in which the assessee was riding. After recording reason to believe that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment, proceedings were initiated in relation to the same by the issuance of notice under Section 148.

The expected demand on assessment, including penalty, would be a substantial amount exceeding two crores. The competent authority of the Department ordered provisional attachment of the Bank accounts of the assessee under section 281B.

The matter reached the Kerala High Court.

The High Court held that the word 'property' is a word of very wide connotation. It is relevant to note that section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of 'any property'. The prefix 'any' to the word 'property' has much significance. It indicates that the word 'property' occurring therein is not to be comprehended in a restricted sense.

Therefore, 'any property' mentioned in section 281B(1) would take within its sweep, money lying in the bank account also. Section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of any property belonging to the assessee in the manner provided in the Second Schedule to the Act. The Second Schedule to the Act is titled, 'Procedure for Recovery of Tax'. Evidently, except for the property exempted from attachment under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), other properties are liable to attachment.

Section 60 CPC provides the property liable to attachment. Noticeably, section 60(1) CPC specifically states that money is an attachable property. Properties that are not liable to attachment have been specified in the proviso to the section. Therefore, money in a bank account is property liable to attachment.

There could be instances where the assessee does not own immovable property sufficient enough to secure the likely demand, but there are sufficient funds in the bank account. The power for provisional attachment is provided to protect the interest of the revenue. There is no warrant to hold that money lying in a bank account is not liable to attachment.

Introduction

In 2025, courts across India delivered several landmark rulings that substantially shaped the interpretation and enforcement of Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) and banking laws, addressing critical issues of regulatory compliance, financial discipline, and economic governance. These decisions examined the scope of money-laundering offences, procedural safeguards in enforcement actions, priority of claims, recovery mechanisms, one-time settlements, and the extent of judicial review over actions of banks and financial institutions. This write-up aims to curate the Top Landmark FEMA and Banking Law Judgments of 2025, offering valuable insights for legal practitioners, compliance professionals, regulators, and academics seeking to understand the latest judicial trends influencing India's financial and regulatory framework.

1. Discharge rightly denied where accused aided co-accused in bank forms and cheques, knowing link to proceeds of crime: SC

K. Murali Krishna v. Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement [2025] 180 taxmann.com 462 (SC)

In the present case, the question before the Supreme Court was whether the petitioner was entitled to discharge under section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, in a prosecution for the offence of money laundering under section 3 read with section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.

The Supreme Court observed that, at the stage of considering a discharge application, the court is not expected to examine the truthfulness or sufficiency of the allegations, as such an exercise falls within the domain of trial. It was further noted that the scope of section 3 of the PMLA cannot be narrowly construed for the purpose of discharging an accused at the threshold.

The Court noted that the allegations against the petitioner indicated that he had indirectly assisted the main accused in filling up bank account opening forms and handling cheque leaves and was, therefore, alleged to be knowingly a party to activities connected with the proceeds of crime.

The Supreme Court held that since these allegations required appreciation of evidence and adjudication during trial, they could not be examined at the initial stage of discharge. Accordingly, it was held that there was no valid ground to interfere with the order of the High Court confirming rejection of the discharge application.

2. Attachment order under PMLA can be made without prior communication under Section 66(2): HC

Directorate of Enforcement v. Prakash Industries Ltd. [2025] 180 taxmann.com 189 (Delhi)

In the present case, the Supreme Court was called upon to examine the interplay between Section 3 read with Section 24 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002(offence of money laundering) and Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (discharge of accused).

The petitioner had filed an application under Section 227 Cr.P.C. before the Trial Court seeking discharge on the ground that he was not connected with the banking transactions underpinning the alleged money-laundering offence and had merely assisted Accused in filling bank account forms without knowledge of Accused's identity, contending he was wrongly implicated.

The Trial Court rejected this application. The High Court, in the impugned order, upheld that the scope of Section 3 of the PMLA is wide and cannot be narrowly circumscribed at the discharge stage.

The court further retreated that at the discharge stage under Section 227 Cr.P.C. is not to assess the truthfulness of allegations but only to determine whether prima facie a case is made out, leaving detailed factual inquiries for trial. It observed that, as per the complaint under Sections 44 and 45 of the PMLA, the petitioner was alleged to have "indirectly assisted" in filling account and cheque forms and was knowingly a party to activities connected with proceeds of crime — allegations which, if accepted, fall within the ambit of the offence under Section 3 read with the statutory presumption under Section 24 of the PMLA.

Therefore constituted prima facie material for trial, not a fit case for discharge. On this basis, the High Court confirmed the Trial Court's order, and the Supreme Court found no valid ground to interfere with the impugned order.

In the wake of the rising non-performing assets crisis, the Indian legal system seems to be grappling with major challenges than before. While turnaround of debt remains a problem, wilful default of debt adds to this menace. As banks and the government are dead beat trying to prosecute Mr. Vijay Mallya for wilful default of loans and Mr. Karti Chidambaram on money laundering charges, they continue to evade law by residing out of India. The Fugitive Economic Offenders Bill, 2017 (the "Bill") seems to be a knee-jerk reaction which attempts to remedy such regulatory fiascos. The Bill was put in public domain on May 19, 2017 for comments.

Background

To state that the existing legal framework to deal with high value multi-jurisdictional economic offences is inadequate would be an understatement. The RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters (July 01, 2015) provides for barring a wilful defaulter from (a) raising any loans from banks, financial institutions and non-banking companies; and (b) floating a new venture. The other remedies available to banks and financial institutions are contained in the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 and the Recovery of Debt due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 which are time consuming since they involve prolonged litigation.

Moreover, even though the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 aims to provide for a speedy bankruptcy process, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal by holding that the timelines prescribed in Section 7, 9 and 10 of the Code are directory in nature1 has reduced its effectiveness to an extent. Further, liquidation/ bankruptcy process is not a sufficient deterrent in case of high value economic offences. The provisions of civil law in India do not address the issue of high value multi-jurisdictional fugitive economic offenders whereas the process prescribed under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is time consuming and hence inefficient.

The Explanatory Note appended to the Bill states that fleeing of economic offenders leads to several "deleterious" consequences such as (a) hampering investigation in criminal matters; (b) wasting the precious time of the court; (c) undermining the rule of law; and (d) cases which involve non-payment of bank loans cause strain on the banking system. The Bill is aimed to deter a fugitive economic offenders by providing for confiscation of all properties of a wilful defaulter prior to conviction.

Key features

The key features of the Bill are as follows:

1.

Definition of Fugitive Economic Offenders : The Bill defines a "Fugitive Economic Offender" as any individual against whom a warrant for arrest in relation to a scheduled offence2 has been issued by any court in India who (a) leaves or has left India so as to avoid criminal prosecution; or (b) refuses to return to India to face criminal prosecution. Further, in order to ensure that the courts are not overburdened with such cases, only such cases where the total value involved is INR 100 crores or more shall be within the purview of the Bill. This is a higher threshold and must be reduced.

2.

Applicability: The provisions of the Bill shall apply to any individual who is, or becomes, a Fugitive Economic Offender on or after the date of coming into force of this law. It may be argued that the Bill (when becomes law) will be an ex post facto law i.e. it will impose penalties retroactively3. It may appear that such a provision shall the violate Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India. In case this line of argument is upheld by the court, by application of doctrine of severability, the remainder of the Bill may survive as good law which means that those individuals who fall within the definition of a "Fugitive Economic Offender" on the date of enactment of the Bill may be excluded from penalties under the Bill4.

3.

Process : The Director5 or any authorised officer shall make an application to the Special Court6 for declaring an individual as a Fugitive Economic Offender. The Director or any authorised officer may pass an order attaching the properties as described in the application. Such attachment shall be valid for a period of 180 days from the date of the order.

The Special Court shall serve notice and call upon the said individual to present himself before the Special Court within a stipulated time period. The Special Court may terminate such proceedings if the said individual appears in person within the specified time. However, prescribed time may be provided by the Special Court if the individual seeks to be represented by a counsel. If the Special Court concludes that the individual is a Fugitive Economic Offender, the Special Court is required to record the reasons in writing.

The Finance Act, 2006 has introduced the provisions of "Provisional attachment of the property. Please explain the situations in which these provisions can be used and also specify the authority who can give the permission of such attachment.

6. Section 73C has been newly introduced by the Finance Act, 2006 and according to it where a proceeding is pending under section 73 or 73A then to protect the interest of the revenue the Central Excise Office can attach the property of the person to whom notice under section 73 or 73A is issued.

Since this is very delicate provision, the Central Excise Officer has to get approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise.

Here it should be noted that section 73 is related to the recovery of service tax and other sum due from any person under the service tax law on account of recovery of service tax not levied or short-levied or short-paid or erroneously refunded.

Section 73A is also newly introduced by, Finance Act, 2006 and is related to recovery of service tax collected by a person when it is not required to be collected or there is excess service tax collection by any person from the recipient of the service.

If the amount due under section 73 or 73A is not paid by the person who is required to pay the same to the Central Government, then the Central Excise Office is empowered to issue a notice to such person; and if during the pendency of proceedings under both these sections, Central Excise Office is of the opinion that to protect the interest of the revenue it is necessary to attach the property of such person, then he can provisionally attach the property of such person with the previous approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise.

How long the provisional attachment will be effective and on which type of property it can be issued ?

7. The provisional attachment can be made of each and every type of property of the person subject to such attachment and it will include all the movable and immovable property of the person subject to such attachment.

Once issued, the attachment order is valid only for the period of 6 months from the date on which is it issued. Though the Chief Commissioner of Central Excise, after recording the reasons in writing of doing so, has the power to extend this period further, and this extension can not go beyond the period to make overall validity of the original attachment order more than 2 years.

Hence, the original provisional attachment order is valid for 6 months from the date of its issuance and the Chief Commissioner can further extend it for 1 year and 6 months so as to make total validity for 2 years.

PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT - VARIOUS STAGES

Provisional attachment under section 24 of the PBPT Act, 1988 has various statutory stipulations governing the procedure to invoke the said provisions. There are various stages involved in the process of such attachment. These are:-

Initial stage: The IO in consequence of material in his possession and after recording his satisfaction can issue a notice to the benamidar asking him to show cause within such period as indicated in the notice as to why the property should not be treated as benami property under section 24(1). This is the starting point of initiation of proceeding under the PBPT Act, 1988. A copy of this notice need be sent to the beneficial owner, if his identity is known. No approval from Adjudicating Authority is required for issue of initial SCN. [24(1)]

Second stage: Where the IO is of the opinion that the person in possession of the property held benami, may alienate such property, during the period allowed to him in the show cause notice under section 24(1), he may attach the subject property provisionally in the prescribed manner as specified Rule 5 of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transaction Rules, 2016. The procedure of attachment should be in the same manner as provided in Second Schedule of the Income-tax Act, 1961. This attachment shall be for a period not exceeding any 90 days from the last day of the month in which show cause notice under section 24(1) is issued (with effect from 1-9-2019). This can be done with previous approval of the Approving Authority. This is provided in sub-section (3) of section 24 of the PBPT Act, 1988. This order should be in writing specifying the property and indicating his satisfaction in resorting to provisional attachment. [24(3)]

Third stage: Where provisional attachment has been made under sub-section (3) of section 24, IO may, after making such enquiries, calling for such details as he may require and collecting evidence and taking into account all relevant materials, may extend the initial period for attachment. The section requires that the initial period of attachment can be continued by the IO only after consideration of relevant material in his possession. This means that the extension is not the ipse dixit of the IO. This extension can be made after consideration of relevant materials within a period of 90 days from the last day of the month in which show cause notice under section 24(1) is issued with effect from 1-9-2019.[S. 24(4)]

Fourth stage: After consideration of all relevant materials and evidences collected on enquiry, the IO may,

Continue the provisional attachment of the property made under this section with previous approval of the Approving Authority till passing of the order by the Adjudicating Authority under sub-section (3) of section 26. [24(4)(a)(i)], or

Revoke the provisional attachment of the property wherever it is not necessary with the previous approval of the Approving Authority. [24(4)(a)(ii)]

Fifth stage : Where no provisional attachment has been made under sub-section (3), the IO may pass an order provisionally attaching the property with previous approval of the Approving Authority till passing of the order under section 26(3) by the Adjudicating Authority [24(4)(b)(i)]. He may also decide not to attach the property as indicated in the SCN with previous approval of the Adjudicating Authority. [S. 24(4)(b)(ii)]

Sixth stage: Where the IO passes an order continuing the provisional attachment of the property under sub-clause (i) of clause (a) of sub-section (4) or passes an order provisionally attaching the property under sub-clause (i) of clause (b) of that sub-section, he shall, within fifteen days from the date of the attachment, draw up a statement of the case and refer it to the Adjudicating Authority. [S.24(5)]

The provisional attachment at all stages as indicated above shall be made after making enquiry, considering evidence or reports and taking into all relevant materials in possession of IO and with previous approval of the Approving authority. Attachment is made provisionally so as to thwart any attempt by the benamidar who was put to notice under section 24(1) not to alienate the subject property. However, the benamidar can approach the Court challenging the notice of attachment or its continuance by way of a writ where there is fatal jurisdictional error committed by the IO which goes to the root of the matter.

Q.14 Whether the provisions of Benami Law violate Article 20(1) of the Constitution? Ans. The benami law does not violate fundamental rights as enshrined in the Constitution of India and more particularly the violation of Article 20(1) of Constitution of India. There is no violation of Article 20(1) of Constitution of India for the reason that the proceedings under benami law are not Criminal proceedings. They are adjudicatory proceedings which are of civil nature. [General]

Q.15 Whether the authorities acting under the PBPT Act, 1988 enjoy protection from criminal action?

Ans. Under section 64 no prosecution, suit or other proceeding shall lie against the Government or any officer of the Government or the Appellate Tribunal or the Adjudicating Authority established under this Act, for anything done or intended to be done in good faith under this Act. The General Clauses Act defines good faith as "A thing shall be deemed to be done in good faith where it is in fact done honestly whether it is done negligently or not." There should be an element of honesty in ones act while performing his duties. [General]

Q.16 What is the meaning of the expression "Benami"?

Ans. The term "Benami" has its origin from a Persian compound word. This comprises of 'Be' which means 'without' and 'Nami' which means 'name'. This literally means without name. In a benami transaction, the benamidar is the ostensible owner of the property and the beneficial owner is the real owner who pays consideration and enjoys the benefit from the property. [Ref. Chapter 2]

Q.17 What is the distinction between a benami transaction and sham transaction?

Ans. Benami transactions are entered into solely to create an advantage for the creator himself. It has a dubious purpose. In the eye of law, a sham transaction has no existence. It is good in appearance but false in facts. Prior to enactment of the PBPT Act, 1988, a sham transaction was not considered as a benami transaction. However, after enactment of PBPT Act, 1988, sham transactions have been brought into the scope of benami transaction by bringing these transactions within the ambit of clauses (B), (C) and (D) to section 2(9) and by widening the scope of benami transaction under section 2(9)(A), which is the basic definition. [Ref. Chapter 3]

Q.18 Whether re-transfer of a benami property by the benamidar to beneficial owner is permissible?

Ans. It is barred. [Ref. Chapters 4 &12]

Q.19 What is scope of definition of 'property' in the Principal Act, 1988 and in the PBPT Act, 1988 ?

Ans. In the definition in the Principal Act, property referred to property of any kind without making the definition explicit leaving some scope for interpretation. Definition of property in the PBPT Act, 1988 refers to asset of any kind whether movable or immovable, tangible or intangible, corporeal or incorporeal, any right or interest, a legal document or instrument evidencing title or interest in property. The new definition has provided clarity, thereby reducing any debate in the matter of interpretation of the expression. [Ref. Chapter 5]

Q.20 Whether Benami Act applies to a property situated outside India?

Ans. No. This has been clarified the Finance Minister in Rajya Sabha that the benami property located outside India is beyond the scope of Benami Act. Such acquisition will be dealt with under Black Money Act. [Ref. Chapter 6]

Q.21 What is the effect of non-identification of Benami property ?

Ans. The proceedings under section 24(1) will be null and void, for the reason that the proceeding under this section is initiated for provisional attachment in respect of such property. [Ref. Chapter 6]

Q.22 Whether benami property only refers to immovable property?

Ans. No. Section 2(26) of the PBPT Act, 1988 has widened the definition of property to include both immovable and movable property of various kinds and forms. [Ref. Chapter 6]

Q.23 Whether a part of the property can be regarded as benami property?

Ans. Yes. In a multi-storeyed building where a person acquires a property in benami name such portion can be covered under benami transaction. [Ref. Chapters 6 & 17]

Q.24 What will be the position when proceeds of benami property are deposited in bank?

Ans. Such bank deposits will take the character of benami property. If this deposit is converted into fixed deposit or in any other form, such property will also be considered as benami property. But the same should exist on the date of initiation of section 24(1) of PBPT Act. [Ref. Chapter 6]

IPs are then left with the only option to file an application under Section 35(1)(n) of the Code before Adjudicating Authority for seeking necessary direction to get these attached assets released. Bhushan Power and Steel Limited (BPSL) has been among one of the initial twelve cases referred for initiation of CIRP under IBC which has been subject to various litigation due to which the entire resolution process has come to a standstill. The topmost litigation being the attachment of the BPSL assets amounting to Rs. 4025 Crores by Enforcement Directorate (ED) in connection with money laundering investigation initiated under PMLA. The Appellate Authority vide its order dated 14 October 2019 directed ED to immediately release the confiscated assets of BPSL in favour of the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor.

Another plea taken by ED in BPSL case is that Section 32A is prospective and hence, shall not be applicable where the plan is already approved by committee of creditors and Adjudicating Authority prior to the said amendment in the Code. Accordingly, ED again filed an application with Appellate Authority against approval of resolution plan of JSW Steel Limited in BPSL where Appellate Authority in its order dated 17 February 2020 took note of the newly introduced Section 32A and set aside the attachment order passed by ED and granted immunity from prosecution by the ED.

It is rather remarkably interesting to note that by taking this plea of "prospective law" ED is contradicting one of its stands which it adopts in every single case. ED normally pleads that even if an asset is procured before the PMLA Act came into force, the same can still be attached, as it might have been used for laundering the money, i.e. the asset could be a part of the conspiracy for committing the scheduled offence and thus their cannot be an argument or dispute on retrospective or prospective effect.

Although the issue of attachment by the ED has been discussed at length and some clarity already given vide the judgment in Directorate of Enforcement v. Axis Bank, 2019, still the ambiguity remains as even this judgements lays stress on approaching the respective authority for the detachment.

Introduction of Section 32A of the Code

Seeing such anomaly and difficulties in resolving stressed units, Section 32A of the Code was inter-alia introduced by way of an amendment dated 28 December 2019. Section 32A was introduced with the purpose to provide immunity to Corporate Debtor against any offence committed prior to initiation of insolvency proceedings for the Corporate Debtor and to give protection to New Resolution Applicant against any coercive action that could have been taken by the Regulatory Authority in pre-existing scenario. This shall surely induce the Resolution Applicants who were previously targeting the assets of such companies but were afraid to buy-out through resolution process considering legal complexities. This would certainly change the valuation profile of such companies and would benefit the lenders in the long run. It would enable the banks to recover the maximum public money stuck in such companies facing insolvency or liquidation proceedings.

However, despite the amendment in the Code, an air of uncertainty still exists due to which the benefit of Section 32A does not get passed to insolvency process or being availed in scheme for compromise or arrangement as provided under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013. The ED attachment on assets have posed a challenge for the IPs to manage the companies as going concern and liquidate the assets within a reasonable time as per law, especially in absence of any clarity available on the issue. This aggravates the situation further when the bank accounts of the Corporate Debtor are also attached by ED, leaving no cash flows with the IPs to manage the business operations, ultimately resulting in closure of business and deterioration/complete erosion of value of assets. Companies (specifically that are having operations) that undergo liquidation are already facing the liquidity crunch and the IPs make every effort to ensure the Corporate Debtor continues to sustain till it is transferred to a potential applicant at a reasonable value. All the efforts made by the IPs are in consonance with the intent of the Code to revive the Corporate Debtor or to liquidate it through sale of assets lest the delays start affecting business leading to erosion in value.

Adjudicating Authority through its recent judgement in the matter of Varrsana Ispat Limited and REI Agro Limited have provided a wave of relief wherein the Adjudicating Authority allowed the benefit of newly introduced Section 32A of the Code to the liquidator of these companies and allowed him to liquidate the assets. However, at the same time, the order does not vacate the attachment order and instead states that the successful applicant can approach the relevant authority for releasing the assets. Buyers, in most of these cases, don't prefer to indulge in any litigation and that too with ED and want the property title free of such encumbrances.

This amendment is a departure from the liberal approach, which was practiced so far. On the one hand, the Government wants to promote voluntary compliance and on the other hand it seeks to enact the law of provisional attachment even before the completion of adjudication proceedings. The only silver lining is that the order of attachment has to be approved by highest authorities, i.e., Commissioner or Chief Commissioner, as the case may be. Similarly provisions are already there in other legislation, e.g., section 281B of Income-tax Act, 1961. One only hopes that such provisions will be used sparingly and in extreme cases.

The Tribunal further held that if the intention of the Legislature were to impose a penalty of only Rs. 100, then there would have been a comma after words ‘rupees one hundred’.

The notice would provide the name, description, etc., of the property proposed to be attached provisionally and would also make a mention that till the disposal of the proceedings of provisional attachment, the assessee or his authorized agent should not cause the transfer of title or debase the title of such property. u Moreover, the revenue authorities have to comply with all the principles of natural justice before passing an order of attachment even when some of the principles have not been provided specifically by the Act or the Rules. In the case of S.K. Modi v. Union of India 2002 (144) ELT 59 (Delhi), the Hon’ble High Court had held that the principles of natural justice have to be complied with before order of attachment against petitioner could be passed.
