Powers under rule 86A are drastic and far reaching powers. The powers cannot be used as tool of harassment. Utilisation of credit is a vested right - S S Industries v. UOI (2021) 87 GSTR 71 = 57 GSTL 13 (Guh HC) - quoted and followed in PMW Metal v. UOI (2024) 91 GSTL 4 = 23 Centax 317 (Guj HC DB). Rule 86A of CGST Rules is not a machinery provisions for recovery of tax or dues under CGST Act but an emergent measure for protection of revenue by temporarily not allowing debit of available ITC in ECL. Hence, negative blocking of ECL (Electronic Credit Ledger) is not permissible - Super Products (Regd) v. DGGSTI (2025) 30 Centax 456 (Del HC DB).

Electronic Credit Ledger cannot be blocked if there is no credit in the ledger. There cannot be blocking of Electronic Credit Ledger if there is no balance in Electronic Credit Ledger - PMW Metal v. UOI (2024) 91 GSTL 4 = 23 Centax 317 (Guj HC DB) * Samay Alloys v. State of Gujarat (2022) 61 GSTL (Guj HC).

Provisional attachment not for cash credit account - Provisional attachment can be only when there is balance in bank account. An account with debit balance (cash credit account) cannot be attached - Bindal Smelting P Ltd. v. ADG, DGGSTI [2020] 80 GST 318 = 116 taxmann.com 28 (P&H HC DB) - following Kaneria Granito Ltd. v. ACIT [2016] 71 taxmann.com 276 = 241 Taxman 315 (Guj HC).

Cash credit account is not property of account holder. It cannot be attached - Skytech Rolling Mill v. Joint Commissioner (2025) 110 GST 570 = 175 taxmann.com 551 (Bom HC DB).

Cash Credit facility is not a debt and cash credit account cannot be attached - J L Enterprises v. ACST (2023) 98 GST 368 = 151 taxmann.com 111 (Cal HC).

Really, if cash credit account is blocked, the account cannot be operated even if the person has limit available in cash credit account. Thus, he surely suffers.

Provisional attachment ceases after final order passed - Once final order is passed under section 74(9) of CGST Act, proceedings under provisional attachment order come to an end - Usha Industries v. Dy. Commissioner (2021) 88 GST 646= 128 taxmann.com 269 (P&H HC DB).

Procedure for provisional attachment and release of property - Order for provisional attachment shall be in form GST DRC-22. Objection to order of attachment shall be in form GST-DRC-23A. If payment is made by defaulter, or on expiry of a period of one year from the date of issuance of order under rule 159(1), whichever is earlier, the property can be released by issuing order in form GST DRC-23 - rule 159(2) of CGST Rules, 2017 [words in italics inserted w.e.f. 26-10-2023]

Departmental guidelines for provisional attachment - CBI&C, vide letter No. CBEC-20/16/05/2021-GST/359 dated 23-2-2021, has issued guidelines for provisional attachment. The guidelines are summarized below -

The powers of provisional attachment are extraordinary and should be resorted to with utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution.

Collective evidence should indicate prima facie case against tax payer before going ahead with provisional assessment.

If property attached is perishable/hazardous nature, it shall be released to taxable person after payment of market price of such property or amount payable by taxable person, whichever is lower.

Provisional attachment should not be resorted to in case of violations of technical nature. These should be resorted mainly in cases of evasion of tax or availment of wrongful Input Tax Credit. Like bogus invoices, frauds etc.

Normally, only immovable property should be attached. Movable property should be attached only if immovable property is insufficient to protect interests of revenue.

Property attached should not be excessive. More than one property can be attached and at different points of time.

Attachment should not hamper normal functioning of taxable person. Thus, raw materials and inputs for production or finished goods should not be normally attached.

Title deeds of immovable property should be checked

After provisional attachment, investigation and adjudication should be completed fast so that tax, interest and penalty can be recovered and purpose of provisional attachment is achieved.

Following property cannot be attached - (a) Property exempted from attachment by Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (b) Property for sale for execution of a decree of Civil Court.

In order to protect the interest of revenue and safeguard recovery in search cases, Finance Act, 2017 has inserted new sub-sections (9B) to (9D) provide for provisional attachment of any property belonging to an assessee.

In terms of the provision, an authorised officer may provisionally attach any property in the following manner:

he should be satisfied that provisional attachment is necessary in the interest of the revenue;

he should record the reason in writing; he should take previous approval of Principal Director General or Director General or the Principal Director or Director;

he should pass an order in writing for provisional attachment of property;

the property to be attached should be belonging to an assessee;

such attachment should be made:

-

during the course of search or seizure; or

-

within 60 days from the date on which last of the authorisations for search was executed.

It is also provided that for the purpose of provisional attachment of property, provisions of the Second Schedule shall, mutatis mutandis, apply.

Finance Act, 2017 has inserted new sub-section (9C) to provide that every provisional attachment of property made under sub-section (9B) would be valid only for six months from the date of order passed under the said sub-section.

The above amendment will take effect from 1-4-2017.

11.1-5a Valuation of the property attached [Sub-section (9D)] - Finance Act, 2017 has inserted new sub-section (9D) to enable the authorized officer to make reference to a Valuation Officer for the purpose of estimating the fair market value of the property.

during the course of search or seizure; or

within 60 days from the date of execution of last authorisation.

On making reference, a Valuation Officer shall:

estimate the fair market value of the property in the manner provided under section 142A; and

submit a report of the estimate to the said officer within 60 days from date of receipt of reference.

The above amendment will take effect from 1-4-2017.

11.1-5b Reason for amendment - The Memorandum explaining the provisions of Finance Bill, 2017 states the reason as under:

11.1-5c Substitution of Explanation 1 of section 132 - Finance Act, 2017 has substituted Explanation 1 of section 132 to provide that for the purposes of sub-sections (9A), (9B) and (9D) ('specified sections'), with respect to 'execution of an authorisation for search', the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 153B shall apply.

Section 133 empowers certain income-tax authorities to call for information for the purpose of any inquiry or proceeding under the Act.

Accordingly, in terms of sub-section (6) and first proviso, such authority may require any person to furnish information in relation to such points/matters or statement of accounts and affairs which may be useful for or relevant to any enquiry or proceeding under the Act. (iii) Giving of Opportunity for making submissions - On receipt of the proposal of attachment, the jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise, or where he is acting on his own, and if he is satisfied that circumstances of the case justify provisional attachment, he may serve a notice on the person on whom a SCN is already served under section 73 or 73 A of the Act. The purpose of serving the present notice is to give the person concerned an opportunity to make submissions, in writing or in person or both, as to why the property belonging to him, and as may be specified in the notice, be not provisionally attached. According to the circular, the said notice should also specify the condition that the noticee should not sell, transfer, mortgage, charge, lease or otherwise alienate or encumber the property specified in the notice, till the decision of the said notice. In case of proposal for provisional attachment of immovable property, the notice should also be sent to the concerned registration authorities with a direction not to allow any sale, transfer, mortgage, etc., of the property.

Note : The person on whom the notice is served by the jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise for provisional attachment of property is required to make submissions within fifteen days of serving of the notice.

(iv) Granting of Approval - Based on the materials placed before him, and after hearing the person concerned, the jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise may grant approval to the provisional attachment of the property, within fifteen days of holding of personal hearing.

(v) Attachment of property - On receipt of approval from the Commissioner, the Central Excise Officer before whom the proceedings under section 73 or 73A are pending, may, by order in writing, proceed to attach the said property. Where proceedings are pending before the Commissioner himself and he has formed the opinion to attach the property, he shall order the attachment of the property, within fifteen days of holding of personal hearing.

Note : A copy of the order of provisional attachment should be served by the Central Excise Officer in the same manner as prescribed under section 37C of the Central Excise Act, 1944, as made applicable to service tax vide section 83 of the Finance Act, 1994.

(vi) Timing of Attachment - In terms of the circular, the provisional attachment of the property of the concerned person by arrest or distrain shall be made after sunrise and before sunset and not otherwise.

(vii) Inventory - The circular instructs that after provisional attachment of the property, the Central Excise Officer shall prepare an inventory of the property attached. He shall specify in the inventory the place where the property attached is lodged or kept and shall hand over a copy of the same to defaulter or the person from whose charge the property is distrained.

(viii) Attachment of property jointly held - In this respect, the Circular states that where the property to be provisionally attached consists of the share or interest of the concerned person in property belonging to him and another as co-owners, the provisional attachment shall be made by a notice to the concerned person prohibiting him from transferring the share or interest or charging it in any way.

Property which can be attached by the department

5. As per the definition of ‘property’ given by the Rules, it includes immovable property but as a matter of fact, only those immovable property/properties which are used for commercial purpose may be provisionally attached. And where immovable property available for attachment is not sufficient to protect the interests of revenue, the attachment may be extended to movable property. It should also be ensured that such attachment does not hamper normal business of the assessee, implying that inputs required for provision of a service should not be attached by the department. Further, the attachment shall not be excessive, i.e., the property provisionally attached should be of value as nearly as may be equivalent to that of the amount of pending revenue against the person committing default.

21. Money in bank accounts is a property liable for provisional attachment under Section 281B: HC

Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax v. Mohammed Salih [2025] 171 taxmann.com 23 (Kerala)

The police seized a huge amount of cash from a car in which the assessee was riding. After recording reason to believe that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment, proceedings were initiated in relation to the same by the issuance of notice under Section 148.

The expected demand on assessment, including penalty, would be a substantial amount exceeding two crores. The competent authority of the Department ordered provisional attachment of the Bank accounts of the assessee under section 281B.

The matter reached the Kerala High Court.

The High Court held that the word 'property' is a word of very wide connotation. It is relevant to note that section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of 'any property'. The prefix 'any' to the word 'property' has much significance. It indicates that the word 'property' occurring therein is not to be comprehended in a restricted sense.

Therefore, 'any property' mentioned in section 281B(1) would take within its sweep, money lying in the bank account also. Section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of any property belonging to the assessee in the manner provided in the Second Schedule to the Act. The Second Schedule to the Act is titled, 'Procedure for Recovery of Tax'. Evidently, except for the property exempted from attachment under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), other properties are liable to attachment.

Section 60 CPC provides the property liable to attachment. Noticeably, section 60(1) CPC specifically states that money is an attachable property. Properties that are not liable to attachment have been specified in the proviso to the section. Therefore, money in a bank account is property liable to attachment.

There could be instances where the assessee does not own immovable property sufficient enough to secure the likely demand, but there are sufficient funds in the bank account. The power for provisional attachment is provided to protect the interest of the revenue. There is no warrant to hold that money lying in a bank account is not liable to attachment.

Scope and ambit of section 73 and rule 3

1. Section 73C of the Finance Act, 1994 provides for provisional attachment of property of an assessee. It reads as follows:

"73C. Provisional attachment to protect revenue in certain cases.—(1) Where, during the pendency of any proceeding under section 73 or section 73A, the Central Excise Officer is of opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interests of revenue, it is necessary so to do, he may, with the previous approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise, by order in writing, attach provisionally any property belonging to the person on whom notice is served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A, as the case may be, in such manner as may be prescribed." [Emphasis supplied]

An analysis of the above section makes it clear that the following ingredients are essential for issuance of an order of attachment thereunder:

(i)

The attachment should be during the pendency of any proceeding under section 73 or section 73A;

(ii)

notice should have been served on the assessee under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A;

(iii)

the Central Excise Officer before whom proceedings are pending is of opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interests of revenue, it is necessary to attach the assessee's property;

(iv)

previous approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise is necessary for the attachment;

(v)

the attachment order should be in writing; and

(vi)

the attachment is provisional.

It is pertinent to note that the officer competent to proceed for attachment under sub-section (1) of section 73C is "Central Excise Officer."

In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 94 read with section 73C of the Finance Act, 1994, the Central Government has made the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008. Rule 3 of the said Rules reads as follows:

"3. Procedure for provisional attachment of property.—(1) If the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise or the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise is satisfied that it is necessary or expedient, for the purpose of protecting the interests of revenue, during the pendency of any proceeding under section 73 or section 73A of the Act, to attach provisionally any property belonging to a person on whom notice has been served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A of the Act, shall after due verification of the facts, and the circumstances of the case, forward a proposal for provisional attachment of property of such person, to the Commissioner of Central Excise, in the format annexed to these rules." [Emphasis supplied].

The legal implication of the terms used in rule 3 (1) is far-reaching.

ATTACHMENT AND CONFISCATION

Attachment of property is one of the modes of execution of a decree in a civil suit. Failure to pay the decretal amount in the execution of its decree, the Court may resort to attachment of the movable and immovable property and recover the amount which is due to the decree-holder by the disposal of attached assets. It is a measure of safe guarding the interest of the decree holder. Sections 60 to Section 64 and Rules 41-57 of Order 21 of CPC 1908, deals with the procedure of attachment of property. Under Section 2(5) of PBPT Act, 1988 "attachment" means the prohibition of transfer, conversion, disposition or movement of property, by an order issued under the Act. This power of confiscation is vested the Adjudicating Authority under section 27(1). The distinction between the two is that a provisional attachment can be made by the Competent Authorities under benami law in anticipation that the benamidar may alienate the benami property before finalization of the proceeding. Provisional attachment and subsequent confiscation are limited to benami property only. It does not amount to disposition of a property till final order under section 27(1) is passed in a benami proceeding, subject to order of Appellate Tribunal. On the other hand, confiscation relates to a legal form of seizure of the benami property by the State without payment of any compensation. It is a measure of penalty. Under benami law, confiscation follows provisional attachment and final adjudication.

INTRODUCTION

Provisions relating to attachment of benami property are akin to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 which empowers the Court to attach before judgment such portion of the property as may be sufficient to satisfy any decree that may be passed in the suit. This power is to be exercised where the Court is satisfied that the defendant, with intent to obstruct or delay the execution of any decree, may dispose of whole or any part of the property. The powers of provisional attachment in any statute are extraordinary powers which should be exercised judiciously after due application of mind. This is the basic tenant of law. As per the provisions of section 2(5) of the PBPT Act, 1988 attachment means the prohibition of transfer, conversion, disposition or movement of property by an order passed under the Act.

The term ‘personal property’ is defined in rule 2(d) to mean any movable or immovable property belonging to a proprietor or partner or director in relation to business activity. Further, rule 3(3) also provides that the Commissioner of Central Excise should not attach the personal property of proprietor or partner or director, as the case may be. The instructions issued vide Circular dated July 1, 2008 provides for the property which can be attached as follows:

"(a )Personal property of a sole proprietor or partners shall not be attached. Personal property means any movable or immovable property which is in personal use of the sole proprietor or partner. (b )Movable property should be attached only if the immovable property available for attachment is not sufficient to protect the interests of revenue.

It will, thus, be seen that the intention of the Government is not to hamper the business activity.

When the property is attached, private alienation is void in following cases :

"(a )where a notice has been served on a person for provisional attachment, the person on whom such notice has been served or his representative in interest shall not be competent to mortgage, charge, lease or otherwise deal with any property belonging to him except with the written permission of the Commissioner of Central Excise.

Conclusion

6. There are number of assessees who are habitual defaulters. They normally do not own fixed asset. The land and building is taken on lease, plant and machinery are mortgaged to the bank for obtaining finance, movable property or stock of raw materials, work in process, etc., are mortgaged to the bank against overdraft.

Recovery of taxes from such person requires very stringent measures and the Rules notified is one such measure adopted by the Government to ensure recovery of amount. However, implementation of the same should be carefully made in order to avoid harassment to genuine person. The authorities shall not recklessly adopt provisional attachment of properties unless there are very justifiable reasons for the same. In conclusion it can be said that the rules are framed with very good objective but it is to be seen that its implementation shall not destroy the object.

Section 132(1)(c) permits search to be undertaken by the department if there is reason to believe that a person is in possession 'of any money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article or thing and such money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article or thing represents either wholly or partly income or property which has not been, or would not be, disclosed' for the purposes of the Act, referred to as 'the undisclosed income or property'. For the purposes of the instant petitions, the emphasis would be on the expression 'any money' and 'other valuable article or thing' as appearing in section 132(1). The context in which these words occur cannot possibly exclude money in a bank account. The contention that this could only mean 'cash' and not money in a bank account may be an attractive argument but not in the context in which the above expression occurs. It is certainly a valuable thing. In other words, a sum in a bank account is not outside the ambit of section 132(1) and can be subject to search and seizure. [Para 53]

Thus, a person could be in possession of undisclosed income not only in his or her own account but in someone else's account. In the context of the instant petitions, therefore, when pursuant to the search warrant, the department proceeded to search and seize not only valuable things etc. found in the premises of 'M' but also those in the accounts of the 8 petitioner companies as well as that of VS who was actively involved in the day to day management of various companies controlled by 'M' and worked closely with him, they could do so as long as they were satisfied that what constitutes M's undisclosed income was in the accounts of the 8 companies and VS. [Para 54]

The second proviso to section 132(1) read with section 132(3) permits the department to require the bank in which the account that is subject to search is located to freeze it since it may not be possible 'to take physical possession' immediately of such 'valuable article or thing and remove it to a safe place.' Section 132B deals with the powers of the authorised officer to deal with the valuable thing which has been so seized and the conditions on which the restraint placed may be lifted. [Para 55]

The assertion by petitioners that this is realization of the debt owed by the bank to the petitioners and that the amount therein cannot be transferred to the department is based on an incorrect understanding of the legal position under section 281B. The said provision states that in order to protect the interests of the revenue, it may be necessary to go in for a provisional attachment. Therefore, the direction issued to RBL by the department does not mean that the money is finally taken over by the revenue. It will undoubtedly be kept in a suspense account like a PD Account to await the final orders in the assessment proceedings and the issues raised as a consequence thereof. For this purpose, the argument that this does not constitute 'assets' or 'money' within the meaning of section 132(1) read with section 133 has not merit. [Para 57]

For the aforementioned reasons, both the petitions are dismissed. [Para 60]

17.2

PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT - VARIOUS STAGES

Provisional attachment under section 24 of the PBPT Act, 1988 has various statutory stipulations governing the procedure to invoke the said provisions. There are various stages involved in the process of such attachment. These are:-

Initial stage: The IO in consequence of material in his possession and after recording his satisfaction can issue a notice to the benamidar asking him to show cause within such period as indicated in the notice as to why the property should not be treated as benami property under section 24(1). This is the starting point of initiation of proceeding under the PBPT Act, 1988. A copy of this notice need be sent to the beneficial owner, if his identity is known. No approval from Adjudicating Authority is required for issue of initial SCN. [24(1)]

Second stage: Where the IO is of the opinion that the person in possession of the property held benami, may alienate such property, during the period allowed to him in the show cause notice under section 24(1), he may attach the subject property provisionally in the prescribed manner as specified Rule 5 of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transaction Rules, 2016. The procedure of attachment should be in the same manner as provided in Second Schedule of the Income-tax Act, 1961. This attachment shall be for a period not exceeding any 90 days from the last day of the month in which show cause notice under section 24(1) is issued (with effect from 1-9-2019). This can be done with previous approval of the Approving Authority. This is provided in sub-section (3) of section 24 of the PBPT Act, 1988. This order should be in writing specifying the property and indicating his satisfaction in resorting to provisional attachment. [24(3)]

Third stage: Where provisional attachment has been made under sub-section (3) of section 24, IO may, after making such enquiries, calling for such details as he may require and collecting evidence and taking into account all relevant materials, may extend the initial period for attachment. The section requires that the initial period of attachment can be continued by the IO only after consideration of relevant material in his possession. This means that the extension is not the ipse dixit of the IO. This extension can be made after consideration of relevant materials within a period of 90 days from the last day of the month in which show cause notice under section 24(1) is issued with effect from 1-9-2019.[S. 24(4)]

Fourth stage: After consideration of all relevant materials and evidences collected on enquiry, the IO may,

Continue the provisional attachment of the property made under this section with previous approval of the Approving Authority till passing of the order by the Adjudicating Authority under sub-section (3) of section 26. [24(4)(a)(i)], or

Revoke the provisional attachment of the property wherever it is not necessary with the previous approval of the Approving Authority. [24(4)(a)(ii)]

Fifth stage : Where no provisional attachment has been made under sub-section (3), the IO may pass an order provisionally attaching the property with previous approval of the Approving Authority till passing of the order under section 26(3) by the Adjudicating Authority [24(4)(b)(i)]. He may also decide not to attach the property as indicated in the SCN with previous approval of the Adjudicating Authority. [S. 24(4)(b)(ii)]

Sixth stage: Where the IO passes an order continuing the provisional attachment of the property under sub-clause (i) of clause (a) of sub-section (4) or passes an order provisionally attaching the property under sub-clause (i) of clause (b) of that sub-section, he shall, within fifteen days from the date of the attachment, draw up a statement of the case and refer it to the Adjudicating Authority. [S.24(5)]

The provisional attachment at all stages as indicated above shall be made after making enquiry, considering evidence or reports and taking into all relevant materials in possession of IO and with previous approval of the Approving authority. Attachment is made provisionally so as to thwart any attempt by the benamidar who was put to notice under section 24(1) not to alienate the subject property. However, the benamidar can approach the Court challenging the notice of attachment or its continuance by way of a writ where there is fatal jurisdictional error committed by the IO which goes to the root of the matter.

The introduction of Section 32A to the IBC has significantly altered the legal landscape by providing statutory immunity to the Corporate Debtor and its assets from prosecution and attachment for prior offences, provided the resolution plan has been approved and management has changed hands.

Some of the below judgments have given paramount importance to section 32A and 238 of the IBC' act- LANDMARK 2025: THE SUPREME COURT'S MANDATE

5.1 Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power & Steel (September 2025)

The Bhushan Power case is perhaps the most significant in IBC history. After JSW Steel acquired BPSL, the ED attached assets worth Rs. 19,000 crores. In 2025, the Supreme Court ruled:

Section 32A is Absolute: Once a resolution plan is approved and the management changes to an unrelated party, the liability of the Corporate Debtor for pre-CIRP offences ceases.

Immunity of Assets: The protection extends to the assets themselves. The ED cannot continue attachments once the NCLT approves a plan.

Jurisdictional Boundary: The Court clarified that while the NCLT cannot "quash" an ED attachment (as it is a criminal law function), the attachment ceases to operate by operation of law upon plan approval

5.2 Directorate of Enforcement v. V Hotels Ltd. (November 2025)-

In this crucial update, the Supreme Court confirmed the setting aside of a Provisional Attachment Order (PAO) after the successful resolution of V Hotels. The Court held that the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA), who steps into the shoes of the debtor as a "clean" entity, cannot have their properties liened by the ED for the sins of the erstwhile management.

Hon'ble Supreme Court held that- "In view of Section 32A of the IBC, the name of the Corporate Debtor shall be deleted from the array of accused in Supplementary Prosecution Complaint dated 12.07.2024 in Spl. Case, while continuing with the prosecution of the erstwhile directors and/or persons in control or conspirators or abettors and confiscation of their attached/restrained properties/entitlements, if any.

Needless to state, the benefit of Section 32A of IBC is subject to the condition that the SRA is neither connected with the erstwhile Directors of the Corporate Debtor nor is the SRA a beneficiary of proceeds of crime derived from the alleged scheduled offence. If this foundation is eroded in the ongoing investigation, the Directorate of Enforcement shall be at liberty to take appropriate steps in accordance with law, including questioning the resolution plan.

SCOPE OF PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT - MADRAS HIGH COURT'S VIEW

In Dinesh Chand Surana v. Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax on 2 July, 2018, Madras High Court held that since the order passed under section 24(4) of the Act being an order of provisional attachment, the petitioner cannot be stated to have been aggrieved over such order, especially, when the adjudicating authority under the Benami Act has already initiated proceedings under section 24(4) of the Act. The whole idea is to see that effective steps are taken for the purpose of getting at the resources of tax evaders, so that their obligations under the Act are discharged, and to search for and seize the assets in whatever shape they may be, and that is why the language in a wide form as "valuable things" has been used in section 132. The debts are intended to be outside the operation of section 132. There is enough indication in both sub-section (3) and sub-section (5) of section 132 that the assets dealt with under the respective provisions were only to be temporarily subject to seizure of attachment, as the case may be. In the case of the seized assets, there is a specific provision made for seeing that the assets are not retained beyond the period of ninety days, after seizure. Within that period, the ITO will have to estimate the undisclosed income and provide for the tax as well as interest, etc. He can retain only that portion of the assets necessary to meet the said obligations and refund the balance. In the case of sub-section (3), the position of the language is not very much different. In other words, that is also a provision intended to be operative temporarily. This is clear from the language of sub- section (3) itself. It provides that the authorised officer may, where it is not practicable to seize the assets, serve an order on the owner, who is in immediate possession or control thereof, that he shall not remove, part with or otherwise deal with them except with the previous permission of the said officer and such officer may take such steps as may be necessary for ensuring compliance with the sub-section. The previous permission can be applied for at any time, even within the period of ninety days. When such an option was given, there was no need for fixing any time-limit. If the assessee satisfies the officer about his having to deal with the particular assets, then the permission of the officer would have to be granted subject to such safeguards as the officer may consider necessary. Thus, the non-specification of a time-limit under sub- section (3) cannot be construed as showing that the authorised officer can subject the assets to attachment for an indefinite period of time. In the instant case, no steps were taken by the respondent for the purpose of obtaining permission for dealing with the assets in any particular manner and, therefore, there was no scope for the authorised officer to allow it to deal with the assets subject to any safeguard that may be considered necessary. It is not possible to read the time-limit in sub- section (5) into sub- section (3) as the Parliament has not imposed any such time-limit with reference to sub- section (3) for good and valid reasons as seen already. It may be that Parliament considered a specific time-limit necessary in the case of seized assets, as the person concerned is deprived of the assets for the said period, while in the case of the attached assets there is no deprivation of assets. The assets continue to be in the possession or control of the said person subject to the prohibitory order from removing it or dealing with it from the said place. The order of attachment cannot, in these circumstances, be construed as if it is indefinite.

Section 226, applies to cases where there is an unsatisfied demand and the assessee is in default. Section 281B applies to the cases where the proceedings are pending. If after the completion of the assessment or even during the pendency of the assessment, the assessee, whose assets are subject to attachment, applies, it may be that the ITO may take recourse to section 226 or 281B, or may think fit to release them if the assessee makes appropriate arrangement for payment of tax. Thus, the provision of sub- section (3) cannot be utilised so as to continue the attachment indefinitely. If in any case any person whose assets are subject to attachment satisfied the court that sub- section (3) has been utilised only for the purpose of circumventing the time-limit as specified in sub- section (5), it would be open to him to approach the court, so that the matter can be examined and appropriate relief granted on proof of such a grievance. The possibility of sub- section (3) being misused in such a manner cannot justify the importing of the time-limit as specified in sub- section (5) into sub- section (3) contrary to what Parliament has done. If Parliament really intended that the procedure contemplated by sub- section (5) should be attracted to sub- section (3), it could have so provided, as has been done in sub- section (7).

Thus, having gone into the several objections put forward by the petitioner in relation to the attachment of the bank account, it was not possible to agree with him that the said attachment, in the circumstances of the case, was in any manner wrong.

The appellant was only a facilitator to carry the cash to be handed over to the Football Association.

In other words, powers under sub-section (3) of section 74 cannot be exercised for expanding or enlarging the liability arising out of show-cause notice under sub-section (1) from the same period. In that view of the matter, the respondents are wholly incorrect in issuing a fresh show-cause notice for the same period of July 2017 to 20-02-2018, which notice was already issued under sub-section (1) of section 74 purportedly under exercising powers to suggest that once a notice has been issued under sub-section (1) of section 74, if the authorities find that the liability of tax, interest or penalty larger than one indicated in the statement referred to in sub-section (1) is likely to arise, the competent authority is remedy-less. However, his remedy does not lie in issuing second notice under sub-section (3) of section 74. The impugned notice dated 19-3-2018 therefore, shall have to be quashed. [Para 12]

As regards last surviving question of attachment of bank accounts, as per the departmental authorities, the petitioners had not paid GSTs on branded goods. The tax liability would be Rs. 36,88,706. There could be possible interest and penalty liability on such tax amount. It prima facie appears that the department had issued second show-cause notice dated 19-03-2017 (which is proposed to be quashed) including even the unbranded goods for recovery of GSTs. Having perused the relevant literature, even otherwise it is found that GSTs on unbranded goods has been specifically exempted. As of now, thus, only notice for recovery of tax that survives is one seeking to recover GSTs of Rs. 30 lacs approximately with interest and penalty. At the same time, one must also realize that if the petitioners are not correct in contending that no service tax can be levied on branded goods because the brand belongs to the directors of the company, such liability may eventually arise with interest and matching penalty. [Para 13]

Under sub-section (1) of section 83, the competent authority has power of provisional attachment, where during pendency of any proceedings under the Act he is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of government revenue, it is necessary so to do. Such provisional attachment could be of any property including the bank account of the taxable person. Sub-section (2) of section 83, however, provided that every such provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of a period of one year from the date of which such order has been made. [Para 15]

In the instant case, nothing is demonstrated by the department either in the orders of attachment or in the affidavit filed. The reason why exercise of such drastic power of attachment of bank accounts was necessary. Therefore, such attachments are set aside. At the same time, some security is provided so that eventually, if the tax liability is confirmed, the department is not left with no means to recover the same. [Para 16]

■

The main ground, on which, the present impugned orders of attachment are assailed is on the aspect of power of the department to issue fresh attachment orders again and again without assigning any reasons, since the impugned orders under section 281B have been issued in a mechanical manner for the fourth time and in a routine fashion stating that for the purpose of protecting the interest of the revenue, it is necessary to attach the immovable properties of the assessees.(Para 6)

■

It is the case of the assessees that they have been duly filing ITRs and indirect tax statutes. However, a surprise search was conducted both at the place of business premises of the assessees and residences of the promoters and employees of the assessees and certain materials were seized. In furtherance of such search, notices under section 132(9B) were issued to the assessees, whereby the properties were attached for three times, vide notices dated 28.02.2022, 23.08.2022 and 17.02.2023 and by virtue of the instant impugned orders dated 16.08.2023, the properties belonging to the assessees were attached for the fourth time and the reason assigned by the authorized officer for issuance of such attachment orders was by merely stating that to protect the interest of the revenue for the welfare of the State.(Para 7)

■

It is the grievance expressed by the assessees that since the department has resorted to such draconian measure of provisional attachment of their properties, not for the first time, but for the fourth time, due to which, their business has almost come to a standstill, since, the properties, which were attached by the department were all the properties, which they have offered as securities to the banks, and because of such mortgaged properties were came to be attached, the banks are refusing to part with further working capital loans, at any moment, they would declare the assessees as non performing assets, if this situation continues, it will jeopardize the entire business of the assessees and it would also have a cascading effect of 5000 workers loosing their job, resulting in 5000 families landing on streets suffering for food and shelter. Therefore, the assessees contended that unless and until, the attachments are lifted, the banks will stop extending their loan facilities, resulting in the assessees’ closing down their business, and even the department will not be assured of their revenue, which they intend to protect.(Para 8)

■

Thus, from the above backgrounds of the case it is clear that the first charge holders of the properties are the bankers and the department are only the second charge holders of the assessees’ properties. Therefore, the first charge holders of the assessees’ properties, being the bankers, the assessees have to first satisfy the bankers, for availing loan facility and only the bankers are satisfied they would come forward to lend loan facility to the assessees. The assessees have earned good reputation and credibility amongst the general public, based on which, the bankers have come forward to extend the loan facility and this is a continuous arrangements entered into between the bankers and the assessees, for the sake of running the business smoothly, and when the banks, having extended working capital loan facility to the assessees, certainly, they will monitor the same so as to protect their interest. The question of non-repayment would arise due to deficit in service of working capital loan extended to the assessees. Therefore, the department could have enabled the assessees to get their working capital loans extended by the bankers, and thereafter, monitor the assessees, whether such loan is being utilized by the assessees for the purpose, for which, such additional loan is extended, and by doing so, the interest of the revenue, is not going to be affected in any away, rather, it would promote much financial gain, and thereby, the interest of the revenue would also be safeguarded. Therefore, the department ought to have acted in such a way, in order to protect the interest of the revenue. Whereas, in the instant case, it is seen that, on earlier occasions, i.e., on 28.02.2022, 23.08.2022 and 17.02.2023, the department has issued the attachment orders and the same got lapsed on 27.08.2022, 22.02.2023 and 16.08.2023 respectively. Finally, for the fourth time, the department has issued the provisional attachment orders dated 16.08.2023 and the reasons assigned is that to protect the interest of the revenue.(Para 9)

This is the most important section in a benami proceeding. The provisions of this section triggers the process of provisional attachment leading to confiscation of the benami property. This section deals with provisional attachment of benami property by the Initiating Officer. The attachment process commences with issue of notice under section 24(1) of the PBPT Act,1988. It is the first step in action to initiate a proceeding for 'Attachment, Adjudication and Confiscation'. Hence, the foundation for initiation of proceeding under section 24(1) should be in conformity with legal parameters as stipulated in this section. If the initiation of proceeding under section 24(1) is bad in law from the beginning and lacks jurisdictional foundation, all other consequential actions which follow the same, would also be bad in law. In this regard, reference may be made to the decisions in the case of CIT v. Kelvinator of India Ltd. [2002] 123 Taxman 433 (Delhi) affirmed by Supreme Court in [2010] 87 Taxman 312. The decisions in cases of Rawatmal Harakchand v. CIT [1981] 129 ITR 346 (Cal) and P.V. Doshi v. CIT [1976] 113 ITR 22 (Guj.). The CBEC’s circular, however, states that where a provisional attachment has been made, any private transfer or delivery of the property attached or of any debt, dividend or other moneys, contrary to such provisional attachment, shall be void as against all claims enforceable under the provisional attachment. (xiii) Does provisional attachment of a property also affect the rights of a person co-owner therein ? - The Rules once again do not make any provision in this regard. The CBEC’s circular, however, provides that where the property to be provisionally attached consists of the share or interest of the concerned person in property belonging to him and another as co-owners, the provisional attachment shall be made by a notice to the concerned person prohibiting him from transferring the share or interest or charging it in any way.

(xiv) Are any properties exempt from provisional attachment ? - Except for personal property(ies) of the proprietor/partners/directors, the Rules do not grant immunity from provisional attachment to any other property. However, as per CBEC’s circular any property which is exempted from attachment and sale for execution of a decree of a civil court in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, shall also be exempt from provisional attachment in terms of section 73C. Further, as regards what property is entitled to exemption, the decision of the Commissioner of Central Excise shall be final.

HEADNOTE: Section  2(8),  read with sections  24  and  26, of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 -  Benami property (Provisional attachment of)  - A survey under section 133A was conducted upon bank branch where it was found that six persons deposited huge cash in dummy bank accounts maintained in branch - Statements under section 131 were recorded where two of them admitted that cash was deposited by them in dummy accounts for conversion of demonetized currency notes to benefit beneficiaries in bank account of one 'Green traders ' and later on said sum was transferred to account of appellant - On basis of same, Initiating Officer provisionally attached property of assessee under section 24(1) - Appellant challenged same on ground that reasons to believe were not recorded in writing and incorporated in show cause notice and argued that sum deposited was received for earth-filling work - Whether perusal of record and more specifically show cause notice under section 24(1) revealed that reasons to believe were recorded in writing and were duly specified in notice conveyed to assessee - Held, yes - Whether further, there is no mandate to send a separate copy of reasons to believe - Held, yes - Whether since appellant did not provide any contract or firm details, receipt of money in appellant's account during demonetization, without substantiation, constituted clinching evidence of a benami transaction - Held, yes - Whether therefore, confirmation of provisional attachment was justified - Held, yes [Paras 17, 18,21 and 23] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: ■

During the demonetization period, a survey under section 133A of the Income-tax Act was conducted on 21-12-2021 at Axis Bank. Multiple dummy accounts controlled by two groups were found to have received large cash deposits. Statements under section 131 of the Income-tax Act recorded admissions that cash deposited in these dummy accounts did not belong to them and was used to convert demonetized currency and was deposited by into the Green Traders account and, on his instruction, was transferred through RTGS to the appellant.

■

Based on the material, the IO initiated action under section 24(1) of the PBPT Act, recorded reasons to believe in writing, and issued a show cause notice. The IO analyzed sworn statements and bank statements, treated Green Traders as benamidar and the appellant as beneficial owner, and passed a provisional attachment order with a reference to the Adjudicating Authority.

■

The Adjudicating Authority, by order dated 29- 12-2023 under section 26(3), confirmed the provisional attachment and answered the reference.

■

On appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, the appellant contended that the section 24(1) notice was invalid for lack of recorded or conveyed reasons; that the Initiating Officer acted solely on borrowed information from the Income Tax Department; that sum received via RTGS was consideration for earth-filling work at Bhavnagar and the appellant was unaware of the proprietor of Green Traders; and that there was no evidence linking the appellant to depositing cash in Green Traders’ account.

HELD: ■

The perusal of the record and more specifically the show cause notice under section 24 (1) reveals that 'reasons to believe' were recorded in writing and were duly specified in the notice conveyed to the appellant. The reasons were framed prior to the issuance of the notice and only thereafter found mention in the show cause notice. The allegation is that the 'reasons to believe' has to be recorded prior to the issuance of the notice, as only after recording 'reasons to believe' a notice can be issued. It is found that the reasons were recorded in writing and therefore they were incorporated in the show cause notice. [Para 17]

■

There is no mandate to send a separate copy of reasons to believe. The reasons to believe have been disclosed in the show cause notice which shows that required exercise was undertaken and for that the Initiating Officer had carefully analyzed the statement recorded apart from the bank statements. It is after analyzing the aforesaid, the show cause notice was issued. Thus, it cannot be said that reasons to believe were not recorded by the Initiating Officer and was conveyed to the appellant even though there is no mandate for it under section 24 (1). [Para 18]

■

The appellant submitted that the notice was issued by the Initiating Officer without having its independent satisfaction, rather it is based on the report given by the Income Tax Department and therefore also the impugned order deserves to be set aside. This argument is found to be in ignorance of the notice to show cause under section 24 (1). [Para 20]

The AO may invoke the guarantee in following situations:

(a)

Where a notice of demand specifying a sum payable is served upon the assessee and the assessee fails to pay that sum within the time specified in the notice of demand, the AO may invoke the guarantee, wholly or in part, to recover the amount.

(b)

If the assessee fails to renew the guarantee, the AO shall in the interest of the revenue invoke the bank guarantee. He shall invoke it 15 days before the expiry of the guarantee.

(c)

If the assessee fails to furnish a new guarantee from a scheduled bank for an equal amount, the AO shall, in the interest of the revenue invoke the bank guarantee 15 days before the expiry of the guarantee.

11.5-2 Utilisation of the amount realised by invoking the guarantee

The amount realised by invoking the guarantee shall be first adjusted against the existing demand which is payable by the assessee.

The balance amount if any shall be deposited in the personal deposit account of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner in the branch of any of the following banks:

(a)

RBI;

(b)

SBI;

(c)

Any subsidiary of SBI;

(d)

Any bank as may be appointed by RBI as its agent under section 45(1) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

Such account shall be at the place where the office of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner is situate.

11.5-3 Release of guarantee

Where the AO is satisfied that the guarantee is not required anymore to protect the interests of the revenue, he shall release that guarantee forthwith.

11.5-4 Acceptance of guarantee is mandatory

Once the assessee furnishes the guarantee satisfying the aforesaid conditions the AO is bound to revoke the attachment. This is because section 281B(3) provides that the AO 'shall' by an order in writing revoke such attachment.

11.5-5 Satisfied

The AO has to be 'satisfied' that the guarantee for an amount lower than the FMV is sufficient.

The term 'satisfied' has been explained as follows:

It is not the personal whim, wish, view or opinion or the ipse dixit of the President de hors the material but a legitimate inference drawn from the material placed before him which is relevant for the purpose. In other words, the President has to be convinced of or has to have sufficient proof of information with regard to or has to be free from doubt or uncertainty about the state of things indicating that the situation in question has arisen [S. R. Bommai v. UOI AIR 1994 SC 1918/[1994] 1 SCC 3 (SC)].

However, once he is satisfied it appears that he has no discretion not to reduce the amount of guarantee.

11.5-6 Opportunity of being heard

The section does not provide for any opportunity of being heard to the assessee before the guarantee is invoked. In this connection the observations of the Supreme Court in Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 300 ITR 403/169 Taxman 328 are apposite :

"If the statute conferring the power is silent with regard to the giving of a pre-decisional hearing to the person affected and the administrative decision taken by the authority involves civil consequences of a grave nature, and no full review or appeal on merits against that decision is provided, courts will be extremely reluctant to construe such a statute as excluding the duty of affording even a minimal hearing, shorn of all its formal trappings and dilatory features at the pre-decisional stage, unless, viewed pragmatically, it would paralyse the administrative process or frustrate the need for utmost promptitude. In short, this rule of fair play must not be jettisoned save in very exceptional circumstances where compulsive necessity so demands. The court must make every effort to salvage this cardinal rule to the maximum extent possible, with situational modifications. But, the core of it must, however, remain, namely, that the person affected must have reasonable opportunity of being heard and the hearing must be a genuine hearing and not an empty public relations exercise." (p. 666).

It is a moot point whether the aforesaid observations would be applicable before the invocation of the guarantee.

11.5-7 Direct acceptance of guarantee is not possible

The section envisages the situation where the assets are first attached and then a guarantee is accepted in lieu of the assets attached. It does not envisage a situation of acceptance of bank guarantee at the first stage itself without attachment of assets.

The provision of section 5(1) of the Act of 2002 would reveal that the Director or any other officer not below the rank of Deputy Director authorised by the Director of the Enforcement can cause provisional attachment of the property on the basis of material in his possession that a person is in possession of proceeds of crime and such proceeds of crime are likely to be concealed, transferred or dealt with in a manner to frustrate the proceeding of confiscation. The provision of section 5(1)(a) and (b) does not refer to possession of proceeds of crime in the hands of the accused but it can be with 'any person' referred under clause (a) to sub-section 5(1) of the Act of 2002. The proviso appended under section 5(1) qualifies the condition for attachment of the property. The provisional attachment initially remains for 180 days and to lapse if it is not confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority, otherwise, to continue as per section 8 of the Act of 2002. [Para 13]

Section 8 of the Act of 2002 was also referred by the Counsel for the appellant to submit that the attachment or seizure of the property to continue during investigation for a period not exceeding 365 days or the pendency of the proceedings relating to any offence under the Act of 2002 before the Court or under corresponding law of any country. In the instant case, the Prosecution Complaint against the appellant has not been filed and thereby the Counsel for the appellant prayed for lapse of the attachment. The argument was made in ignorance of the fact that as per Section 8(3) (a) of the Act of 2002 the continuation of the investigation for a period not exceeding 365 days or pendency of the proceedings is in reference to the offence under the Act before the Court and does not mandate a Prosecution Complaint against the person in whose hands the property has been provisionally attached. (Para 14)

■

Section 5 and 8 of the Act 2002 does not refer proceeds of crime for attachment only in the hands of the accused, rather, Section 5(1)(a) of the Act of 2002 refers to "any person" in possession of the proceeds of crime. The Apex Court in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India [2022] 140 taxmann.com 610 (SC)/ (2022) SCC Online SC 929 had refused to accept the similar arguments when it was urged that the property has been attached in the hands of a person not named as an accused. (Para 15)

■

A perusal of the para quoted above reveals that the attachment of the property can be in the hands of a person other than an accused as exist in the present matter. If the provision of the Act of 2002 is given interpretation to allow attachment of the property only in the hands of the accused, the very object of the Act of 2002 would frustrate in case of proceeds of crime comes in the hands of third person. In the instant case, the accused is involved in commission of predicate offence and derived proceeds of crime. It was transferred to the Companies held by the appellant. Finding proceeds of crime in the hands of a person not directly involved in the predicate offence, even then the attachment of the property was permissible in reference to Section 5(1) of the Act of 2002. If the interpretation taken by the appellant is accepted then it would become very easy for the accused to acquire the proceeds of crime and transfer or divert it to third person then according to the appellant proceeds cannot be attached. Thus, argument of the appellant in reference to Section 5(1) of the Act of 2002 to allow attachment of property only in hands of accused, can not be accepted. (Para 16)

NCLAT'S LATEST PRONOUNCEMENT ON THE IBC–PMLA CONFLICT: AN ANALYSIS OF ANIL KOHLI, RESOLUTION PROFESSIONAL OF DUNAR FOODS LTD. v. DIRECTORATE OF ENFORCEMENT [2025] 176 taxmann.com 218 (NCLAT – New Delhi)-

In the said appeal before NCLAT, following questions were rose pertaining to supremacy of IBC on provisional attachment by PMLA -

ISSUE I: Whether the provisional attachment of assets by the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) under the PMLA violates the moratorium imposed under Section 14 of the IBC?

It was held by the NCLAT that if the property is alleged to be "proceeds of crime" and is already under adjudication by competent authority under a penal statute, such property cannot be deemed to be part of the freely available resolution estate. The PMLA provides its own adjudicatory process and remedy for challenging attachments, which is separate from the IBC. Therefore, the issuance of the PAO by ED under the PMLA does not violate the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC.

ISSUE II: WHETHER THE IBC, BY VIRTUE OF SECTION 238, OVERRIDES THE PMLA IN CASE OF INCONSISTENCY, PARTICULARLY IN THE CONTEXT OF RESOLUTION PROCESSES INVOLVING TAINTED ASSETS

NCLAT held that Crux of this issue lies in a potential conflict between two central legislations viz. the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA). The IBC is a commercial legislation aimed at facilitating time-bound insolvency resolution of financially distressed companies. On the other hand, the PMLA is a penal statute that seeks to identify, attach, and confiscate properties derived from criminal activities such as money laundering.

Section 238 of the IBC is intended to ensure that the objects of the Code are not frustrated by competing statutory provisions. In 'Innoventive Industries Ltd. (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that: Section 238 overrides all other laws, including company law provisions, to the extent of inconsistency. This ensures that once IBC applies, other statutes cannot interfere.

In the present factual matrix, the IBC cannot be said to override the PMLA merely because the ED's attachment interferes with the CIRP. The ED does not act as a creditor, but as a public enforcement agency.

ISSUE III: WHETHER THE NCLT/NCLAT HAVE JURISDICTION TO INTERFERE WITH CONFIRMED ATTACHMENTS UNDER THE PMLA

Hon'ble SC in its judgment in Kalyani Transco's case (supra) discussed the powers of NCLAT vis a vis provisions under PMLA 2002.

It is absolutely clear from the above Judgement of the Hon'ble SC that NCLAT lacks jurisdiction to interfere with the PAO which has been subsequently confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority under the PMLA.

1.4-3 Provisional attachment of property involved in money-laundering.

Section 5(1) of PMLA deals with provisional attachment of proceeds of crime. Section 5(1), as amended by the Finance Act, 2015 provides that where the Director or any other officer not below the rank of Deputy Director authorised by the Director for the purposes of this section, has reason to believe (the reason for such belief to be recorded in writing), on the basis of material in his possession, that—

(a)

any person is in possession of any proceeds of crime; and

(b)

such proceeds of crime are likely to be concealed, transferred or dealt with in any manner which may result in frustrating any proceedings relating to confiscation of such proceeds of crime under this Chapter,

he may, by order in writing, provisionally attach such property for a period not exceeding one hundred and eighty days from the date of the order, in such manner as may be prescribed.

First proviso to section 5(1) provides that no such order of attachment shall be made unless, in relation to the scheduled offence, a report has been forwarded to a Magistrate under section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974), or a complaint has been filed by a person authorised to investigate the offence mentioned in that Schedule, before a Magistrate or court for taking cognizance of the scheduled offence, as the case may be, or a similar report or complaint has been made or filed under the corresponding law of any other country.

Second proviso to section 5(1) provides that that, notwithstanding anything contained in the first proviso, any property of any person may be attached under this section if the Director or any other officer not below the rank of Deputy Director authorised by him for the purposes of this section has reason to believe (the reasons for such belief to be recorded in writing), on the basis of material in his possession, that if such property involved in money-laundering is not attached immediately under this Chapter, the non-attachment of the property is likely to frustrate any proceeding under this Act.

Introduction

Money laundering is a felony, which, per se, is not new to the world. Given its nature, it is essential to have written law in place, which should be amended, time and again, to adequately deal with the on-going changes in the economical environment. In India, the enactment of Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 ('PMLA') was a remarkable and important step towards ensuring the same. Since its initial introduction, the law has undergone various amendments over the years. The Interim Budget for 2019-2020 has made several changes in enactments, which also include changes in PMLA. The amendment is part of the Finance Bill, 20191, and is yet to be notified.

PMLA is a comprehensive law which deals with all the major aspects of money laundering, which includes defining what constitutes as money laundering, the process of attachment and adjudication, management of confiscated properties, obligations on reporting entities like banks and financial institutions, etc.

Background to the amendment

Chapter III of the PMLA deals with "Attachment, Adjudication and Confiscation". Section 5 under the Chapter, gives powers to the Director or Deputy Director (appointed authority under PMLA by the Central Government) to provisionally attach the property in case he has reason to believe that the property is involved in money laundering. This is an interim action which prevents any likelihood of further transfer of/ or launder of property or money. The initial attachment is merely allowed for a period of 90 days.

The aforesaid complaint is transferred to the Adjudicating Authority (AA), which further investigates the matter in accordance with the provisions of section 8 of PMLA. At this stage, it is pertinent to understand the definitions of 'attachment' and 'investigation'; both the expressions are defined as under:

"attachment" means prohibition of transfer, conversion, disposition or movement of property by an order issued under Chapter III.

"investigation" includes all the proceedings under this Act conducted by the Director or by an authority authorised by the Central Government under this Act for the collection of evidence.

While attachment is an act to stop any movement of the property, investigation is a lawful process, which allows collection of evidence of money laundering, leading to punishment and confiscation. If on investigation, the AA concludes that the property is involved in money laundering, it shall confirm the continuation of the provisional attachment, which becomes final after the final order of confiscation is passed by the court.

Text prior to amendment

Section 8(3)(a)

(3) Where the Adjudicating Authority decides under sub-section (2) that any property is involved in money-laundering, he shall, by an order in writing, confirm the attachment of the property made under sub-section (1) of section 5 or retention of property or [record seized or frozen under section 17 or section 18 and record a finding to that effect, whereupon such attachment or retention or freezing of the seized or frozen property] or record shall—

(a)

continue during investigation for a period not exceeding ninety days or the pendency of the proceedings relating to any offence under this Act before a court or under the corresponding law of any other country, before the competent court of criminal jurisdiction outside India, as the case may be; and

(b)

become final after an order of confiscation is passed under sub-section (5) or sub-section (7) of section 8 or section 58B or sub-section (2A) of section 60 by the Special Court.

Post amendment

The amendment has substituted the words 'ninety days' with 'three hundred and sixty five days'. While the amendment seems minor, it actually extends the time period of attachment by a total of 275 days. Resultantly, the attachment shall continue for one year during pendency of proceedings before a criminal court, under PMLA or a corresponding foreign law.

While the provisional attachment period remains unchanged, extending the attachment period before final confiscation, gives the authorities increased time in hand to deal with a given case. With the increased number of cases of money laundering, this is a relief for the authorities investigating matters under PMLA.

Additionally, the amendment inserts explanation to sub-section (3) above; accordingly, the aforesaid period of 365 days shall exclude any period for which the respective investigation is stayed by any court of law. Since investigation is construed to be ineffective while it is stayed, and the number of attachment days is calculated in reference to the investigation, the period of stay should be excluded.

Conclusion

In essence, the amendment adds flexibility to the proceedings under PMLA and gives more time to the authorities, which can be invested into finding relevant evidence and records.

As a re¬sult, Department is burdened with the responsibility to recover the huge arrears existing in its records, with little possibility of actual recovery in many cases. The Board has, therefore, decided that in cases where demand of Rs. 5 lakh and above in big cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Kolka¬ta, Chennai, Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Pune and Bangalore and Rs. 1 lakh and above elsewhere, is likely to be created and it appears that the recovery, in full or in part, could become difficult, it shall be the responsibility of the Assessing Officer, during the assessment proceedings itself, to enquire into all assets of the assessee and place under provisional attachment, in terms of provisions of section 281B, before the assessment is completed, the assets sufficient to cover the demand in question (or to the maximum extent, as the case may be). In each of these cases, the Assessing Officer shall mention in an Office Note to the Assessment Order in question, the efforts made to locate the assets of the assessee, the details of assets located, the details of assets placed under provisional attachment, etc.

3. In search and seizure cases, huge demands are raised under block assessment and the recovery of the same is tedious and time-consuming. In this regard, it is extremely important for Assessing Officers in Central Charges to explore the possibility of invoking the provisions of section 281B. The above acts/omissions shall entail proceedings under section 73 or 73A which may be followed by attachment of property under section 73C. (ii) Is there any threshold limit for invoking attachment provision ? - Neither section 73C nor the Rules lay down any threshold limit for initiating attachment proceedings. However, the CBEC’s Circular No. 103/06/2008-ST, dated July 1, 2008, provides that it should be resorted to only in a case where the service tax or CENVAT credit alleged to be involved is more than Rs. 25 lakh.

(iii) Against whom can the provisions of attachment be invoked ? - As per section 73C, provisional attachment can be ordered in respect of any property belonging to a person on whom a notice has been served under section 73(1) or 73A(3). It may be noted that under section 73(1), a notice can be served on the person chargeable with the service tax which has not been levied or paid or which has been short-levied or short-paid or the person to whom service tax has been erroneously refunded, whereas, a notice under section 73A(3) can be served on - (1) a person liable to pay service tax who has collected any amount in excess of the service tax assessed or determined and paid on any taxable service from the recipient of the taxable service, or (2) any person who has collected any amount as service tax, which is not required to be collected, from any other person.

(iv) Which property can be attached under the provision of service tax ? - As noted in FAQ 3, provisional attachment under section 73C can be ordered in respect of any ‘property’ belonging to the specified person. Rule 2(c) of the Rules defines the term ‘property’ to include immovable property. Further, rule 4(2) of the Rules provides that movable property shall be attached only if the immovable property is not sufficient to protect the interest of revenue.

The CBEC, vide its circular dated July 1, 2008, has clarified that immovable property/properties which is/are used for commercial purpose may be provisionally attached.

(v) Can personal property(ies) of proprietor/partner(s)/ director(s) be also attached ? - As per proviso to rule 3(3) of the Rules, personal property of proprietor or partners or directors, as the case may be, shall not be attached. As per rule 2(d), ‘personal property’ means any movable or immovable property belonging to a proprietor or partner or director, which is not in relation to business activity.

Accordingly, the CBEC in its circular dated July 1, 2008 has also clarified that any movable or immovable property which is in personal use of the sole proprietor/partner/director cannot be attached.

(vi) What shall be the extent of attachment ? - In terms of rule 4(1), the provisional attachment of property shall be to the extent it requires to protect the interest of revenue. In other words, the value of property attached shall be as nearly as may be equivalent to that of the amount of ‘pending revenue’.

The term ‘pending revenue’ is defined under rule 2(b) to mean "any service tax that has not been levied or paid or has been short-levied or paid or erroneously refunded in respect of which a notice has been served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A". Thus, the term ‘pending revenue’ refers to the amount demanded in the proceedings under section 73 or 73A.

(vii) What can be the possible justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary ? - If the Central Excise Officer reasonably believes that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, any of his property(ies) liable to attachment, it can be considered as sufficient justification necessitating attachment of property. The belief must, however, be based on substantial grounds.

(viii) What precautions should the Central Excise Officer take before initiating attachment proceedings ? - Although section 73C and the Provisional Attachment of Property Rules, are both silent in this regard, the CBEC has in its circular dated July 1, 2008, stated emphatically that the remedy of attachment is of extraordinary nature and should be resorted to in the utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution. There should be sufficient justification to hold the view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interests of revenue. The Central Excise Officer should, in his proposal for attachment, clearly state the grounds on which he entertains the reasonable belief that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, the property and the sources of his information, if any.

The circular further states that appropriate disciplinary action shall be initiated against the officers who may be found to have exercised the powers of provisional attachment of property frivolously and without sound reasons.

SCOPE OF ATTACHMENT UNDER PBPT ACT, 1988 AND UNDER PMLA ACT, 2002

In the PBPT Act, 1988, there is no specific provision which mandates that any movable or immovable property of the benamidar can be attached as in Section 2(u) of PMLA, 2002, which is another Special Act. Any provision of PMLA, 2002 cannot be invoked under Benami law. Under Benami law, only benami property or proceeds of such property can be attached. This was so held in case of V. N Nandhini Devi v. Sh. K. Visakh, Dy. Commissioner of Income Tax, Chennai, FPA/PBPT/57/CHN/2018.
